note: 966 asks what could be gained, neither fame nor heaven, by going after those who despise you. 1255 is a direct reply from inside love: people with this sickness can't know that kind of honour. The ethics chapter on honour isn't refuted, but declared unavailable.

The sneeze appears in two contrary ways: in 1203 it threatens and doesn't come, which she reads as him not thinking of her. In 1253 it comes uncontrollably, like her desire. So his love fails to arrive and hers can't be stopped.

The same phrase, மறையிறந்து மன்று படும், in both. 1138 presents it as a general truth about women's love, with Parimelazhagar seeing her own case in it. In 1254 she says it in the first person, having once thought herself an exception.
Both tell the same story in the first person: she went to sulk, and her heart went to join him. Whichever is read first, the second confirms that this is a repeating pattern, and that she knows it.

position: 'Today' is the day of her death and மேல் is the next birth: remembering him at the moment of death is how she can reach him in the next life.
quote: இவ்வெல்லைக்கண் நினைந்தால் மறுமைக்கண் அவரை எய்தி அன்புறலாம்;

position: The verse is about this life: if she forgets, her body will fail, and the address means 'you who have no pain'.
quote: தம்மழகினை நீக்கி வளை முதலான அணிகலங்களையும் கழலவிடும்

position: The heart puts out branches, swelling and rising as a tree does, with sorrow gone.
quote: என் நெஞ்சு வருத்தமொழிந்து மேன்மேற் பணைத்தெழாநின்றது.

position: The heart climbs a tree to look for him, because from the top one can see someone coming from afar.
quote: என்னெஞ்சம் மரத்தின் மேலேறிப் பாராநின்றது

position: The man, stuck on campaign, says to himself that he wants to join his wife; மனை here stands for the wife.
quote: வேந்தற்கு உற்றுழிப் பிரிந்த தலைமகன் வினை முடிவு நீட்டித் துழித் தலைமகளை நினைந்து தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது.

position: The woman speaks: let the king win, and I will prepare a feast at home, with மனை meaning the kitchen.
quote: நம் காதலர்க்கு விருந்து செய்வே மாக

position: The man speaks: if the leader wins, he will feast with his wife.
The man fears that she may die before he gets back, and it can't be her voice, since then it would be a lament and not impatience.
quote: இது தலைமகள் கூற்றாயவழி இரங்கலாவதல்லது விதுப்பாகாமை அறிக.

position: The woman answers the friend who says that he will come: what use, if my own heart has already broken?
quote: இது வருவா ரென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் கூறியது.

note: 1151 tells him to bring promises of quick return to those who will still be alive. 1270, in Parimelazhagar's reading, has the man finally arriving at that thought himself, from the other end of the journey and perhaps too late. The warning was given at the start of the separation, and he feels it only at the end.

591 says ஊக்கம், inner resolve, is the only true possession. In 1263, the woman names a very similar quality in உள்ளம் as his companion in leaving her. The virtue the Book of Wealth values most is what she has been left for.

If Parimelazhagar's speaker is correct, evening is a coming feast for the man in 1268, and for the woman in 1224 it comes like a killer to the execution ground. They are thinking about the same hour, far apart, and with opposite expectations.

1267 is a plan: sulk, embrace or both. 1259 records how such a plan works out: she goes to sulk, and her heart gives way. The planner in 1267 hasn't learned anything from the experience, or she has and enjoys planning anyway.

position: It's an intent that he can't himself identify, and he asks her friend to find out what it is.
quote: மடந்தையது அணியகத்துக் கிடந்து புறத்துப் புலனாகின்றதொரு குறிப்பு உண்டு.

position: It's a hidden sorrow, which shows though she conceals it.
quote: இவள் மறைக்கவும் தோற்றுகின்றதொரு துன்பம் உண்டு

position: The man tells the friend that she has hidden from him out of a false fear, and the cure is for the friend to explain that he isn't leaving.
quote: என்கண் இல்லாத தொன்றனை உட்கொண்டு அது காரணமாக என்னை மறைத்துப் போன குறிப்பு

position: The friend tells the man, in courtship, that the woman's slipping away coyly means that his plea will succeed.
quote: எதிர்ப்பட்ட தலைமகற்கு நின்குறை முடியும்; நீ இவ்விடைச் செல்லென்று தோழி கூறியது.

position: He hasn't physically left: 'left yesterday' means he made up his mind then, shown by yesterday's tenderness.
quote: 'நெருநற்றுச் செய்த தலையளியாற் பிரிவு துணியப்பட்டது' என்பாள், 'நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார்' என்றும்

position: He has actually left, and she was grieving before he went.
quote: இஃது அவர் பிரிவதன் முன்னும் பிரிவரென் றேங்கி, இன்புற்றில் மென்று தலைமகள் கூறியது.

position: The man answers: he praises her decision to go with him, as a way of telling her friend he won't be leaving at all.
quote: தன் பிரிவின்மைக் குறிப்பினை அறிவுறுப்பான், அவள் பெண்மையினைப் பிறர்மேலிட்டு வியந்து கூறியவாறு.

position: The friend speaks to the man, having seen the woman's response to news of his leaving.
quote: இது பிரிவுணர்த்திய தலைமகள் குறிப்புக்கண்டு தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

note: In Parimelazhagar's reading, 1120 is the man refusing to elope because her feet can't bear even swan's down. In 1279 she looks at those same feet, her way of saying she will walk. The compliment had been an excuse, and her glance answers it.

706 says the face shows what is in the heart, as crystal shows what is next to it, in the chapter on reading signs in court. 1273 uses crystal the same way, with a thread inside it. Courtier and lover both depend on the transparency of the surface.
In 1152 the fear of parting spoils union, and Parimelazhagar cites a poem where unusual fussing is the warning sign. 1276 makes that the very argument: too much tenderness is proof of a departure.
Both have bangles announcing the departure of the lord of the shore. In 1157 they announce it to others, and in 1277 they tell her, before she herself knows. The sign has moved inward.

position: The friend tells the man that she has seen the woman's eagerness, and uses 'us' for them both.
quote: தலைமகள் புணர்ச்சி? விதுப்பு அறிந்த தோழி, தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

position: The woman speaks to the man herself, having let go of the wish to sulk.
quote: இது புலவிக்குறிப்பு நீங்கின தலை மகள் தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது

position: The man speaks during a sulk that won't yield to his pleading, in order to end it.
quote: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

position: The woman, seeing that he desires union, tells her own heart that this isn't the moment to sulk.
quote: இப்பொழுது ஊடுவையாயின், இக்காமஞ் செவ்விதப்பு மென்று புணர்ச்சி வேட்கையால் தலைமகள் நெஞ்சோடு கூறியது.

note: 104 says that those who know value a favour the size of a millet seed as if it were a palmyra. 1282 uses the same pair for love and sulking. The scale of ethical gratitude is used for measuring love's excess, and this time the small thing is to be removed altogether.

Both state that he doesn't truly cherish her (பேணாது) and that the eyes can't rest without seeing him (காணாது அமை-). In 1178 this is a complaint on her eyes' folly, and in 1283 it's her reason for not quarrelling. The same fact has moved from grief to an explanation.

In 1127 she won't line her eyes because he's within them and would be hidden. In 1285 the stick is what the eye can't see. In the absence, kohl was an obstacle. In his presence, he himself is like the stick, too close to be seen.

90 says that a guest wilts at a cold look as an anicham flower wilts when smelled. 1289 makes love softer still than a flower. In both, what is finest about a relationship fails at a slight change in the other person's face.

1259 tells it in her voice: I went to sulk, my heart gave way. 1290 tells it in his: she sulked with her eyes and came faster than I did. Each tells the other's defeat as a private pleasure, though for her it's defeat, and for him it's a fond memory.

position: உயிர்க்காதல் means the heart loves its own life: it won't die, and so it plans reconciliation.
quote: உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு - உயிர்மேல் காதலையுடைய என் நெஞ்சு

position: It's a heart whose love is as dear as life, and it thinks on his greatness.
The man speaks, in a sulk that won't yield, whose heart still wants her.
quote: உணர்ப்புவயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

position: The woman replies to the friend who asks who would help.
quote: இது தலைமகள் துணையாவார் யாரென்ற தோழிக்குக் கூறியது.

note: 796 says ruin has one benefit: it's a measuring rod for friends. 1293 applies this proverb to one's own heart, which she treats as a friend who proves false. The inner dialogue has absorbed a whole social ethic of friendship.

In 1244 her eyes eat her alive with longing, and in 1296 her heart does. The same verb is used for what are, in effect, her own organs, and these chapters keep treating her as a person being consumed by her parts.
1247 demands that the heart give up either love or shame. 1297 tells us what happened: shame got forgotten. The chapter between them, on breaking restraint, is how.

ஏதிலர், the 'stranger', has been her word for him in the town's mouth, in 1129 and 1130. In 1300 the same word is used for a stranger, and now the one who isn't one's own is one's own heart. By the end, the outsider is inside.

position: She means courtesans: go back to them, she tells the man returning from them, since they'll suffer without you. It's sarcasm.
quote: நும்மைப் பெறாது புலந்தூடியிருக்கின்ற பரத்தையரைப் போய்ப் புலவி நீக்கிப் புல்லீராயின், அவராற்றார்

position: It's a general truth about lovers: leaving a sulking partner unreconciled is cruel.
She again means the other women, and she adds that she has no right to sulk, since she has their sons to look at; so go to them.
quote: நும்மோடு ஊடிய பரத்தையரை ஊடலுணர்த்திக் கூடாதொழிதல்

position: It's about any partner who stays aloof from a sulking lover.
The man, reconciled, reflects to himself that even faultless men find this sulking lovely.
quote: தலைமகளைப் புலவி நீக்கிக் கூடிய தலைமகன் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது.

position: The friend tells the woman that sulking suits courtesans, and that she shouldn't sulk at those not worth it.
quote: இது பரத்தையரோடு புலந்து கூறிய தலைமகட்குத் தோழி கூறியது.

position: The man praises both kinds of quarrel after making up.
quote: இவ்விரண்டும் வேண்டும் என்று வியந்து கூறியவாறு.

position: The woman speaks, saying that there is some good in the sulking that is then healed.
quote: இஃது உணர்தற்கு நல்லது உளதென்று தலைமகள் கூறியது.

position: The man is himself sulking, because she won't yield to his pleading.
quote: இவள் நம் காதலியல்லள்; அன்மையின், இந்நோவு அறியாள்

position: The friend tells the man this when she has come inside, knowing about his sulking.
quote: அதனை யறிந்து அகம்புக்க தோழி அவனுக்குச் சொல்லியது.

note: உப்பு is the word in both. In 1302 the salt is the sulk, measured carefully. In 1328 the salt is the sweetness of the union that follows, as Parimelazhagar glosses it. The cook's image runs through both chapters, with the same word for the seasoning and the taste.

1191 calls requited love the stoneless fruit, the ideal of enjoyment with nothing in the way. 1306 says love without quarrels is fruit gone bad or not yet ripe. So the obstacle that 1191 wishes away, 1306 says is what makes the fruit ripe.

366 warns the renunciant to fear craving (அவா), because it deceives. In 1310, the sulking man names the same craving as what drives his heart to her. He uses the moral vocabulary correctly, with no intention of following it.

position: பெண்ணியலார் means courtesans, who, lacking other virtues, have only the nature of women. They look at him as his procession passes.
quote: பரத்தையர்க்குள்ளது பெண் இயற்கை மாத்திரமே என்னுங் கருத்தால், 'பெண் இயலார்' என்றாள்.

position: It simply means all women, who think of his chest as common property.
quote: நின் மார்பைப் பெண்மை யுடையா ரெல்லாரும் தமக்குப் பொதுவாக நினைத்துக்

note: The same folk belief at two points in the story. In 1203 she longs for a sneeze as proof he's thinking of her. In 1317 he sneezes in front of her, and the same belief proves someone else is thinking of him. A sign that means what one fears can't be falsified.

In 1125, the man is clever at the friend's expense: I would remember her if I forgot. 1316 shows the woman turning this logic on him: you say you remembered, so you forgot. His own wit has become the trap.

On Parimelazhagar's reading of 1262, she keeps him in mind at death so as to reach him in the next birth. In 1315, 'this birth' is what makes her cry. Rebirth, for the renunciant a fate to escape, is in this book something lovers want to share.

In 1113, he went over her body part by part, comparing it to shoots, pearls and spears, and she was pleased to be praised. In 1320 she treats that very habit of comparing part by part as evidence that he has others in mind. The praise of chapter 112 is the root of the suspicion.

position: It is jealousy: his love is so delightful that others surely enjoy it too, and she can't stand the thought.
quote: யான் எய்தற் பாலதாய இத்தலையளி ஒழிந்தாரும் எய்துவர் எனக்கருதி, அது பொறாமையான் ஊடல்நிகழா நின்றது

position: He reverses the direction: the quarrel, between faultless lovers, builds up their love.
Water takes on the character of the ground it's in, so men take on the nature of the women they touch, which is the reason for her sulking. It's a surprisingly suspicious reading of a famous image.
quote: நீர் தான் நின்ற நிலத்தியல்பிற்றாமாறு போலக் காதலரும் தாம் கூடிய மகளிரியல்பினராகலான்

position: Earth and water together combine heat and coolness, and in the same way lovers experience joy and pain as one.
quote: நிலத்தொடு நீரியை தலால் அவை வெப்பமுந்தட்பமுங் கூடியிருக்குமாறு போல்

position: புத்தேள்நாடு isn't a divine world but a new one, which removes heaven from the verse.
The woman answers the friend's question about what will end this sulk.
quote: 'அப்புலவி இனி யாதான் நீங்கும்?' என்றாட்குச் சொல்லியது.

position: He calls the group at this point the man's speech.
quote: இவையெட்டும் தலைமகன் கூற்று .

note: 1103 asks whether the Lotus-eyed one's world is sweeter than sleeping on the arms of one's beloved. 1323 repeats the challenge to heaven with a stranger choice: it's the quarrel that outdoes heaven now. Between these two verses, love has come to value its own frictions most.

In 1088, a warrior laments his strength being broken by her forehead, and takes it as defeat. In 1327, the man has worked out that losing is the way to win. The book's military imagery, which begins with injury, ends in a pleasantly ruined scoreboard.

In 1169, the woman in separation says the long nights are crueller than the cruel man himself. In 1329, the man in reunion prays for night to lengthen. The same long night is torment or wish, depending on whether the other person is there.

942 says the body needs no medicine if one eats only after the last meal has digested. 1326 takes the same physician's advice and makes it a rule of love: the pause between meals is what keeps appetite and health.

Both say soft words are the weapon that breaks her defences. In 1258 she says it with bitterness and calls him a thief, and in 1324 she says it with something like eagerness. The weapon hasn't changed, and what she wants from it has.

Verse 1 says the world has ஆதி பகவன் as its first (முதற்றே உலகு), as letters have அ. Verse 543 uses the same word for the king's sceptre: it stands as the ஆதி of the antaṇar's books and of aram (அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய் நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as their cause (காரணம்). The pairing shows the book giving the world one 'first' in its opening and giving aram itself a second, political one in Book 2.

Verse 2: what has learning yielded, if one does not bow at the good feet (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்)? Verse 315: does understanding achieve anything (அறிவினான் ஆகுவதுண்டோ) if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own? Both are rhetorical questions that judge knowledge by a test outside knowledge, worship in one and compassion in the other.

Verse 2 asks what use learning is (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயன் என்கொல்) if the learned do not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge. Verse 356 states the fruit positively: those who learn here and see the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not returning. Parimelazhagar reads verse 2's fruit as ending rebirth too, so 356 spells out what verse 2 leaves as a question.

Verses 3 and 6 end on the same words, நீடுவாழ்வார், 'will live long'. Verse 3 gives this to those who reach the feet (மாணடி சேர்ந்தார்); verse 6 gives it to those who stand in the path of conduct free of falsehood (பொய்தீர் ஒழுக்க நெறி நின்றார்) of the one who quenched the five. The repeated ending puts devotion and conduct side by side as routes to the same result.

Verse 4 describes the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no affliction. Verse 350 turns the same description into an instruction: hold to the hold of the one without attachment (பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை), in order to let attachment go (பற்று விடற்கு). Parimelazhagar notes that பற்றற்றான் is chosen to match the invocation chapter; 350 supplies the mechanism verse 4 leaves unstated.

Both verses turn on the word வேண்டாமை but use it differently. In verse 4 it is paired with வேண்டுதல் as something the Lord lacks, which Parimelazhagar glosses as aversion (வெறுத்தல்). In 362 வேண்டாமை is desirelessness, the thing to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்) so that birthlessness comes. A reader should not carry one sense into the other.

Verse 4 says there is no இடும்பை at any time for those who reach the feet of the one free of liking and aversion. Verse 628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure and calls இடும்பை natural (இன்பம் விழையான் இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்) does not come to pain. The Book 2 verse keeps the link between absent desire and absent suffering but drops the devotional route, and it concedes that the affliction itself still arrives.

Verse 5 says both kinds of deed, which belong to darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும்), do not attach to those who dwell on the Lord's praise; Parimelazhagar explains that good deeds too are a cause of birth. Verse 38 says that doing good (நன்றாற்றின்) with no day lost is the stone that blocks the road of one's days, which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read as ending rebirth. On those readings one verse counts good deeds among what binds and the other makes them what frees.

Verse 5 ties the two kinds of deed to இருள், which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar gloss as delusion. Verse 352 says that for those of stainless sight who have left confusion (மருள்நீங்கி மாசறு காட்சியவர்க்கு), darkness goes and joy comes (இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும்). The later verse gives knowledge as what removes the darkness that verse 5 only names.

Verse 5 speaks of the praise of இறைவன், the chapter's word for the Lord. Verse 388 says a king who does justice and protects is set down as இறை for the people (மக்கட்கு இறையென்று வைக்கப்படும்). The shared word shows that the title used for the deity in chapter 1 is one a human ruler earns by conduct in Book 2.

Verse 6 promises long life to those who stand in the path of the one who quenched the five. Verse 126 gives the human practice and its reward: if one can draw in the five like a tortoise in one birth (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), it is a protection for seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Verse 126 says அடக்கல், holding in, where verse 6 says அவித்தான், quenched, so the follower's task is stated more modestly than the exemplar's.

Verse 7 says it is hard to remove the mind's anxiety (மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது) except for those who reach the feet of the one without equal. Verse 622 says a flood of affliction perishes when a person of understanding thinks in his own mind (அறிவுடையான் உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்). The conflict holds if மனக்கவலை is ordinary mental distress, as Manakkudavar's gloss allows; Parimelazhagar narrows it to the sufferings of rebirth, which 622 does not address.

Verse 7 makes freedom from mental anxiety rare, reserved for those who reach the Lord's feet. Verse 1072 says, with irony, that the base are better off than those who know the good, because they have no distress in their hearts (நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்). Read beside verse 7 it marks that mere absence of worry is not the state the invocation is praising, since the base have it too.

Verse 8 calls the deity அறவாழி அந்தணன், joining அந்தணன் to aram. Verse 30 defines the word: those called அந்தணர் are the people of aram (அறவோர்), because they act with kindness toward every living being (செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுகலான்). Verse 30 gives the reason for the pairing of title and virtue that verse 8 assumes.

Verse 8 uses ஆழி for the deity (அறவாழி), read as 'sea of aram' by Parimelazhagar, who also records the reading 'wheel of aram'. Verse 989 calls the worthy சான்றாண்மைக்கு ஆழி and says they do not shift even if the age shifts; there Parimelazhagar reads ஆழி as the shore of the sea of worth. The same word is attached to a virtue in both verses, to a god in one and to people in the other, and its sense is disputed in both.

Verse 8 says the other seas are hard to swim (பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது) except for those who reach the feet of the antaṇan who is a sea of aram; Parimelazhagar takes the other seas to be wealth and pleasure and the feet to be the raft. In 1164 the woman says the sea of kāmam is there and the safe raft to swim it is not (காமக் கடல் ... அதுநீந்தும் ஏமப் புணை ... இல்). Book 3 shows from inside one of the seas that Parimelazhagar finds in verse 8, with the raft named and missing.

Verse 9 treats a sense organ that does not grasp (கோளில் பொறி) as the type of uselessness, while verse 6 praises the one who quenched the five of the sense-gates (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்). Parimelazhagar reads what is quenched in verse 6 as the five desires that travel by the senses, not the senses. Taken together the two verses of the chapter support that reading: a dead sense is a defect, and what is praised is something else.

Verse 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the one of eight qualities is without worth, like a sense organ that does not grasp (கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே). Verse 418 says ears not pierced by listening are of a deaf kind even though they hear (கேட்பினும் கேளாத் தகையவே). Both measure a part of the body by one proper use and call it dead without that use; the use is worship in one and learning by ear in the other.

Verse 9 compares the unbowing head to an organ that is present and does not sense. Verse 574 asks what eyes without kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be in the face (உளபோல் முகத்து எவன் செய்யும்). The figure of the organ that is there and useless is applied in Book 2 to a ruler's compassion.

Verses 8 and 10 both speak of swimming a sea with the Lord's feet as the condition. Verse 10 names the sea as birth (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல்); verse 8 says only 'the other seas' (பிறவாழி), which Parimelazhagar takes as wealth and pleasure. On his reading the chapter has two different seas; without it, verse 8 can look like a first statement of verse 10.

Verse 10 makes reaching the Lord's feet the condition for crossing birth: those who do not reach them do not swim it (நீந்தார் இறைவனடி சேராதார்). Verse 349 gives a condition with no deity in it: the moment attachment is cut, that cuts birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). The next verse, 350, joins the two by telling one to hold to the one without attachment in order to drop attachment, so 349 shows what reaching the feet has to accomplish.

Verse 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of birth and others do not. In 1167 the woman says she swims the fierce flood of kāmam and sees no shore (நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன்), alone even at midnight. The swimmer who cannot cross, stated as doctrine in verse 10, is spoken in the first person in Book 3.

Verse 31 says aram yields wealth and asks what greater gain a living being has. Verse 169 admits the opposite case occurs: the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are to be thought about (நினைக்கப்படும்). Parimelazhagar says such outcomes cannot come from crookedness or uprightness and sends the wise to look for a cause in past deeds; either way 169 limits how far verse 31 can be read as a promise visible in one life. His gloss on 31 itself takes செல்வம் as heavenly goods.

Verse 31 says aram yields distinction and yields wealth too (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்). Verse 754 uses the same construction with the terms turned round: wealth that came by known means and without wrong yields aram and yields pleasure too (அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). Book 1 has virtue producing wealth and Book 2 has rightly earned wealth producing virtue, in matching words.

Verse 32 says no ruin (கேடு) surpasses forgetting aram. Verse 117 gives the other side: the world will not count as ruin (கெடுவாக வையாது) the low state of one who stays fair and rests in the good. Together they define ruin by one's relation to virtue and not by one's circumstances.

Verse 32 names forgetting (மறத்தல்) of aram as the greatest ruin. In the chapter on heedlessness, 532 says forgetfulness kills renown (பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை) as unrelieved poverty kills understanding. The idea that the damage comes through lapse of attention, without any act of wrongdoing, is carried from ethics into statecraft.

Verse 33 asks for aram everywhere and without a break (ஓவாதே ... எல்லாம் செயல்). Verse 297 says that if one keeps to not lying, then not doing the other virtues is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று). On Parimelazhagar's reading of 297, that it is better to hold one virtue unfailingly than to take on many and fail in some, this is advice to narrow what verse 33 tells one to spread as widely as possible.

Verse 33 limits its command with ஒல்லும் வகையான், 'in the way that is possible'. Parimelazhagar explains this for the householder as acting in proportion to one's means, and 477 says so directly: give knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து ஈக), for that is the way to guard wealth while giving. Verse 477 gives the practical content of the qualifier in verse 33. This edition prints அறவறிந்து in 477; the commentary reads அளவு அறிந்து.

Verse 33 says to do the work of aram by whatever means one can (ஒல்லும் வகையான்), without ceasing, wherever it can go (செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம் செயல்). Verse 673, on how to carry out a task, uses the same words: where it is possible the deed is good, and where it is not, act looking for a way that goes (ஒல்லும்வாய் ... செல்லும்வாய் நோக்கிச் செயல்). The rule for virtue and the rule for state action are built from the same vocabulary of the possible. This edition prints the first word of 673 as ஙல்லும், a typo for ஒல்லும், as its own commentary shows.

Verse 34 sets inner cleanness against outward show. Verse 298 makes the same division and adds how the inner kind is known: outer purity is had by water, and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). It gives a test for the state that verse 34 only asserts. This edition prints புறள்தூய்மை for புறந்தூய்மை.

Verse 35 lists envy (அழுக்காறு) first among what aram must avoid. Verse 161 turns that item into a positive rule: take as your way of conduct (ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க) a nature that has no envy in the heart. The chapter on envy opens by treating as a discipline what verse 35 states as an exclusion.

Verse 35 defines aram by the absence of four faults. Verse 431 defines a sound prosperity the same way for a ruler: the increase of those without arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும் இல்லார்) has dignity. Anger is on both lists; Parimelazhagar glosses சிறுமை in 431 as lust, which would bring the two lists closer still.

Verse 36 calls aram a companion that does not perish (பொன்றாத் துணை). Verse 233 says that apart from high renown nothing in the world stands unperishing (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்று இல்), using the same word. Read literally the second excludes the first. Parimelazhagar's reading of 36, that the merit goes with the soul into another body, puts it outside 'the world' of 233; Kalaignar reads 36 itself as lasting fame, which removes the conflict another way.

Verse 36 says aram done now stays as a companion at death. Verse 398 says the learning one has acquired in one birth is a protection through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). Both speak of something gained in this life that is not lost with the body; Book 2 says of learning what Book 1 says of virtue.

On the reading of Parimelazhagar and Pope, verse 37 explains the difference between palanquin rider and bearer by aram done before. Verse 270 reasons the same way about a whole society: the reason the have-nots are many is that those who do tavam are few and those who do not are many. Both read present inequality as the result of past practice; Parimelazhagar adds that wealth and want in 270 also mean understanding and its lack.

Verse 37 says there is no need to state the way of aram: look between the one who carries the palanquin and the one who rides (பொறுத்தானொடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை). Parimelazhagar and Pope take this to mean that the fruit of virtue can be seen in who rides and who carries. Verse 973 says those who are not high are not high even when seated high (மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர்), and Parimelazhagar reads the seating there as wealth and poverty. On those readings one verse lets position show merit and the other denies that position shows anything about the person. The Tamil of 37 is elliptical and does not itself say which of the two is the virtuous one.

Verse 38 says daily good is a stone that shuts the road of one's வாழ்நாள்; Parimelazhagar takes வாழ்நாள் as the days of living in a body, so that shutting the road means no more births. Verse 326 says Death does not advance on the வாழ்நாள் of one who keeps to not killing. On Parimelazhagar's reading the same word names something virtue ends in 38 and something virtue protects in 326. On Kalaignar's reading of 38, where the stone smooths life's road, there is no conflict.

Verse 38 treats each day as something that can fall away unused or be filled with good. Verse 334 says what a day is: it shows itself as one thing called a day, and it is a blade sawing through life (உயிர் ஈரும் வாள்), for those who perceive it. Verse 334 gives the reason for the daily urgency of verse 38.

Verse 39 says only what comes by aram is joy (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்) and the rest lies outside and has no renown either. Verse 156 allows that those who retaliate do get joy, for one day (ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம்), while those who forbear have renown for as long as things last (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்; until the world perishes, in Parimelazhagar's gloss). It keeps verse 39's pairing of joy and renown but concedes a short pleasure outside virtue, so the 'only' of 39 reads as a judgment of worth and not a denial that such pleasure is felt.

Verse 40 names blame (பழி) as the thing to escape. Verse 280 says neither shaving nor growing the hair is needed if one gives up what the world has blamed (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்துவிடின்). Both make avoidance of the blameworthy the working test, verse 280 applying it to the ascetic in place of outward marks.

Verse 40 gives a two-sided rule: what one should do is aram, and what one should escape is blame (செயற்பாலது ... அறனே, உயற்பாலது ... பழி). Verse 466 gives the same two sides to a ruler as consequences: one is ruined by doing what is not fit to do, and ruined also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Book 2 restates the pair as policy and makes the omission as costly as the wrong act.

Verse 40 says blame is what a person should escape. Verse 656 tests that rule at its hardest: even if one must see the hunger of the mother who bore one, do not do the deed the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை). It shows that the avoidance of blame in verse 40 is meant to hold against a competing duty, and it names whose blame counts.

242 ends பல்லாற்றால் தேரினும் அஃதே துணை: however many ways you examine, அருள் alone is the companion. 132 ends with the same words, தேரினும் அஃதே துணை, said of ஒழுக்கம் (conduct). The identical closing with its exclusive ஏ is given to two different things; read strictly the two claims compete, read as emphasis each chapter is crowning its own subject.

242 tells one to search by a good path and hold to அருள் (நல்லாற்றான் நாடி அருளாள்க). 324 asks what the good path is (நல்லாறு எனப்படுவது யாதெனின்) and answers: the way that keeps in view not killing anything (யாதொன்றும் கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி). 324 gives content to the நல்லாறு that 242 leaves open, and ties அருள் to not killing.

243 says those whose hearts are joined with அருள் (அருள்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்) do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 5 says the two kinds of deed joined with darkness (இருள்சேர் இருவினையும்) do not join (சேரா) those devoted to the Lord's praise. Both build on சேர், what one is joined to: in 5 darkness is a quality of deeds (Parimelazhagar: மயக்கம்), in 243 it is a place one enters, and joining something else keeps it away.

243: no entry into the dark painful world for hearts with அருள். 121: restraint leads among the immortals, lack of restraint drives into thick darkness (அடங்காமை ஆரிருள் உய்த்து விடும்). Both use darkness as the destination of a failed virtue, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as a hell; 243 states only the exemption, 121 states both directions.

244 pairs மன்னுயிர் and தன்னுயிர்: care for other lives frees one's own life from fear. 268 uses the same pair the other way round: one who has fully gained his own life (தன்னுயிர் தான்அறப் பெற்றானை) is worshipped by all other lives (ஏனைய மன்னுயிரெல்லாம் தொழும்). Together they show the relation running in both directions, from care of others to one's own safety and from self-mastery to others' reverence.

244: one who tends living beings and holds to அருள் (மன்னுயிர் ஓம்பி அருளாள்வாற்கு) has no deed his own life need fear (தன்னுயிர் அஞ்சும் வினை இல்). 326: on the days of one who lives by not killing, Death that eats life does not advance (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று). Both say that sparing other lives secures one's own, once in terms of deeds and once in terms of Death.

244 promises that the one who protects lives has nothing his own life need fear. 327 uses the same word, தன்னுயிர், to command not taking another's life even if one's own life goes (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க). 327 shows that the safety promised in 244 is not the condition for the rule: the rule holds even where one's own life is lost.

245 calls the wide earth where the wind moves a witness (ஞாலம் கரி) that those who hold to அருள் have no distress. 25 calls Indra witness enough (இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி) to the power of one who quenched the five senses. Both close an unprovable claim about a virtue's power by naming a கரி, a witness; 245 appeals to the whole visible world, 25 to one figure from story.

245 says flatly that those who hold to அருள் have no distress (அல்லல் அருளாள்வார்க்கு இல்லை), and Parimelazhagar takes this to cover this life. 169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright (செவ்வியான் கேடும்) are to be pondered, which concedes that the upright do meet ruin. The conflict holds if அல்லல் includes worldly ruin and if 169 is read as admitting such cases occur; Parimelazhagar softens 169 with 'if they occur' (உளவாயின்).

246 says those who leave அருள் and go on doing wrong have, they say, parted from பொருள் and forgotten (பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்). 32 says there is no ruin greater than forgetting virtue (அதனை மறத்தலின் ஊங்கில்லை கேடு). Both treat wrongdoing as a kind of forgetting; Parimelazhagar reads the பொருள் of 246 as the lasting good, i.e. virtue, which brings the two closer, while Kalaignar reads it as being without wealth.

246 describes the cruel as people who have forgotten (பொச்சாந்தார்); Parimelazhagar says what they forgot is their own suffering. 250 prescribes an act of memory: when going against the weaker, think of yourself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Within the chapter, 250 supplies the remedy for the forgetting that 246 diagnoses.

247 puts wealth and அருள் in parallel (பொருளில்லார்க்கு இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி யாங்கு). 248 then breaks the parallel: those without wealth may flower one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished and can hardly become anything again (அற்றார் மற்றாதல் அரிது). The simile of 247 holds for what each lack costs, not for whether the loss can be repaired.

248: loss of wealth can be reversed, loss of அருள் cannot (அற்றார் மற்றாதல் அரிது). 134: even if forgotten, the recited text can be learned again (மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும்), but a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct declines (பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்). Both set a recoverable possession against an unrecoverable loss of character, in the domains of wealth and of learning.

249 compares virtue done by one without அருள் to an unclear person seeing the true thing (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்று). 355 defines understanding by the same phrase: seeing the true thing in whatever thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). 355 shows why the comparison in 249 bites: seeing the true thing is what clarity consists in, so without clarity it does not happen, or happens only once by chance as Parimelazhagar reads it (ஒருகால்).

316 gives the general rule: what one has oneself felt to be painful one must not do to another (இன்னா எனத்தான் உணர்ந்தவை ... பிறன்கண் செயல்). 250 applies the same use of one's own experience to a difference in strength: recall your own position before the stronger when you stand over the weaker. 250 is the rule of 316 turned into a specific exercise of memory.

321 asks what virtuous action is and answers not killing (அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை); killing brings all other deeds. 254 uses the same question form for அருள்: what is அருள் and what is not comes down to not killing and killing (யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்). Read together, not killing is the content of both அருள் and virtuous action, which joins the chapter on அருள் to the chapter on not killing. (The first letter of 254 is missing in this edition: ருளல்லது for அருளல்லது.)

321 makes not killing the answer to what virtuous action is. 297 says that if one keeps up not lying, it is good not to do other virtues (பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற செய்யாமை நன்று). Each verse lets one virtue stand for the whole, and they pick different ones; the conflict holds if both are read as claims of sufficiency and not as chapter emphasis. 323 settles the order inside this chapter by putting not lying second.

322 puts feeding and sustaining lives at the head of the virtues. 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and that comes behind the strength of those who remove hunger (அப்பசியை மாற்றுவார் ஆற்றலின் பின்); Parimelazhagar takes the first group to be ascetics. 225 supplies a ranking that fits 322: not harming is completed by actively keeping others alive.

323 ranks not lying behind not killing. 292 says even falsehood stands in the place of truth if it yields good free of fault (புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்), and Parimelazhagar's example is a false word that saves a life from death. 292 shows the ranking of 323 at work inside the chapter on truth: where truthful speech and a life pull apart, the life decides.

324: if asked what is called the good path, it is the way that keeps in view not killing anything (யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும் கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி). 291: if asked what is called truth, it is speech with no harm at all in it (யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). The two definitions share their wording, எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும், and both define a positive term by the complete absence of harm, in action and in speech.

325 says that among all who renounced fearing their condition (நிலைஅஞ்சி நீத்தாருள்), the one who fears killing and keeps not killing in view is chief. 261 defines the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை). 261 states the two parts of the ascetic's practice; 325 says which part decides rank among ascetics.

325 ranks the renouncer who keeps to not killing first. 984 says austerity lies in the goodness of not killing (கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை), and sets it beside worth, which lies in not speaking others' faults. The same claim about renouncers appears in the third part of the book of wealth, used there as the measure for a layman's virtue.

327: even at the cost of your own life, do not do the deed that takes a life. 656: even if you must see your mother hungry, do not do the deed the worthy condemn (ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும் செய்யற்க). Both have the form 'even at this extreme cost, செய்யற்க', and both name a வினை as what is forbidden; the first is addressed to the virtuous life, the second to a minister's conduct of affairs.

327 puts another's life above one's own. 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்). In both, one's own life is not the highest value; what outranks it is another creature's life in 327 and one's own sense of shame in 1017.

328 refuses gain that comes by killing, however great. 311 says that even if one could get wealth that brings distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்), not doing hurt to others is the settled stand of the stainless. The two adjacent chapters make the same refusal for the lesser harm and the greatest one.

328: for the worthy (சான்றோர்க்கு), gain got by killing is the lowest (கடை). 657: the utter poverty of the worthy is above gain got with blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவே தலை). Both judge ஆக்கம் by its source from the standpoint of the சான்றோர், with கடை in one and தலை in the other; 328 belongs to the book of virtue and 657 to the conduct of state business.

329 treats killers as the settled example of baseness. 551 takes that example as a measure and says a king who takes up harassing his people and does wrong is crueller than those who have taken up killing (கொலைமேற்கொண்டாரிற் கொடிதே). The book of statecraft uses the low point fixed in 329 to rank a bad ruler below it.

330 infers a past deed from a present condition: the wretched are those who took life. 37 says there is no need to say 'this is the way of virtue': look between the one who carries the palanquin and the one who rides (சிவிகை பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை). On Pope's and Parimelazhagar's reading both argue from visible fortune back to deeds, 37 for good fortune and 330 for bad; Kalaignar reads 37 differently, as about how the virtuous bear life.

330 explains diseased and failing lives by past killing. 270 explains why the have-nots are many: those who practise austerity are few and those who do not are many (நோற்பார் சிலர் பலர் நோலாதவர்). Both give a cause in conduct for an unequal condition seen in the world, 330 for individuals and 270 for the proportion in a population.

330 says those with afflicted bodies and a failing, evil life (செயிர் உடம்பின் செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கையவர்) are, they say, people who separated life from body. 326 says Death does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. The two verses are the chapter's pair of consequences, both stated in terms of body and lifespan: the non-killer's days are spared and the killer's body and living are spoiled. Parimelazhagar places the killing of 330 in a former birth; the Tamil does not say which birth.

381 calls the king who has all six limbs (படை, குடி, கூழ், அமைச்சு, நட்பு, அரண்) 'அரசருள் ஏறு', the male beast among kings; 59 says a man whose home lacks a wife who seeks good name has no 'ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை' before those who scorn him. The same figure of the proud male animal is made to depend on what a man has behind him: a kingdom's six supports in one case, a household's good name in the other. (Parimelazhagar takes ஏறு in 59 as a lion; the word itself only says 'male'.)

381 measures a king by possession (ஆறும் உடையான்), and குடி, which Parimelazhagar takes as the land, is one of the six. 740 says a land that has every excellence is still without use (பயமின்றே) if it lacks accord with its ruler (வேந்தமைவு இல்லாத நாடு). Read together, having the limb is not enough: the limb and the king must fit each other.

381 counts the fort (அரண்) among the six things whose possession makes the leading king. 750 says a fort with every excellence (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்) is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). The later verse adds the condition that 381's bare 'உடையான்' leaves out.

382 lists fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive (அஞ்சாமை ஈகை அறிவு ஊக்கம்) as a king's nature. 863 describes the man who is easy prey for an enemy: he fears, does not know, does not fit with others, does not give (அஞ்சும் அறியான் அமைவிலன் ஈகலான்). Three of the four kingly qualities reappear negated, so the weak enemy of chapter 87 is drawn as the reverse of the king of chapter 39.

383 gives three things that stay with a ruler, beginning with தூங்காமை. 605 gives four that are the pleasure-boat of those bound for ruin: delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep (நெடுநீர் மறவி மடி துயில்). The two lists are near-opposites, and 605 covers both senses the commentators give தூங்காமை in 383 (not delaying, not being slothful).

383 names promptness and resolve (தூங்காமை, துணிவுடைமை) as two separate standing qualities, with learning between them. 668 turns them into one instruction for a single task: once a deed has been seen clearly and decided (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), do it without wavering and with delay driven off (தூக்கம் கடிந்து செயல்). The trait list of the king becomes a sequence: decide, then act at once.

384 pairs மறன் and மானம் in the king. 766 opens its list of the four safeguards of an army with the same pair (மறம் மானம்), followed by keeping to the proven path and trustworthiness. The same two qualities are required at the top and in the ranks.

384 asks for honour that does not fall short of valour. 773 says fierceness (தறுகண்) is called great manliness, but helping the foe when something befalls him (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால் ஊராண்மை) is its edge (எஃகு). Parimelazhagar explains 384's phrase with examples of not striking the unequal or the fleeing, which is the restraint 773 states directly.

385 ends the king's four skills with வகுத்தல், apportioning what has been guarded. 377 uses the same verb for what lies outside human skill: even those who have piled up crores can enjoy them only in the way the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை), which Parimelazhagar takes as fate. The pairing sets the king's apportioning inside a larger one he does not control.

385 says the king must create ways for wealth to come (இயற்றல்) without naming them. 756 names three that count as the king's wealth: what falls in unowned, customs dues, and what is taken from defeated enemies (உறுபொருள், உல்கு பொருள், ஒன்னார்த் தெறுபொருள்). Parimelazhagar's note on 385 gives a similar list of sources.

386 says that if a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் அல்லனேல்), his land is spoken of above others. 566 uses the same word for the reverse case: if he is கடுஞ்சொல்லன் and without kindly regard, his long-standing wealth perishes on the spot. One trait is given both its reward and its penalty.

92 ranks the two: being pleasant-spoken with a glad face is better than giving with a glad heart (ஈதலின் நன்றே). 387 does not rank them but joins them, giving 'with' pleasant words (இன்சொலால் ஈத்து), and adds protection. The king's version needs both, where the householder's verse lets speech stand above the gift.

387 says that for one able to give with pleasant words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்து அளிக்க), the world answers to his word. 525 says one who can give and speak pleasantly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by layers of kin. The same two means work at two scales: they hold a family around a man and the world around a king.

387's result clause is that the world becomes as the king says and intends (தன் சொலால் தான் கண்டனைத்து); Manakkudavar reads this as the world lying under his command. 648 says the world quickly takes up the work it is told (விரைந்து தொழில் கேட்கும் ஞாலம்) when it finds those who can speak in order and sweetly. Both make pleasant speech the cause of the world's compliance; 387 adds giving and protection.

388: the king who does முறை and protects is counted as இறை. 547 uses the same two words in a loop: the இறை guards the whole earth, and முறை guards him if he carries it out without fail (அவனை முறை காக்கும்). Justice is what earns the title in 388 and what keeps its holder safe in 547.

388 has the just king set apart as இறை; 702 says one who knows without doubt what is in another's mind should be regarded as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோடு ஒப்பக் கொளல்). Parimelazhagar glosses both with the same phrase, 'though a man by birth'. The book grants this standing for a function performed, justice in one case and insight in the other.

389 praises a king who endures (பொறுக்கும்) bitter words. 160 says those who fast in penance are great, but rank after those who endure the harsh words others speak (இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பார்). Bearing hard speech is rated as the higher discipline for the ascetic and as the quality that holds a kingdom for the king.

389 says the world rests under the parasol of a king who can bear words bitter to the ear (செவிகைப்பச் சொற்பொறுக்கும்). 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his support people who rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை). Parimelazhagar reads 389's bitter words as those of exactly such rebuking companions, so 447 gives the institution and 389 the temperament it needs. Manakkudavar reads 389 differently, as hearing of others' offences and bearing it.

389 states the king's side: he should bear speech that is bitter to hear. 638 states the minister's side: even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to say what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). The duty to speak does not wait on the king having 389's quality.

390 calls the one who has giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people 'வேந்தர்க்கு ஒளி', a light to kings. 556 uses the same word: kings endure through just rule, and without it 'மன்னர்க்கு ஒளி' does not endure. 390 makes செங்கோல் one of four sources of that light; 556 makes it the one without which the light goes out.

390 lists அளி, kindly care, among the four things a king must have. 557 says what its absence is like: as lack of rain is to the earth, so is the king's lack of அளி to the living (துளியின்மை ... வேந்தன் அளியின்மை). An item in a list becomes, in the chapter on the crooked sceptre, something people cannot live without.

541 gives the steps of justice: examine, favour no one, deliberate, act (ஓர்ந்து ... தேர்ந்து செய்வஃதே முறை). 561 defines the king by the same sequence and adds two things: the punishment must match the offence (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது) and aim at the wrong not recurring (தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்). Chapter 57 thus supplies the measure and purpose that 541 leaves unstated.

541 makes the refusal of கண்ணோட்டம் part of the definition of முறை. 577 says those without கண்ணோட்டம் have no eyes, and those who have eyes are never without it. If 577 is read without exception, the judge of 541 is 'eyeless' in the moment of judging; the conflict disappears only if 577 is limited to dealings outside judgment, as 578 suggests.

542: the whole world lives looking to the sky, and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (வானோக்கி ... கோல் நோக்கி). 557 states the same comparison from the side of failure: what lack of rain is to the earth, the king's lack of kindly care is to living beings. The pair shows the rain comparison is about dependence, so that a failed king is a drought.

542 compares subjects' dependence on the sceptre to the world's dependence on rain. In 1192 the woman says the tenderness the loved one gives to the one who loves is like the sky yielding to those who live by it (வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்றால்). The same figure of living by the rain is used for a people before their king and a lover before the beloved, and the word அளி serves for both the king's care (557, 390) and the lover's.

543 makes the sceptre the precondition of scripture and virtue. 19 says that giving and austerity will not last in the wide world if the sky does not give (தானம் தவம் இரண்டும் தங்கா ... வானம் வழங்காதெனின்). Rain in Book 1 and just rule in Book 2 hold the same position: neither is itself virtue, but virtue does not continue without it.

544 says the world holds to the king who embraces his people. Parimelazhagar explains the embrace as speaking pleasantly and giving what is needed in hardship, which is what 387 names: to one able to give with pleasant words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க), this world answers. 387 says how the embrace is done; 544 adds that it goes together with the sceptre.

544: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும்) of the king who embraces his people (குடிதழீஇ) while wielding the sceptre. 1025: the world gathers round as kin (சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு) the man who raises his family and lives without fault. In both the world's attachment is the return for care of one's own குடி, the word meaning the king's subjects in 544 and a man's family in 1025.

545 ties rain to the king's right rule. 55 ties it to a wife's fidelity: she who rises worshipping her husband says 'rain' and it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). In the household and in the kingdom the book makes rain answer to a person keeping to their proper role.

545 says harvest (விளையுள்) comes with just rule. 239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). Both let the moral state of people show in the fertility of the land; 239 does it for any person, 545 for the king.

546's condition is that the கோல் does not bend (கோடாது). 118 praises not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை), like the கோல், here the balance beam, that first levels itself and then weighs. The same word and the same verb serve for the king's sceptre and the scales, so the straightness asked of the ruler is the impartiality asked of the worthy in Book 1.

547: the king guards the earth, and justice guards the king (இறை காக்கும் ... முறை காக்கும்). 57: what can the guard of confinement do? The guard that women keep by their own steadfastness is the chief guard (சிறை காக்கும் காப்பு ... நிறை காக்கும் காப்பே தலை). Both verses, in the same rhyming pattern, say that real protection comes from the guarded person's own conduct and not from outside force.

547 says justice protects the king if he does it without fail. 448 calls the king who has no one to rebuke him 'ஏமரா மன்னன்', a king without a guard, and says he perishes even with no one to ruin him. Together they name what guards a ruler: his own just practice and the people who correct him.

548: a king who is not easy of access (எண்பதத்தான் in the negative, as Parimelazhagar construes it) and does not examine and do justice sinks and perishes. 386: a king easy to see (காட்சிக்கு எளியன்) and not harsh in speech has his land praised. Accessibility is stated as a virtue in chapter 39 and its lack as a cause of ruin in chapter 55.

548 says the unjust, unapproachable king perishes of himself (தானே கெடும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even without enemies'. 448 says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes though no one sets out to ruin him (கெடுப்பார் இலானும் கெடும்). Both describe a ruler's fall with no outside agent, caused by shutting out complaint in one case and criticism in the other.

548 and 553 share most of a line: a king who does not examine and do justice (ஓரா / நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்). In 548 the king himself perishes; in 553 he loses his land day by day (நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The pairing shows the same neglect ruining the ruler and the country.

314 tells a person how to punish those who hurt him: shame them by doing them good and let it go (அவர் நாண நன்னயம் செய்து விடல்). 549 says that for a king, guarding the people and removing offences (குற்றம் கடிதல்) is no stain but his work (வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்). The words 'no stain' answer the doubt that punishing goes against virtue, which Parimelazhagar spells out; 549 limits 314's rule to one's own injuries and exempts the office.

549 makes removing offences the king's work. 436 sets an order for it: if he first removes his own fault and then looks at others' (தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றம் காண்கிற்பின்), what fault can attach to a ruler? The right to punish in 549 is, by 436, clear of blame only for a king who has corrected himself first.

550 compares the king's execution of the cruel to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). 1038, on farming itself, says that after weeding (கட்டபின்) guarding the crop is better than watering it. In the farmer's own chapter weeding is one step and guarding counts for more, which fits 549's order of guarding the people first and punishing second.

483 asks whether anything called அருவினை exists for one who acts with கருவி and knowing காலம். 631 uses the same three words but keeps அருவினை as a separate item the minister must be good at. The pair shows where the minister's list comes from: tools and timing are what make a hard task doable.

631 defines the minister as one excellent in கருவி, காலம், செய்கை and the அருவினை itself. 675 turns nearly the same list into a rule for anyone acting: பொருள், கருவி, காலம், வினை, இடன், 'ஐந்தும் இருள்தீர எண்ணிச் செயல்'. Read together, the minister's defining competence is the checklist of 675, with resources and place added there.

632 lists the minister's qualities: வன்கண், குடிகாத்தல், கற்றறிதல், ஆள்வினை. 382 lists the king's: அஞ்சாமை, ஈகை, அறிவு, ஊக்கம் (383 adds கல்வி and துணிவுடைமை). Firmness, knowledge and drive appear on both lists, so the minister is described on the king's pattern; Manakkudavar even glosses வன்கண் as அஞ்சாமை. Giving is on the king's list only.

187 says those who cannot make friends with pleasant talk 'கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்', split even their own kin, by divisive speech. 633 uses the same verb, பிரித்தல், for a minister's skill, which Parimelazhagar restricts to detaching an enemy's allies. The same act is a fault at home and a craft in statecraft, and what differs is whose bond is being broken.

633 names rejoining those who parted as a minister's skill. 530 says how the king should handle such a return: one who left (உழைப்பிரிந்து) and came back for a reason is to be taken in after thought, 'எண்ணிக் கொளல்'. The pair shows that பொருத்தல் is not unconditional welcome; 530 supplies the caution.

633 says a minister must be able to divide (பிரித்தல்), keep his own side (பேணிக் கொளல்) and rejoin those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 679 ranks one such act: 'ஒட்டாரை ஒட்டிக் கொளல்', bringing the unattached over, is more urgent than doing good to friends. 679 gives a priority among the alliance skills that 633 only lists.

462 tells the one acting that nothing is out of reach if he examines with a chosen circle and thinks it over himself: 'தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு'. 634 describes the minister with the same two verbs, தெரிதல் and தேர்ந்து செயல். The pairing shows the two sides of one arrangement: 462 is the ruler's need for such company, 634 is what that company must be able to do.

634 asks of a minister தெரிதல், தேர்ந்து செயல் and 'ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல்', speaking so that the matter is settled. 671 says 'சூழ்ச்சி முடிவு துணிவெய்தல்': deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and letting that resolve linger is a fault. Parimelazhagar glosses ஒருதலையாச் சொல்லல் as speaking so that துணிவு arises, which makes the minister's decisive word the point where 671's deliberation closes.

441 tells the king to choose the friendship of those who are 'அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார்', 'திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து'. 635 describes the counsel-companion in the same words: 'அறனறிந்து ... திறனறிந்தான் தேர்ச்சித் துணை'. 441 is the instruction to seek such a person and 635 is the portrait of him, with settled speech (ஆன்றமைந்த சொல்) added.

635 asks for one who knows அறன், has full and settled speech, and knows திறன். 644 joins the same three terms in one rule: 'திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லை', since no அறன் or பொருள் is beyond that. The next chapter thus takes the speech item of 635 and makes fitted speech itself the place where knowing virtue and knowing method show.

636 implies that nothing withstands the person who has native subtlety and learning. 503 says that even in those who have studied hard texts and are free of fault (அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார்), close examination rarely finds no blankness: 'இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு'. The praise in 636 concerns outwitting opposing schemes; 503 limits it, since the learned still have gaps.

426 defines அறிவு as living with the world in the way the world lives: 'உலகத்தோடு அவ்வது உறைவது'. 637 gives the working form of this for one who already knows the method: 'உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்'. Together they treat attention to how the world actually goes as part of knowledge and not a concession against it.

638 makes it the duty (கடன்) of the one at the king's side to say what is sound (உறுதி) even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself. 448 gives the stake: a king without those who rebuke, 'இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்', perishes even with no one to ruin him. 448 shows why 638 does not release the minister when the king will not listen.

638 obliges the minister to speak sound counsel regardless of the king's reception. 696 governs the manner: knowing the king's mood and considering the time, say what is needed without what is disliked, so that it is wanted ('வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்'). The duty of 638 stands, and 696 conditions how and when it is discharged.

849 says 'காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்': one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up not seeing himself, while the other keeps to what he saw. 638 requires exactly this of a minister when the king 'அறிகொன்று அறியான்'. The conflict holds if 849 is read as general advice not to instruct the conceited; Parimelazhagar reads it as a report that the instructor is reviled, which would leave 638 as a duty carried at that cost.

639 and 817 use the same construction and the same kind of figure: 'மந்திரியின் ... எழுபது கோடி உறும்' and 'நட்பின் பகைவரால் பத்தடுத்த கோடி உறும்'. In both an inflated count of open enemies is set against one false intimate, a plotting minister in 639 and a friend good only for laughter in 817. Parimelazhagar reads உறும் in 639 as 'that many enemies will come', and notes others read it as 'that many times better', which is how 817 is read.

639 says seventy crore enemies are better than a minister at one's side who plots harm ('பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி'). 882 gives the general rule: do not fear enemies like swords, fear the bond of enemies who are like kin ('கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு'). Parimelazhagar explains 639 on the same ground, that open enemies can be guarded against and the one inside cannot.

640 says those without திறப்பாடு leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order ('முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்'). 664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as said is hard ('சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்'). Both locate failure in the gap between a correct plan and its execution; Parimelazhagar glosses the 'saying' of 664 as stating in order how the task will be done.

640 says sound planning comes to nothing in those who lack the capacity to carry it through. 728 says those who have learned many things are of no use ('பயமிலரே') if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. The same pattern appears in two domains: knowledge or planning is counted worthless without the ability that delivers it.

971 says 'ஒளி ஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை' and 600 says 'உரம் ஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை': the same phrase, abundance of spirit, is called a person's light in one and a person's strength in the other. Each then states the lack: living without it is disgrace (இளி) in 971, and those without it are trees in 600. The repetition shows the chapter on greatness resting on the earlier chapter on ஊக்கம்.

133 says having conduct is what good family is ('ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை') and a lapse becomes low birth. 972 says birth is equal and distinction follows from deeds. Both move rank from descent to what a person does, though 133 keeps the vocabulary of birth and Parimelazhagar reads it within varna.

751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account ('பொருளல்லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்'). 973 says the not-high do not become high by being placed high, which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read as a seat given by wealth. On that reading 973 limits 751: wealth gets a person regarded, and it does not make them great.

57 says confinement does little and the guard a woman keeps by her own steadfastness is the chief guard ('நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை'). 974 takes this as its comparison: like single-minded women, greatness exists only 'தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின்', if one keeps hold of oneself. 974 carries 57's claim about self-guarding into the Porul chapter on greatness, so that greatness, like கற்பு, cannot be kept for someone from outside.

974 says greatness exists only as long as one keeps oneself. 965 shows the loss: even those like a hill sink if they do a lowering thing the size of a குன்றி seed. Together they present greatness as a condition that continues only through conduct and can be forfeited by a small act.

975 says the great carry out hard deeds 'ஆற்றின்', in the right way. 468 states the other side with the same word: effort not made in the right way ('ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம்') collapses even if many stand guard over it. The pair shows that ஆற்றின் in 975 carries weight: hard deeds done by the wrong route fail.

451 says greatness fears small company while smallness takes it as kin ('சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்'). 976 says the small have no thought of attaching themselves to the great. Both describe the same sorting from two ends: the small seek their own kind and do not look upward.

977 says even distinction (சிறப்பு), if it falls to the unworthy, results in acts of excess ('இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்று'). 838 says a fool getting something in hand is like a man already deranged getting drunk. Both say a good thing makes its holder worse when the holder is unfit; 838 says it of possessions and a fool, 977 of distinction and the small. Manakkudavar reads the சிறப்பு of 977 as wealth, which brings the two closer.

1000 says great wealth obtained by one without பண்பு is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel. 977 says distinction landing on the unworthy produces excess. The logic is the same, that the recipient's quality decides what a gift becomes, but 1000 has the wealth spoiled and useless while 977 has the distinction turn into overbearing action.

125 says bowing is good for everyone and for the wealthy it is a further wealth. 978 says greatness bows and smallness decks itself out in self-admiration. Both attach humility to those who have most reason for pride; Parimelazhagar glosses the பணிதல் of 125 as being without பெருமிதம், the word 979 uses.

439 commands 'வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை', never admire yourself, among faults a ruler must avoid. 978 uses the same verb to define smallness: 'அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து'. What 439 forbids as a fault, 978 treats as the mark by which the small are known.

978 says greatness bows always ('பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை'). 963 says bowing is needed in abundance and standing tall is needed in reduced circumstances ('சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு'). Taken plainly, 963 limits the என்றும் of 978; Parimelazhagar reads என்றும் in 978 as 'even when distinction has come', which makes the two verses say the same thing about prosperity.

979 defines greatness as the absence of பெருமிதம் and smallness as riding it to the end. 431 uses the same word with approval: the prosperity of those free of செருக்கு, anger and சிறுமை is 'பெருமித நீர்த்து', which Parimelazhagar glosses as having the quality of eminence. The word means conceit in 979 and dignity in 431, and both verses agree that the person without pride is the one who has real stature.

844 defines வெண்மை, poor understanding, as the pride that says 'we have brightness' ('ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு'). 979 defines smallness as being carried away by பெருமிதம். In both a defect is identified with the claim to its opposite: the foolish are those sure of their intelligence, and the small are those sure of their greatness.

846 and 980 share the words அற்றம், மறை and குற்றம். In 846 covering one's own nakedness is itself poor understanding while one's faults stay uncovered, which Parimelazhagar takes as faults not removed. In 980 greatness covers the அற்றம் of others. The image of covering what is exposed is used for self-deception in one verse and for consideration toward others in the other.

1079 says the base, on merely seeing others clothed and fed, are able to find a blemish in them ('வடுக்காண வற்றாகும் கீழ்'). 980 says smallness tells only faults ('குற்றமே கூறி விடும்'). 1079 adds a cause the Tamil of 980 leaves out: Parimelazhagar reads the fault-finding of the base as coming from being unable to bear others' prosperity.

1091 says the same eyes hold the look that makes him ill and the look that cures it. 15 says rain is both what ruins ('கெடுப்பதூஉம்') and what, as support to the ruined, lifts them again ('எடுப்பதூஉம்'). In both, one source is credited with the harm and with its remedy, once in love and once in the world's subsistence.

1090 says brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it and does not, like love, gladden those who merely see ('கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல்'). 1092 puts a measure on that: the small look her eyes steal ('கண்களவு கொள்ளும் சிறுநோக்கம்') is not an even half of love but more ('செம்பாகம் அன்று பெரிது'). Together they make sight alone a large share of love's pleasure; Parimelazhagar takes the 'half' in 1092 to be half of physical union.

1092 ranks a brief stolen look as more than half of love. 1326 ranks sulking above union ('புணர்தலின் ஊடல் இனிது'), as digesting is sweeter than eating. Both verses place the greater part of love's pleasure in something beside the embrace, one before it and one around it.

In 1093 her look followed by a lowered head is 'water she poured' ('அட்டிய நீர்') into the 'யாப்பு', which Parimelazhagar reads as the crop of love binding the two. 718 says speaking before those able to understand is like pouring water into the bed of something already growing ('வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந்தற்று'). Both use watering for a sign or word given to someone already receptive: the gesture or speech does not start the growth, it feeds it.

1096: though they speak like those unattached ('உறாஅதவர்போல் சொலினும்'), the words of those without anger are quickly understood ('செறாஅர்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்'). 826 has the same frame reversed: though they say good things like friends ('நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும்'), the words of the unreconciled are quickly understood ('ஒட்டார்சொல் ஒல்லை உணரப்படும்'). The shared wording shows one claim applied in love and in statecraft: a spoken mask, harsh or kind, does not long hide the disposition behind it.

1097 lists small harsh words spoken without anger and looks like an enemy's ('செற்றார்போல் நோக்கும்') as the signs of those who are close while seeming distant. 824 warns of the opposite pairing: a sweet smile on the face with bitterness inside ('முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா'). In both the surface is the reverse of the heart; the lover reads the mismatch with relief, the Book of Wealth reads it with fear.

In 1098, when he looks she softens and smiles gently ('பசையினள் பைய நகும்'), and he says there is a certain grace in her then ('உண்டு ஆண்டு ஓர் ஏஎர்'). 1274 says there is something inside the bud of her smile, like scent inside a closed bud ('நகைமொக்குள் உள்ளதொன்று உண்டு'). Both treat her slight smile as holding an unspoken meaning, and both leave that meaning as an unnamed 'something'.

1099 says looking at each other with the common look, like strangers ('ஏதிலார் போலப் பொதுநோக்கு நோக்குதல்'), is found in lovers. 528 uses the same word for a king: he should not look on all in common ('பொதுநோக்கான்') but by rank, and many will live looking to that. In 528 the undifferentiated look is a failure to distinguish; in 1099 it is put on deliberately by the two people who distinguish each other most.

1100: when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words are of no use at all ('வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல'). 705, in the Book of Wealth's chapter of the same name, asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign ('என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்'). Both hold that the eye is the organ for knowing another's mind; 705 says so for court service and 1100 for lovers, where it makes speech redundant.

1100 says that once the eyes agree, words from the mouth serve no purpose. 1280 says that telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading ('கண்ணினால் காமநோய் சொல்லி இரவு') adds womanhood to womanhood. 1280 moves from the fact that eyes can replace speech to praise of the woman who chooses to speak that way.

1151 tells him to announce his quick return to those who will be alive then ('வாழ்வார்க்கு உரை'), implying she will not be. 1160 says many consent to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards ('பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்'); Parimelazhagar reads this as her ironic reply to the friend, meaning she is not one of them. The chapter opens and closes on the same word, 'வாழ்வார்', for the survivors she sets herself apart from.

In 1151 the speaker (the friend for Parimelazhagar, the woman for Manakkudavar) says a promise of quick return is only for those who will survive. In 1263 the woman, after he has gone, says she is still alive through wanting his return ('வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்'). The later speech shows the claim of 1151 as said in the moment: the hope of return that was dismissed there is what keeps her alive here.

1152: once even his look was pleasant, but now union itself holds the pain of fearing separation ('பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு'). 1295: her heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting ('பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்'), so its misery never ends. Both say that the prospect of parting takes away the pleasure of being together; 1295 states it as the heart's standing condition.

1153: trust is hard ('அரிதரோ தேற்றம்'), because parting occurs at some point even with those who understand ('அறிவுடையார் கண்ணும்'). 514: even when people have been trusted after every kind of test ('எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்'), many turn different through the nature of the work. Both say that knowing a person's qualities does not secure their future conduct, one about a lover and one about a king's appointee.

1154 holds up his words 'fear not' and says the fault, if he leaves, is not the believer's. 1209 holds up another of his sayings, 'we are not separate' ('வேறல்லம் என்பார்'), and says her life is ending from thinking on his lack of grace. 1154 is the argument made before the parting; 1209 is the same contrast of word and conduct felt after it.

1151 asks him to say he is not going, and leaves talk of return to those who will survive. 1155 turns to the friend: if you would protect, prevent his parting ('பிரிவோம்பல்'), since once he goes union is hard ('நீங்கின் அரிதால் புணர்வு'). Both reject return as a remedy and allow only not-leaving; Parimelazhagar supplies that what is to be protected in 1155 is her life.

1156 names him 'வன்கண்ணர்' for announcing his departure. In 1222 she asks the evening, which looks as wretched as she is, whether its partner too is hard like hers ('எம்கேள்போல் வன்கண்ணதோ'). The epithet given conditionally in 1156 has become her settled description of him once he is gone.

In 1157 the slipping bangles broadcast ('தூற்றா') his leaving. In 1235 the shoulders that have lost bangles and their old beauty tell of the cruel one's cruelty ('கொடியார் கொடுமை உரைக்கும்'). Both make her thinning body a speaker that reports on him without her consent; 1235 adds a judgment of him to the bare news of 1157.

1158: living in a town without one's own people is painful, and parting from one who is dear is more painful still ('அதனினும் இன்னாது இனியார்ப் பிரிவு'). 839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting brings no pain at all ('பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்று இல்'). Read together, both verses use the pain of parting as the measure of what a bond was worth: none for a fool's friendship, more than exile among strangers for a lover.

1160 says many agree to the hard thing, put away their pain, endure the parting and live on ('பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்'); Parimelazhagar reads it as irony against the friend's advice. 1198 says outright that none in the world are harder than those who live on ('வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்') without a kind word from the beloved. Both treat surviving separation as something that needs explaining, not as the expected course.

Verse 11 gives rain the name அமிழ்தம் because the world's life continues through it. In 1106 the lover says her shoulders must be made of amrita (அமிழ்தின் இயன்றன தோள்) because his life puts out new shoots at each touch (உயிர் தளிர்ப்ப). Both verses award the word for the same reason, that the thing keeps life going, once for the whole world and once in a lover's speech about himself.

Verse 13 says that if the sky proves false (விண் பொய்ப்பின்), hunger stays and torments the world (உள்நின்று உடற்றும் பசி), sea-girt though it is. Verse 734 defines a land as one that severe hunger (உறுபசி), unending disease and destructive enemies do not reach. Read together, the first mark of a proper country in the Book of Wealth rests on something no ruler supplies, the rain of chapter 2.

Verse 14 says ploughing stops when the rain's bounty declines. Verse 1036 says that if the ploughmen's hands fold (உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின்), even those who say they have given up desire cannot hold their state. Verse 14 names one cause that would fold those hands, so the failure of rain reaches as far as the renouncer.

Verse 15 says it is rain that ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them (எடுப்பதூஉம்); Parimelazhagar explains that it ruins by not falling. In 1102 the lover says that for other diseases the medicine is something else, but she is herself the medicine for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). The pattern of one thing being both the harm and the only remedy appears for rain and the world and, in a lover's speech, for the beloved.

Verse 16 says that unless drops fall from the sky (விசும்பின் துளிவீழின் அல்லால்) not even the tip of green grass can be seen. Verse 557 says that what lack of drops (துளியின்மை) is to the earth, the king's lack of tender regard (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him. Verse 16 supplies the picture that 557's comparison assumes: without the king's அளி, the people are the bare ground.

Verse 211 asks what the world does for the rain-cloud in return (மாரிமாட்டு என் ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு) and makes it the model of duty that wants no repayment. Verse 17 says even the long sea loses its nature if the cloud, having taken from it (தடிந்து, as Parimelazhagar reads it), does not give back. On that reading the cloud is not a pure giver: it returns what it drew from the sea, and the sea suffers if it withholds. Manakkudavar takes தடிந்து as lightning flashing, and on his reading the qualification falls away.

Verse 17 pictures the cloud not giving (எழிலி தான் நல்காதாகி விடின்) and the sea itself shrinking as a result.
