The impermanence of wealth taught to the renouncer is restated in the Book of Wealth, where it becomes a reason to value energy and not a reason to withdraw.

437 says the wealth of the miser who does not do with it what should be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது) perishes without anything surviving. 333 says wealth does not stay and should be turned at once into what does. The Book of Wealth gives the same instruction negatively: unused wealth is simply lost.

334 presents each day as a blade cutting life, with no one exempted. 326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days (வாழ்நாள்மேல் செல்லாது) of one who lives by not killing. Read literally, 326 exempts the non-killer from the daily loss of life that 334 treats as universal; the conflict depends on taking 326 as a promise about lifespan and not as praise of the vow.

342 says if you want what renunciation brings, renounce while there is still something (உண்டாகத் துறக்க), which Parimelazhagar takes as 'while there is time'. 335 says to hurry to good deeds before the death rattle. On that reading the next chapter applies the same urgency to renouncing that 335 applies to good deeds.

336 says this world has the 'greatness' that one who was here yesterday is not here today (நெருநல் உளனொருவன் இன்றில்லை). 233 says nothing in the world stands undying except high renown (புகழல்லால் பொன்றாது நிற்பதொன்றில்). 233 agrees with 336 about everything else and names one exception; the renouncer's chapter offers none.

336 says a person who was yesterday is not today (இன்றில்லை). 235 speaks of a death that is really existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு), possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains as the body of fame surviving. The two verses use the same pair, உள and இல், in opposite directions: 336 for the plain fact of death and 235 for the rare death that leaves something that is.

338 pictures the body as a குடம்பை, shell or nest, that the bird leaves empty; 340 pictures it as a lodging (துச்சில்) where life stays as a tenant without a home of its own (புக்கில்). Both make the body a dwelling and life its occupant. 338 shows the departure, and 340 asks why there has to be one; Manakkudavar takes the permanent home to be liberation.

339 presents death and birth as alternating like sleep and waking, which both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read as a cycle that keeps turning. 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). 356 limits 339: the waking that follows each death is the rule only for those who have not seen the real.

341's doubled யாதனின் யாதனின் ... அதனின் அதனின் allows release thing by thing: each thing left stops hurting. 343 demands that everything wanted be let go together (வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு). Parimelazhagar notices the difference under 341, calling giving up everything at once the chief way while granting that giving things up one by one still removes the pain each brings.

341 says that whatever one has left (யாதனின் நீங்கியான்), from that one has no pain (நோதல் இலன்). 626, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, asks whether those who never guarded wealth saying 'we have got it' (பெற்றேமென்று ஓம்புதல் தேற்றாதவர்) would grieve saying 'we have lost it' (அற்றேமென்று). The renouncer's rule reappears in the book of wealth as a habit of mind for someone who still owns things.

341 ties freedom from pain to having left the thing itself (நீங்கியான்). 629 says one who does not crave the pleasure in pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not suffer the pain in pain; Parimelazhagar reads this as someone who goes on experiencing the pleasure without wanting it. The pairing shows the same result claimed for an inward letting go, without the outward leaving.

36 tells one to do virtue without saying 'we will see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம் என்னாது). 342's உண்டாகத் துறக்க is read by Parimelazhagar as 'renounce while there is time', i.e. in youth, so the joys last long; Manakkudavar instead reads it as 'if you want gain for your life'. On Parimelazhagar's reading the chapter on renunciation repeats, for renouncing, the earlier rule against postponing virtue.

46 asks what a person who runs household life by the way of virtue would gain by going to the outside way (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவது எவன்). 342 says that after renouncing there are many things to be had here, and urges renouncing if one wants them (வேண்டின் ... துறக்க). The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Pope does: on that reading 46's rhetorical 'what is gained?' gets the answer 'much' in 342.

342 says that after renouncing, many things come about here (ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல), which Parimelazhagar takes as joys in this life. 369 says joy is unbroken even here (இன்பம் இடையறாது ஈண்டும்) once craving, the sorrow of sorrows, is gone. Both place the reward of letting go in this world (ஈண்டு), not only after death.

6 describes God as the one who quenched the five whose gates are the senses (பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான்) and promises long life to those who keep to his path. 343 lays the same thing on the renouncer as a duty (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை). The renouncer is asked to do what the invocation names as the mark of the Lord.

126, in the householder's chapter on restraint, speaks of drawing in the five like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), which protects through seven births. 343 uses a harder verb for the renouncer: the field of the five must be killed or crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை), and every wanted thing dropped at once. Read together they show two degrees of the same discipline, withdrawal that can be reversed and destruction that cannot.

344 makes possessionlessness the nature of austerity. 263 asks whether the others have forgotten austerity out of a wish to provide for those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). The pairing shows that the ascetic's having nothing is sustained by householders who keep possessions in order to give.

344 says having nothing at all is natural to the vow (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்றின்மை) and that owning anything brings back confusion. 1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing (விட்டேம் என்பார்க்கும் நிலை இல்லை). The renouncer's owning nothing rests on others who produce food.

344 treats having nothing (ஒன்றின்மை) as the proper state of the vow. 1050 speaks of those who have nothing to enjoy (துப்புரவில்லார்) and yet do not fully renounce (துவரத் துறவாமை), calling them death to salt and gruel. Lacking things is therefore not the same as renouncing: poverty without the inner giving up is counted as a burden, not as austerity.

73 says the bond of the precious life with the body (ஆருயிர்க்கு என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is the way that came to be joined with love, so embodiment is given a purpose. 345 says that for those undertaking to cut off births (பிறப்பறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்கு) the body itself is excess and other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) pointless. The value 73 gives the body-bond holds within the life of love; 345 marks where, for the renouncer, it stops holding.

345 says even the body is too much for one seeking to end birth. 627, in the book of wealth, says the great do not take trouble as trouble, knowing the body is a target for suffering (இலக்கம் உடம்பு இடும்பைக்கு). Both start from the body as a liability, but 627 uses that view to keep steady in worldly trouble while 345 uses it to argue for giving up every tie.

50 says one who lives on earth as life should be lived will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வானுறையும் தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப்படும்). 346 promises the one who ends 'I' and 'mine' a world higher than the gods' (வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த உலகம்). Set side by side the two verses give a scale: the good householder reaches the gods, the renouncer goes beyond them.

346 says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods. 72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves (எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்) while the loving belong to others even to their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). The householder's love already loosens 'mine', and even the body as 'I', by giving it to others; renunciation does it by cutting the notion itself.

347 uses பற்று for attachment in general and says its holders are held by griefs. 438, on a ruler's faults, names miserliness as 'the clinging heart' (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) and says it is not to be counted with any other fault. The same word and the same refusal to let go appear in the domain of wealth, where Parimelazhagar glosses it as not releasing goods when they ought to be released.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றினைப் பற்றி விடாஅதவர்க்கு). 940 says that as a gambler loves the game more with each loss, the life grows more fond with each suffering it undergoes (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar and Pope take the object of that fondness to be the body. 940 supplies what 347 leaves unexplained: suffering does not loosen the grip but tightens it.

348 sets those who have fully renounced above everyone else. 276 says none are harder-hearted than those who have not renounced in the heart (நெஞ்சின் துறவார்) and live by deceiving as though they had (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து). The praise in 348 therefore applies to renunciation of the heart; the outward form without it is placed among the worst.

348 gives the prize only to those who renounce thoroughly (தீரத் துறந்தார்). 365 says those called 'freed' are those freed of craving, and the others are not freed in that way (மற்றையார் அற்றாக அற்றது இலர்), whatever else they have given up. 365 specifies what 348's 'thoroughly' requires: the giving up must reach craving, not only things.

361 says craving is the seed that yields unceasing birth for all beings (தவாஅப் பிறப்பீனும் வித்து). 349 says the moment attachment is cut off, that cuts off birth (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும்). One verse names the cause and the other states what follows when the cause is removed; Parimelazhagar makes the same cause-and-effect point under 349.

350 says to hold to the hold of the one who has none. 359 says that if one knows the support and lives so that supports perish (சார்புணர்ந்து சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains due to come will not come. The two are built alike on a repeated word, பற்று and சார்பு, and Parimelazhagar reads the சார்பு that is known as the true reality on which all rests, so 359 states the result of the practice 350 prescribes.

351 says an inglorious birth comes from the delusion that takes what is not real for real (மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு). 1002 ends with the same words: the delusion of thinking everything comes by wealth, and so hoarding without giving, produces an inglorious birth. The book of wealth applies the metaphysical formula to one concrete error, treating money as the thing that matters.

352 has darkness leave and joy arise for those who see truly. 243 says those whose hearts are joined with compassion do not enter the painful world joined with darkness (இருள்சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம்). 243's wording supports Parimelazhagar's reading of இருள் in 352 as a dark world of suffering, and shows the book promising escape from it by compassion as well as by knowledge.

50 says one who lives on earth (வையத்துள்) as one should is placed among the gods who dwell in the sky. 353 uses the same pair, earth and sky (வையத்தின் வானம்), and says the sky is the nearer of the two for one who is clear of doubt. The householder gets there by right living and the knower by certainty, and in both the sky is brought within reach of someone still on earth.

353 says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. 702 says one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை) should be held equal to a god. In both, knowing free of doubt lifts a person toward the divine, once in the knowledge of reality and once in a courtier's reading of minds.

2 asks what learning has achieved (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்) if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge. 354 says command of the five senses has no benefit (பயமின்றே) for those without perception of the real. Both verses grant an attainment and then deny its fruit when the final step is missing, learning without worship in one and discipline without insight in the other.

126 says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a protection for seven. 354 says the attained fivefold awareness yields no fruit without true perception; Parimelazhagar reads ஐயுணர்வு as the mind withdrawn from the senses and held under control, and the missing fruit as release, while Manakkudavar reads it as knowing all that the five senses can know. On Parimelazhagar's reading sense-restraint earns protection across births, as 126 says, but not the end of birth.

355 makes seeing the true thing the definition of understanding. 857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காணார்); Parimelazhagar takes it there as the substance of the texts on right policy that bring success. The same phrase marks, in the book of wealth, what a mind bent on quarrel cannot perceive.

398 says the learning acquired in one birth protects through seven (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து). 356 says those who have learned here and seen the true thing (கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார்) reach the path of not coming back here (மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி). Learning in the book of wealth is an asset carried across births; learning that ends in seeing the real is said to end the births themselves.

356 speaks of those who learn and see the true thing; 357 adds the mind's own work: if the mind examines and knows with certainty what is (ஓர்த்து ... உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையா), one need not think of birth again. Parimelazhagar reads the two as successive means, hearing instruction in 356 and reasoned examination in 357. The printed text here has உணரான், but Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's glosses read உணரின், which the sense requires.

351 says a joyless birth comes from the delusion (மருள்) that takes the unreal for real. 358 goes a step further and calls birth itself a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை); Parimelazhagar explains this as naming the effect in place of its cause. The chapter moves from delusion as the cause of birth to birth and delusion spoken of as one thing, removed together by seeing the real.

358 speaks of 'the folly called birth' departing when the real is seen. 835, in the chapter on folly in the book of wealth, says a fool can in one birth's doing make the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both tie பேதைமை to the chain of births, 358 as its root and 835 through the fool's deeds.

5 says the two kinds of deed do not attach (சேரா) to those devoted to the Lord's praise. 359 says the pains due to attach will not attach (சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்) to one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish; Parimelazhagar takes these as the fruits of stored deeds still awaiting experience, and Manakkudavar takes சார்பு itself as the hold of deeds. Devotion in 5 and knowledge with practice in 359 are credited with the same effect on karma.

347 says griefs hold and do not let go of those who hold on to attachment. 359 gives the other case: for one who knows the support and lives so that supports fall away (சார்புகெட ஒழுகின்), the pains that were due do not come to cling. 347 states the bondage and 359 the way out, in the same language of things that cling.

360 says pain perishes when desire, anger and confusion perish down to their names (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் ... நாமம் கெட); Parimelazhagar glosses the three as wanting, aversion and ignorance. 4 describes God as the one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet have no suffering. The state 360 sets as the goal is the nature 4 gives to the Lord, with the same result, the end of suffering.

360 lists desire, anger and confusion as what must perish for pain to end. 431 lists three faults whose absence gives a ruler's prosperity its dignity: arrogance, anger and smallness (செருக்கும் சினமும் சிறுமையும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as pride, anger and lust. A similar triad, sharing anger and, on that gloss, desire, is the obstacle to release in one book and to good rule in the other.

34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல் அனைத்து அறன்). 364 defines purity as the absence of craving (அவாவின்மை). Taken together, 364 names the stain that 34 leaves unnamed.

275 warns that the hidden conduct of those who say 'we are free of attachment' (பற்றற்றேம் என்பார்) brings many harms. 365 says who may rightly be called freed (அற்றவர் என்பார்): only those freed of craving. 275 shows the claim made falsely; 365 gives the inner criterion that the claim has to meet.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, one of which is craving (அழுக்காறு அவா வெகுளி இன்னாச்சொல்). 366 says craving is what deceives a person (வஞ்சிப்பது அவா), and that fearing it is itself virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). 366 takes one item from the list in 35 and gives the reason for singling it out: it works by deceit, so it needs constant watch.

428 says fearing what should be feared is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்) and leaves the object open. 366 names an object, craving, and calls the fear of it virtue (அஞ்சுவதோரும் அறனே). The general rule about right fear in the book of statecraft gets a specific content in the renouncer's chapter.

Fear and craving appear together in both verses with opposite roles. In 1075 fear is the whole conduct of the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), with a little more if there is something they crave (அவாவுண்டேல்); Parimelazhagar takes the fear as fear of punishment. In 366 fear is directed at craving itself and is called virtue. The pairing separates fear that serves craving from fear that guards against it.

266 says those who do austerity do their own work, and the others, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவஞ்செய்வார் ஆசையுட் பட்டு). 367 says that if craving is cut off thoroughly, the deed that does not fail (தவாவினை) comes in the way one wishes. They state the same link from opposite sides: desire makes action futile, and its removal makes action unfailing.

309 says all that one has thought of is reached at once if one does not think of anger in the heart (உள்ளியதெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 367 says the unfailing deed comes as one wishes (தான் வேண்டுமாற்றான் வரும்) once craving is cut. Each verse removes one passion, anger or craving, and promises that what one intends then arrives.

341 says a person has no pain from each thing he has left (யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல் அதனின் அதனின் இலன்), taking objects one by one. 368 says those without craving have no sorrow at all (அவாஇல்லார்க்கு இல்லாகுந் துன்பம்). 368 moves from the objects given up to the craving behind them, so the relief is complete instead of item by item.

347 says sorrows hold and do not let go of those who hold attachment and do not let go (பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள்). 368 says that where craving exists sorrow keeps coming without fail, one after another (தவாஅது மேன்மேல் வரும்). Both describe suffering as continuing for as long as its cause is kept.

628, in the chapter on not being undone by trouble, says one who does not desire pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow (துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). 368 says those without craving have no sorrow. The renouncer's doctrine reappears as practical advice for a person at work in the world, where Parimelazhagar relates it to the pains of effort.

The two verses share one sentence frame. 369: joy is unbroken if the sorrow of sorrows called craving perishes (அவாவென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). 854: it yields the joy of joys if the sorrow of sorrows called hostility perishes (இகலென்னும் துன்பத்துள் துன்பங் கெடின்). The same title, sorrow of sorrows, is given to craving in the book of virtue and to hostility in the book of statecraft, each as the worst thing in its own field.

370 says that giving up craving gives, in that very state (அந்நிலையே), a nature that does not shift (பேரா இயற்கை). 349 says the moment attachment ends (பற்றற்ற கண்ணே) it cuts off birth. Both make the result immediate on the cause ending, with no further step between.

370 says craving has a nature that is never filled (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா). 940 gives a picture of that: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும்), a living being's love grows with each suffering (துன்பம் உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்); Parimelazhagar takes this as love of the body. 940 shows why satisfying craving cannot end it, which is why 370 says it has to be given up.

617 says the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி) and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the one without sloth. 371 says sloth (மடி) and its opposite are themselves produced by the fate of loss and the fate of gain. In 617 fortune depends on whether one is slothful; 371 adds that whether one is slothful depends on fate.

371 says tireless effort arises from a fate of gain and sloth arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 618 says lacking good fortune (பொறியின்மை) is no one's disgrace, but lacking effort after learning what should be known is a disgrace (ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). If sloth itself is produced by fate, as 371 says on a plain reading, the line 618 draws between blameless fortune and blameworthy idleness is hard to hold.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப் படுக்கும் இழவூழ்); Parimelazhagar adds that this happens even to one who has understanding. The protection 429 promises rests on understanding, and 372 says understanding itself can be taken away by fate.

372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ் உற்றக் கடை). 859 says that when gain is coming a person does not look at hostility (இகல்காணான் ஆக்கம் வருங்கால்), and to bring ruin on himself he looks to excel at it. In both, approaching gain or ruin shows first as a change in the person's own judgement.

823 says that even after learning many good things it is hard for the unworthy to become good in heart (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும் மனநல்லர் ஆகுதல் மாணார்க்கு அரிது); Parimelazhagar applies this to enemies. 373 says that after much study a person's own understanding still prevails. The same limit on what books can change is stated once for understanding and once for the heart.

169 says the prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்), and gives no answer; Parimelazhagar says the wise look for the earlier deed behind it. 374 notes a like mismatch between wealth and understanding and gives it as the two-fold nature of the world. One verse separates wealth from goodness and the other separates it from wisdom.

374 states as a general fact that wealth and clear understanding are separate lots. 408 judges one result of that: wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). 408 takes for granted the mismatch that 374 explains.

483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the right means and knowing the time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). 375 says that in making wealth all that is good turns bad and bad turns good (நல்லவை எல்லாஅந் தீயவாம்); Parimelazhagar takes the good and bad things to be time, place, means and action, reversed by fate. On that reading the favourable conditions 483 relies on do not secure the result, and the two conflict. Kalaignar reads 375 differently, as good and bad deeds turning out contrary to intent.

376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however carefully it is guarded (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if thrown out. 659 says all that is taken with others' tears leaves with tears, and what is of the good kind (நற்பாலவை) pays later even if lost. Both say some goods stay and some go whatever one does; 659 gives a test the person controls, the way the wealth was gained, where 376 gives only fate's allotment.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்), and treats this as the miser's own failing. 377 says even those who have gathered crores can enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). Both separate owning from enjoying; 377 places part of enjoyment outside the owner's choice, which limits the blame in 1005.

344 says having nothing is natural to austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை). 378 looks at those who already have nothing through poverty and says they would renounce, but for what fate makes them undergo. Parimelazhagar makes the connection: they have already lost what a renouncer gives up, and still suffer because their intent differs. Having nothing is the condition of austerity in 344, and 378 shows it is not enough by itself.

379 asks why those who see things as good when good comes should grieve (அல்லற்படுவது எவன்) when it does not. 626 asks whether those who never clutched at wealth saying 'we have got it' would grieve (அல்லற்படுபவோ) saying 'we have lost it'. Both are rhetorical questions with the same verb and the same symmetry between gain and loss. 626 adds the practical point that grief at loss depends on how one held the gain.

380 says fate is the strongest thing and gets ahead of any plan. 619 grants that a thing may not come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), and adds that effort still pays the wage of the body's labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). 619 accepts the limit that 380 states and marks out what remains for effort within it.

391 treats right conduct as what should follow flawless learning. 823, on false friends, says that even after studying many good things (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்தும்) it is hard for the unworthy (மாணார்) to become good at heart. It limits 391: study does not by itself produce the standing-by-it, which is why 391 has to command it separately.

391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw (கசடறக் கற்க), then stand in keeping with it (நிற்க அதற்குத் தக). 834 names the person who does the first and skips the second: one who has studied, understood and even taught others but is not himself restrained (தானடங்கா) is the greatest of fools. The pair shows that the second half of 391 is not an afterthought: learning without it is classed as folly.

392 makes numbers and letters the eyes of the living. 445 says a king goes about with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with care. Both treat sight as something acquired from outside oneself, through learning in one case and through chosen advisers in the other.

393 denies real eyes to the unlearned. 418 says ears not pierced by listening (கேள்வியால் தோட்கப்படாத செவி) are of a deaf kind even though they hear. The next chapter repeats the pattern for the other sense: an organ counts only when it has been trained by learning or listening.

394 describes the learned as people whose company others want again after it ends. 643 defines speech as what binds those who heard it and makes even those who did not hear want it (கேளாரும் வேட்ப). 643 gives the means, speech, for the effect 394 describes.

394 says the work of the learned is to meet so that others are glad and to part so that others think of them (உள்ளப் பிரிதல்). 839 says, ironically, that friendship with fools is very sweet because parting from them (பிரிவின்கண்) brings no pain at all. Both judge a person by what the parting leaves behind; the fool is the case where it leaves nothing.

395 praises learning in the stance of one who lacks before one who has. 724 tells even the learned to state what they have learned before the learned and take more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). The asking stance of 395 is thus not only for beginners; it continues among the learned.

395 uses the poor standing before the rich (உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல்) as its figure for the learner, and on Parimelazhagar's reading those who learned standing so are foremost while those who would not are lowest. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even asking water for a cow. Read together, the posture the book calls degrading when the object is goods is the one it honours when the object is learning.

397 says that for the learned any land is one's land and any town one's town (யாதானும் நாடாம் ஊராம்). 753 says the unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind (எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று) and cuts away the darkness there. Learning and wealth are each credited with making foreign places open to a person.

399 assumes the learned person's learning gives the world joy. 650 says those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others grasp it (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom without scent. It adds the condition 399 leaves unstated: the world's delight depends on being able to convey the learning.

400 gives the title of real wealth to learning. 241 gives it to grace (அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), with the reason that wealth of goods is found even among the base. The same move appears in the Book of Virtue with a different winner, and 241's reason, who can hold it, differs from 400's, whether it can be lost.

400 says learning is the imperishable, excellent wealth and other things are not wealth (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை). 411 says the wealth of the ear is the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துளெல்லாம் தலை). Adjacent chapters use the same 'true wealth' figure for study and then for listening, without ranking the two against each other.

401 says holding forth in an assembly without full book-learning (நிரம்பிய நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்) is like playing dice without a marked board. 728 says those who have learned many things are still of no use if they cannot speak well and tellingly in a good assembly. Together they give both halves: speech without learning has nothing to stand on, and learning without speech yields nothing.

402 compares the unlearned man's desire to speak (சொற்காமுறுதல், as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it) to a woman without breasts desiring womanhood. 727 compares the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies. Both use a figure of lacking what one's role requires, and they cover the two opposite failures: wanting to speak without learning, and having learning without the nerve to speak. Kalaignar reads 402 differently, as desiring to hear the unlearned man's words.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 715 says the best of all good things is the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு). 715 turns the rule 403 gives the unlearned into a general virtue of the assembly that binds capable speakers too.

403 counts silence before the learned as the unlearned person's merit. 729 says those who have studied and understood yet fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). Silence is therefore not good in itself: it is right for the one with nothing to say and a failing in the one who has something.

404 says that however good an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்) may be, those with understanding do not accept it. 423 says understanding is seeing the true substance of a thing from whoever's mouth it is heard (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). If 404 means the wise set aside what the unlearned say even when it is good, it conflicts with 423's rule to judge the matter and not the speaker; on Parimelazhagar's reading, that they only decline to credit him with real brightness because an occasional hit is accidental, the conflict is smaller.

404 says native brightness without learning is not accepted by the wise. 636 says nothing over-subtle can stand before those who have keen native intelligence together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 636 states positively what 404 implies: natural intelligence gains its force when joined to study.

405 says an unlearned person's standing collapses once he converses. 717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines out (விளங்கும்) among those able to examine words without fault. Conversation with the competent is the test in both, with opposite results for the unlearned and the learned.

405 says the unlearned person's self-regard gives way when he engages and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar supplies that the talk is with a learned person. 1046 says that even when the poor speak of good matters well understood, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The same closing phrase marks two ways speech fails: in 405 for want of learning in the speaker, in 1046 for want of standing with the hearers, though the content is sound.

406 grants the unlearned existence only and compares them to land that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). Both reduce a person lacking a quality to mere existence and express it through land, as barren soil in one and as weight on the ground in the other.

406 says the unlearned are no more than 'they exist' (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are like barren saline ground that yields nothing. 730 says those who, fearing the arena, cannot convey what they have learned are, though they exist, equal to those who do not (உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்). The same bare-existence wording puts the learned who cannot speak in nearly the place of the unlearned.

407 says good looks without understanding are worth what a clay doll's are. 667 says not to scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), since the great chariot has its small linchpin. Both deny that appearance measures a person, 407 for the handsome and empty, 667 for the slight and capable.

407 compares the good looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding to a well-decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 1020 compares the movements of those with no shame within to a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) made to seem alive by its string. Both use a doll for a human form missing its inner part, understanding in one and shame in the other.

408 says wealth is worse than poverty when it sits with the unlearned (வறுமையின் இன்னாதே). 558 says having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை) under a ruler who does no justice. Both invert the usual ranking of wealth over poverty under a stated condition: the holder's lack of learning in one, the king's injustice in the other.

408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good. 837 shows what happens when a fool gets great wealth: strangers feast and his own people go hungry. 837 gives one concrete form of the harm; Manakkudavar likewise reads 408 as harm done to others.

409 says the unlearned, though born high, do not have the worth (பாடு) of the learned born low. 133 says having conduct is good family, and lapse from it becomes low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Both make birth give way to something acquired, learning in 409 and conduct in 133.

410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). 420 calls those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear மாக்கள், and asks what it matters whether they die or live. The next chapter carries the comparison on, from those who have not studied to those who do not even listen.

410 makes book-learning the difference between people and beasts. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and that the distinction of human beings is having shame (நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). The two verses give different answers, learning and shame, to what sets humans apart.

410 says the unlearned differ from the learned as beasts from people, though all are human in form. 1071 says the base look exactly like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a likeness the speaker has seen nowhere else. Both deny full human standing to some who have the human shape, for lack of learning in one and for baseness in the other.

412 treats listening as food for the ear (செவிக்குணவு) and lets the stomach have a little (சிறிது) only when that food is absent. 420 turns the same ear-and-mouth pairing into a judgment: for those who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear (செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்), living and dying come to the same. The chapter's ranking of the two appetites starts as a rule for mealtimes and ends as a measure of a life.

412 allows the stomach only a little (சிறிது), and Parimelazhagar explains the word by saying heavy eating multiplies disease and desire. 946, in the chapter on medicine, says well-being stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்) and disease with the heavy eater (கழிபேர் இரையான்). The same restraint at the table is asked for in the name of listening in one verse and in the name of health in the other.

413 makes listeners equal to the oblation-fed (ஆன்றாரோடொப்பர்). 702 says one who knows without doubt what is inside another (அகத்தது உணர்வான்) should be taken as equal to a god (தெய்வத்தோடொப்பக் கொளல்). In both, a human being is ranked with the gods for a faculty of taking in what others carry: their teaching in one, their unspoken thought in the other.

403 says even the unlearned are very good if they can keep from speaking before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 414 addresses the same person (கற்றிலனாயினும்) and tells him to listen (கேட்க). The silence that 403 only recommends as damage control becomes in 414 the means of gaining what he lacks.

415 says the words from the mouth of those with conduct (ஒழுக்கமுடையார் வாய்ச்சொல்) are like a staff where the ground is slippery (இழுக்கல் உடையுழி). 139 says of the same people (ஒழுக்கமுடையவர்க்கு) that speaking evil with the mouth, even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்), is not possible. 139 gives the reason 415 needs: those who do not slip in what they say are the ones whose words can steady someone who is slipping.

415 presents the words of people of conduct as the staff that keeps a person upright on slippery ground. 447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையார்). Both verses locate safety in another person's speech; 447 applies it to a king and makes the helpful words explicitly unwelcome ones.

417 says well-grounded listeners do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும்). 139 says that for those who have conduct, speaking evil even by a slip (வழுக்கியும்) is not possible. The same guarantee, speech that holds even under error, is attached to listening in the Book of Wealth and to conduct in the Book of Virtue.

417 says those whose wide listening rests on their own close inquiry (இழைத்துணர்ந்து ஈண்டிய கேள்வியவர்) do not speak folly even when they have misunderstood (பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார்). 199 says those of stainless vision, free of delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say empty things even in forgetfulness (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லார்). The two verses have the same shape, a kind of person whose speech stays sound even when the mind lapses, and they credit it to different sources: listening in one, clear vision in the other.

418 denies real hearing to ears that listening has not opened. 577 says those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்), and those who have eyes do not lack it. The form of argument is the same, an organ is counted as present only when it is used for its higher purpose, applied to instruction in 418 and to kindness in 577.

95 says being humble and sweet-spoken (பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல்) is a person's ornament, and nothing else is. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to come by without fine listening. 95 holds humble speech up for everyone, and 419 adds a condition: it has to be prepared for by listening.

419 says humble speech is hardly to be had without fine listening. 844 defines வெண்மை, shallowness of understanding, as the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம் என்னும் செருக்கு). The pair links lack of instruction and self-praise from both ends: 419 says the uninstructed will not speak humbly, and 844 says boasting of one's understanding is itself the mark of lacking it.

420 treats those without the ear's taste as people whose death and life are the same. 214 says only one who knows what is fitting truly lives (உயிர்வாழ்வான்), and anyone else is counted among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). The book repeatedly denies real life to those who lack one defining quality; here the quality is listening, and in 214 it is knowing one's duty to others.

406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like saline ground that yields nothing (பயவாக் களர்). 420 says of those who have no taste for what the ear takes in that their dying or living makes no difference (அவியினும் வாழினும் என்). The chapters on not learning and on listening reach the same verdict, a life that merely exists; Manakkudavar reads 420, as Parimelazhagar reads 406, as about being of no use to others.

420 asks what it matters whether they die or live, those மாக்கள் who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for all living beings (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல), and the distinction of மாந்தர் is having shame. Both verses treat eating as what humans share with every creature and put human worth elsewhere, in the ear's taste for one and in shame for the other.

421 names understanding as the tool that guards against ruin (அற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி). 781 asks what guard is as hard for hostile action to get past as friendship (வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு). The Book of Wealth offers two protections that are not walls or weapons, one within the person and one between persons, and praises each in the vocabulary of defence.

24 says one who guards the five with the goad called firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்) is a seed for the highest ground; the goad makes the senses elephants, as Parimelazhagar spells out. 422 gives understanding a similar job, not letting one go where one has gone (சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா), which Parimelazhagar explains with a rider directing a horse. 422 goes a step past 24's holding back: it also sorts good from evil and steers toward the good.

422 says understanding does not let one go wherever the mind has gone, but draws away from evil and directs toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). 787 says friendship removes one from what ruins and sets one on the path (அழிவினவை நீக்கி ஆறுய்த்து). The two verses use the same pair of actions and the same verb of steering (உய்); what understanding does for a person from inside, the friend does from outside.

424 makes it part of understanding to put things so that hearers take them in easily. 650 says those who cannot lay out what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like a cluster of flowers in bloom with no scent. 650 gives the failure case of 424's first half: learning that cannot be conveyed is counted as lacking something essential. The first word of 650 is misprinted in this edition, though the image is clear from the commentary.

424 says understanding sees the fine meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள்); Manakkudavar takes this as seeing what they mean without their spelling it out. 701 praises one who knows what is intended by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 701 carries the second half of 424 one step further, from reading what lies within words to reading what is never put into words.

115 says loss and increase are not absent from life, and that not bending in the heart (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Parimelazhagar records a second reading of 425, in which the opening and closing are expanding in wealth and shrinking in want. On that reading the two verses say the same thing, that a person should stay the same through gain and loss, one under the heading of fairness and the other of understanding.

425 says embracing the world is brightness (உலகம் தழீஇயது ஒட்பம்). 544 uses the same verb twice: the world stands embracing the feet (அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு) of the king who rules embracing his people (குடிதழீஇ). In 544 the embrace is returned, which gives a concrete reason why 425 counts drawing the world close as intelligence. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' in 425 to the high-minded.

425 says understanding is what has neither opening nor closing (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது), which Parimelazhagar reads as steadiness in friendship with the high-minded, unlike a pond flower that opens and shuts. 782 says the friendship of the wise fills like the crescent moon and that of fools shrinks like the moon after full. Both verses judge attachment by a natural cycle; 782 praises the bond that grows, while 425 asks for one that does not swing in either direction.

426 makes accord with the world part of what understanding is. 850 says one who says 'it is not' of what the world says is (உலகத்தார் உண்டென்பது இல்லென்பான்) will be set down as a demon on earth. 850, in the chapter on shallow understanding, extends 426 from conduct to belief and states the cost of breaking with the world's view.

427 makes knowing what is to come the mark of having understanding, as if it were a trait of the person. 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish (பேதைப்படுக்கும் இழவூழ்) and a fate of gain, when it arrives, widens understanding (அறிவகற்றும் ஆகலூழ்). Read with 372, the division in 427 is not fixed: the same person may see ahead or fail to, depending on what fate is at work.

427 defines those with understanding as those who know what is going to be (ஆவதறிவார்). 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 429 gives the use of the foresight that 427 only defines: knowing beforehand matters because it lets one guard beforehand.

427 separates the wise from the unwise by whether they know what will be (ஆவது). 461 tells one to act after weighing what will be lost, what will come of it (ஆவதூஉம்), and the gain that follows later. 461 turns the foresight of 427 into a procedure, a reckoning of outcomes made before acting.

428 makes fear of the right things the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). 1075 says fear is the whole basis of proper behaviour among the base (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Together they show that fear in itself does not separate the wise from the low; what separates them is that the wise fear what deserves it and the base behave only for fear of being punished.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is ahead have no affliction that comes to shake them (அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்). 435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like a straw-heap before fire. They are the positive and negative statements of one rule; 435 stands in the chapter on faults, where Parimelazhagar supplies 'fault' as what comes, while 429 speaks of harm in general.

429 credits freedom from shock to an understanding that guards against what is coming. 442 tells a ruler to cherish and keep those who can remove the trouble that has come and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). 442 shows that the foresight of 429 need not be the ruler's own: it can be secured by choosing the right people.

430 defines having by understanding: the wise have all, and the unwise have nothing whatever they own. 591 uses the same turn for energy of mind: it is what makes someone 'one who has' (உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம்), and those without it do not really have what they have (உடையது உடையரோ). The book redefines possession in the same words for two different inner qualities.

430 says those with understanding have everything, and those without it have nothing whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்). 841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை), and the world does not count other lack as lack. 841, opening the chapter on shallow understanding, restates 430 from the side of poverty.

431 lists செருக்கு first among the faults whose absence gives prosperity its dignity. 180 names a செருக்கு it approves of, 'வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு', the pride of not wanting, which yields victory (விறல் ஈனும்); Parimelazhagar there glosses the word as wealth. Read together they separate arrogance from a pride that consists in refusing to covet.

432 lists 'மாணா உவகை' among a ruler's faults; Parimelazhagar takes it as joy beyond measure. 531 says why such joy is dangerous: the slackness that comes from the elation of great joy (சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு) is worse than excessive anger. 531 supplies the mechanism for the fault 432 only names.

432 calls honour that has passed beyond the fine a fault in a ruler. 1028 says that for one raising his family, idling and minding his மானம் brings ruin (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). Both treat a misplaced sense of honour as a fault, one in the king and one in the head of a house.

433 describes how those ashamed of blame weigh a small fault of their own. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up raised high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து). 957 adds the public side: in a person of standing a small fault is seen large by others too.

433 says the blame-fearing treat a millet-sized fault as palmyra-sized. 965 says even people like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a குன்றி seed. 965 gives the outward fact, that a tiny act does lower the great, which makes the inward magnifying in 433 an accurate estimate and not an exaggeration.

434 says fault itself is the enemy that brings ruin. 304 asks whether there is any other enemy (பகையும் உளவோ பிற) than anger, which kills laughter and joy. 304 applies to one named fault the claim 434 makes of fault in general: the real enemy is inside.

435: the life of one who doesn't guard before it comes (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand (முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான்) will later grieve over his own error. The same failure is given two outcomes, sudden destruction in 435 and late regret in 535.

437: the wealth of one who clings to it without doing what should be done with it (செயற்பால செய்யாது இவறியான்) perishes without lasting. 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who keep what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) don't know the joy of giving. Both assume hoarded wealth is lost anyway; 228 adds what the hoarder missed in the meantime.

437 says wealth perishes when its owner does not do the things that ought to be done (செயற்பால செய்யாது ... கெடும்). 466 says one perishes by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). The miser of 437 is a case of 466's second half: ruin by omission.

437 says the miser's wealth perishes because he does not do what should be done with it; Parimelazhagar lists these as virtue, increase of wealth and enjoyment. 1006 says one who neither uses his wealth himself nor gives to the deserving (தான்துவ்வான் ... ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்) is an ஏதம், a harm, to great wealth. 1006 spells out the two uses left undone and turns the miser himself into the wealth's affliction.

432 lists இவறல் as one of three faults in a ruler, beside excessive honour and excessive joy. 438, on Parimelazhagar's reading, takes it out of any such list as greater than the rest (எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவதொன்று அன்று). Manakkudavar reads 438 differently, as saying miserliness is not to be valued as anything, and on that reading the two verses simply agree.

438 says the miserliness called the clinging heart (பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை) is not to be counted among any others; Parimelazhagar takes this to mean it exceeds all other faults. 1002 names what lies behind it, the delusion (மருள்) that everything comes by wealth, so that one clings without giving (ஈயாது இவறும்), and gives its result as an inglorious birth. 1002 supplies a cause and a consequence for the fault 438 ranks.

439 commands: never admire yourself (வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை). 474 gives the outcome for one who doesn't live in accord with others, doesn't know his measure and admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்): he perishes quickly. Parimelazhagar connects them in his note on 439, saying that self-admiration keeps one from knowing place, time and strength.

439 ends 'நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை', do not desire a deed that yields no good. 652 ends with the same phrase and extends it: one must always avoid a deed that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை). The rule is given in 439 as part of a ruler's guarding against faults and in 652, on Parimelazhagar's reading, as a rule for ministers.

440: if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without the love being known (காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்), his enemies' designs come to nothing. 866, from the enemy's side, says one of blinding anger and excessive desire (கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is an opponent whose enmity is worth having. Together they show the reasoning: a visible passion is an opening for an enemy, which Parimelazhagar states in his note on 440.

441 tells a ruler to choose, after weighing, the friendship of those who know virtue and are mature in understanding (கேண்மை ... தேர்ந்து கொளல்). 795 tells anyone to examine and take the friendship (நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்) of those able to make one weep, to rebuke, and to teach the right way. The same instruction, to select friends for their capacity to guide, is given for the king's advisers and for ordinary friendship.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before it comes will burn like straw. 442 tells the ruler to cherish and take as his own those whose nature is to remove the affliction that has come and to guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும் பெற்றியார்). The foresight 435 demands of the ruler is, in 442, something he obtains through the people he keeps.

442 describes the people a ruler should keep: they remove the trouble that has come and guard in advance against more. 787 describes friendship in similar terms: it removes what leads to ruin (அழிவினவை நீக்கி), sets one on the path, and shares the suffering when ruin comes. The great adviser and the friend are given the same protective work, though 787 adds a sharing of suffering that 442 does not ask of the adviser.

443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things (அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது). 781 asks what is as hard to make as friendship (செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின்), and what guard is as hard for an enemy's work to get past. Both rank a bond with others as the hardest thing to obtain, and 781 adds that it is also the strongest protection, which is what chapter 45 goes on to claim for the great.

444: to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself are one's own is the chief of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 891: not slighting the power of the able is the chief of all the safeguards of those who guard themselves (போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). The two verses use the same ranking formula for the two sides of dealing with the great, winning them as the highest strength and not offending them as the highest protection.

444 places the chief strength in attaching oneself to those greater than oneself; Parimelazhagar adds that this means following their lead. 985 says the strength of those who accomplish things is to bow (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல்). Both locate strength in deference and not in standing alone.

445 tells the ruler to choose his counsellors after deliberation (சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்), since they serve as his eyes. 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after considering a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). Both put the selection of the people one deliberates with before the deliberation itself.

445 says a ruler proceeds with his counsellors as his eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக) and so must choose them with thought. 581 says a ruler should hold spies and the respected treatise as his eyes (மன்னவன் கண்). The king's 'eyes' are advisers in one verse and intelligence plus learning in the other, and in both he sees through something other than himself. This follows Parimelazhagar's reading of 445; Manakkudavar takes its second line differently.

445 says counsellors must be chosen with care because the ruler sees by them. 639 states the cost of choosing badly: a minister at one's side who plots harm (பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரி) is worse than seventy crore enemies. 639 shows what the care in 445 protects against.

446 says enemies can do nothing against one who keeps the company of the worthy. 460 says there is no support greater than good company (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை) and nothing that brings more affliction than bad company. 460 states as a general rule what 446 applies to a ruler facing enemies.

446: against one who can conduct himself as having the worthy for his company (தக்கார் இனத்தனாய்), enemies have nothing left to do. 868 gives the reverse case: one with no good qualities and many faults is without company (இனன் இலன்), and that is a protection to his opponents. Both verses use the word இனம் and both make a ruler's exposure to enemies depend on who stands with him.

447 speaks of the ruler who keeps rebukers. 638 gives the matching duty of the one beside him: even if the king rejects knowledge and knows nothing himself, the one at his side is bound to tell him what is sound (உறுதி உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்). 638 extends the idea to the case where the king is not the willing listener 447 assumes.

447 values supporters for their rebuking (இடிக்கும்) and says a ruler who has them cannot be ruined. 784 defines friendship by the same act: it is not for laughing but for going ahead to rebuke when one oversteps (மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). Rebuke is treated as the purpose of the bond in both statecraft and friendship.

449 says there is no standing (நிலை) for those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its base. The image of a structure that needs a prop is applied to a king in one verse and to a household in the other.

450 says abandoning one's tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than the enmity of many. 800 says to hold close the friendship of the stainless (மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மை) and to be rid of the friendship of the unfit even at a price. 800 gives the same instruction for friendship and adds its other half, which bonds to drop.

450 weighs losing the good against the enmity of many and finds it ten times worse. 816 weighs close friendship with a fool against being a stranger to the wise and finds the second ten million times better (கோடி உறும்). Both rank relationships by a multiplied comparison, and in both the quality of the person outweighs whether the relation is friendly or hostile.

873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொள்பவன்) is more wretched than the mad. 450 uses the same phrase as its measure: letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than that (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). Read together, what 873 treats as an extreme of folly becomes the smaller of two harms in 450.

451 says greatness fears small company (சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை) while smallness takes it for kin. 201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear them but the excellent do (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). In both, what marks the better person is fear of the thing the worse person is at ease with, once about company and once about deeds.

452 says water takes the nature of the land, and understanding the nature of one's company (இனத்தியல்பு). 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால் காட்டும்) and speech shows the family one was born in. Both treat a person as carrying the mark of the ground they stand in, 452 for the company kept and 959 for birth.

452 uses water changing with the nature of the land it meets (நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர் திரிந்து) for understanding taking on the nature of one's company. In 1323 a lover calls the pair those joined as water with earth (நிலத்தொடு நீர் இயைந்தன்னார்), and Parimelazhagar explains that image by water taking on the land's nature. The same picture of water absorbed into soil is a caution about company in one place and a figure of union in the other.

453 says perception comes from the mind, but the word that one is 'such a person' comes from one's company (இன்னான் எனப்படும் சொல் இனத்தான் ஆம்). 505 says the touchstone of greatness and smallness is each person's own deeds (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as that and nothing else. If 453 is read as saying what a person really is, and not only what people call them, the two name different tests of character: company or deeds.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truthfulness (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 455 says purity of mind comes resting on purity of company. The book thus gives inner purity two supports, one's own truthfulness and the people one keeps.

456 says no deed fails to turn out well for those whose company is pure (இனந்தூயார்க்கு இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை), and Parimelazhagar gives the reason: their deeds are thought through with good company. 462 states that mechanism directly: nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி).

457 says goodness of mind gives gain (ஆக்கம்) and goodness of company gives all praise as well (இனநலம் எல்லாப் புகழும் தரும்). 651 has the same two-step form but says goodness of companions gives gain and goodness of action gives all that is wanted (துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம் வேண்டிய எல்லாம் தரும்); Parimelazhagar there reads companions as giving wealth only. Company holds the higher place in 457 and the lower in 651, where one's own action outranks it.

458 says that even for the worthy who have goodness of mind in full, goodness of company is a safeguard (ஏமாப்பு உடைத்து). 448 says a king without the guard of people who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்) perishes even with no one to ruin him. Both use the same word for protection (ஏமம்), and 448 shows what the company protects against: one's own unchecked faults.

243 says those whose hearts are joined to அருள் do not enter the dark world of pain (அருள் சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சினார்க்கு இல்லை இருள் சேர்ந்த இன்னா உலகம் புகல்). 459 agrees that the next world comes from goodness of mind (மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமை) and adds that even this is made secure by goodness of company. The afterlife that 243 rests on the heart alone is given a second support in 459.

460 is built on the form 'nothing beyond X as support, nothing beyond Y as affliction' (நல்லினத்தின் ஊங்கும் துணையில்லை). 32 uses the same form and the same word ஊங்கு for virtue: no gain beyond virtue, no ruin beyond forgetting it (அறத்தினூஉங்கு ஆக்கமும் இல்லை). The pairing shows good company being given, in the book on statecraft, the kind of unqualified ranking the opening chapters give to virtue.

460 says there is no support greater than good company and nothing that afflicts more than bad company (தீயினத்தின் அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்). 450 says letting go the tie with the good is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many (பல்லார் பகை கொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்து). 460 names keeping bad company as the worst harm and 450 names losing good company; both rank these above open enemies, and Parimelazhagar glosses 460's second half as enmity.

461 lists the outcomes to be weighed before acting: loss, gain and later yield. 471, opening the next chapter with the same imperative, lists the strengths to be weighed: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). The second supplies what the first's calculation of gain and loss depends on.

461 tells one to weigh what will be lost, what will be gained and the later yield, and then act (அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ... ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்). 676 has the same closing command and also three items, but different ones: what it takes to finish, the obstacles, and the great yield at completion (முடிவும் இடையூறும் ... படுபயனும் பார்த்துச் செயல்). 461 is an account of cost and return; 676 keeps the return and adds the course of the work itself.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company and thinking it through themselves (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணி). 568 gives the negative case: the fortune of a king who does not think matters through with his circle (இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன்) and then rages will shrink. Both make deliberation with one's இனம் the condition of success, stated once as promise and once as warning.

463 says the wise do not undertake what loses the principal in hope of gain. 932 asks whether gamblers, who get one and lose a hundred (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்), have any way of living well. The gambler is the plain case of the venture 463 rules out, a small gain pursued at the cost of what one already had.

464 says those who fear the harm called disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவிலதனைத் தொடங்கார் ... அஞ்சுபவர்). 172 has the same form: those ashamed of unfairness do not do blameworthy things out of desire for the gain (பழிப்படுவ செய்யார் நடுவன்மை நாணுபவர்). In both a fear or shame is what holds a person back, in 172 from a wrong act and in 464 from an unexamined one.

428 says not fearing what should be feared is folly and fearing it is the work of the knowing (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்). 464 gives one such fear and what it does: fear of disgrace (இளிவென்னும் ஏதப்பாடு) keeps people from beginning what they have not made clear. The general rule of 428 is applied in 464 to the start of an undertaking.

465 says rising without full deliberation (வகையறச் சூழாது எழுதல்) benefits the enemy. 473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on in enthusiasm and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). 473 names one of the things left unconsidered, one's own strength, and shows the cost to oneself where 465 shows the gain to the enemy.

465 says setting out without thinking through every aspect is a way of setting one's enemies in a planting bed (பகைவரைப் பாத்திப் படுப்பது); Parimelazhagar reads this as establishing them in ground where they grow. 718 says speaking before those who understand is like pouring water into the bed of a growing plant (வளர்வதன் பாத்தியுள் நீர் சொரிந்தற்று). The same garden bed stands for fostering growth in both, wanted in 718 and brought on oneself in 465.

465 pictures a rash attack as planting the enemy in a bed where he will grow. 879, in a chapter on enemies, says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, since when hardened it wounds the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க). Both treat the enemy as a plant whose growth is the danger: 879 says to stop it early, 465 warns against tending it by one's own haste.

466 says one is ruined by doing what is not fit to do, and also by not doing what is fit (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானும் கெடும்). 510 says trusting someone unexamined and doubting someone already examined and trusted both bring unending trouble (தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Each verse sets an error of excess beside an error of defect and gives them the same result, once for action and once for trust.

466 says both doing the unfit and leaving the fit undone bring ruin. 672 gives the same two-sided rule for timing: delay what should be done slowly, and do not delay what must be done without delay (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால தூங்கற்க தூங்காது செய்யும் வினை). 672 carries 466's point, that holding back is no safer than acting, into the question of when to act.

467 fixes the order for action: think first, then resolve, and no thinking postponed until after. 509 fixes the same order for trusting people: trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக). In both the examination belongs wholly before the commitment, and the commitment is then not to be reopened.

616 says effort produces fortune and lack of effort brings want (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்). 468 says exertion that is not made by the right way (ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம்) will give way even if many stand guarding it. 468 puts a condition on 616's praise of effort: it has to follow the proper method, and neither strain nor helpers make up for that.

468 says effort without the right method fails whatever support it has (பலர் நின்று போற்றினும் பொத்துப்படும்). 640 says those without practical capacity leave things unfinished even after planning them in proper order (முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர் திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்). The two are complementary failures: effort without method in 468, and method on paper without the ability to carry it out in 640.

469 says doing good can itself be a mistake if the character of the person is not taken into account. 987 asks what worth has achieved if it does not do what is sweet even to those who have done one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்), which makes the recipient's conduct irrelevant. The conflict holds if 469's நன்றாற்றல் is read as doing good in general, as Pope and Kalaignar take it; Parimelazhagar narrows it to a king's use of gifts and soft words toward other kings, and on that reading the two do not meet.

469 says there is error even in doing good when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word, while the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர் கரும்புபோல் கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 is an instance of the difference in character 469 says must be known first: the approach that works on one kind of person does nothing with another.

470 says to think and do what will not be scorned, because the world does not accept what does not accord with oneself (கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு). 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world lack understanding, however much they have studied (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்). Both make the world's acceptance a test that sound judgement has to meet, 470 for a ruler's choice of action and 140 for conduct in general.

470 tells the one who acts to avoid what the world will scorn and not accept. 280 tells the ascetic that neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if he gives up what the world has condemned (உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்); Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' there as the high-minded. The same measure, what the world rejects, governs a king's policy in one verse and a renouncer's conduct in the other.

471 makes comparing strengths the test of whether to act. 250, in the chapter on compassion, uses the same comparison as a brake: when going against those weaker than oneself (தன்னின் மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து), one should think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Being the stronger party permits action in 471, while 250 asks the stronger party to remember what that position feels like from below.

471 tells one to weigh four strengths before acting: of the deed, oneself, the opponent and the allies (வினைவலி, தன்வலி, மாற்றான் வலி, துணைவலி ... தூக்கிச் செயல்). 675 gives a second checklist with the same closing command, five things to think through until the darkness clears: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன் ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). Read together, 471 measures the parties to a contest and 675 adds the circumstances of the act, and only the deed (வினை) is on both lists.

471 says to weigh one's own strength against the opponent's before acting (தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்). 861 states what follows from that weighing when choosing an enemy: avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursue enmity with the weaker (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). 861 is 471's comparison turned into a rule.

472 says nothing fails for those who know what they can do and what must be known and proceed resting in that (ஒல்வது அறிவது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 462 says nothing is out of reach for those who act after examining the matter with chosen company and thinking it over themselves (தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்). The promise is the same in both and the condition differs: knowledge of one's own capacity in 472, counsel and deliberation in 462.

472 promises that nothing fails for one who knows his capacity (ஒல்வது அறிந்து ... செல்லாதது இல்). 483 asks whether anything is hard for one who acts with the means and knows the time (அருவினை என்ப உளவோ கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து செயின்). The chapters on knowing strength and knowing time each make the same claim for their own subject, which suggests each is meant as one necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

594 says gain asks the way and goes to one whose ஊக்கம் does not waver (அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையான் உழை). 473 says many who did not know their own strength set out on ஊக்கம் and broke midway (வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்). The same word names the quality praised in chapter 60 and the cause of failure here, so 473 limits 594: drive pays only when it is matched to a measured strength.

612 warns against letting a task perish in the middle of doing it (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்), because the world gives up on those who leave work unfinished. 473 describes how that happens: people start on enthusiasm without knowing their strength and break midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 612 demands finishing; 473 puts the remedy before the start, in measuring one's strength.

473 says many who did not know their strength broke midway (இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 899 uses the same figure for a king: if those of exalted resolve are angered, even the king breaks midway and loses his kingship (இடைமுரிந்து வேந்தனும் வேந்து கெடும்). Parimelazhagar reads 473 as starting something against those stronger than oneself, and 899 gives one such case, a ruler who misjudges the power of the great.

474 lists three failings that bring quick ruin: not living in accord (அமைந்தாங்கு ஒழுகான்), not knowing one's measure (அளவறியான்) and admiring oneself. 863 lists the traits of one who is easy for an enemy, and two of them match: he does not know (அறியான்) and does not fit in with others (அமைவிலன்). The chapter on what makes a good enemy to have describes, from the other side, the man 474 says will perish.

474 says the one who admires himself (தன்னை வியந்தான்) perishes quickly. 978 uses the same phrase to define smallness: greatness always bows, and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In 978 self-admiration is a mark of character, and in 474 it is a miscalculation of strength with a practical result.

475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if too many are piled on (பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும்). 667 says not to scorn people for their appearance, since there are those who are like the linchpin of a great rolling chariot (உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு அச்சாணி அன்னார்). Both use the axle of a vehicle to say that size misleads: the light thing can break it and the small thing holds it.

475 says a light load breaks the axle when there is too much of it (அப்பண்டம் சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). Parimelazhagar takes the verse as an indirect statement that a strong king who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength when they combine. 873 says this outright: one who, alone, takes on the enmity of many (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்) is more foolish than the mad.

475 says that feathers, light as they are, break an axle when piled too high. 889 says that enmity within, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. Both warn against judging a danger by the smallness of its unit, 475 because small things add up and 889 because of where the small thing sits.

596 says that whatever one thinks of, one should think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்), and that even if this is thwarted it is as if it were not. 476 says that those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and push beyond it (அஃதிறந்து ஊக்கின்) end their lives. 596 sets no ceiling on aspiration, while 476 sets one on action: there is a point past which striving higher is fatal.

476 says pushing on past the tip of the branch (இறந்து ஊக்கின்) ends one's life. 858 uses the same verb of hostility: leaning away from it is gain, and if one pushes on to excel in it (மிகல் ஊக்கின்), ruin pushes on in turn (ஊக்குமாம் கேடு). In both, the drive that the book elsewhere praises becomes the cause of ruin when it is carried past a limit.

477 says to give knowing the measure, for that is the way of guarding wealth while bestowing it (அளவறிந்து ஈக அது பொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி). 943 says to eat knowing the measure once the last meal is digested, for that is the way to carry the body far (அளவறிந்து உண்க அஃது உடம்பு பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). The two verses have the same build, a command to know the measure followed by 'that is the way', applied to wealth in one and the body in the other. Both verses are printed with அறவறிந்து in this edition; the reading அளவு is from Parimelazhagar's gloss.

478 says a small income does no harm if spending does not exceed it. 463 says those with understanding do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain (ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை ஊக்கார்). Both put keeping what one has ahead of getting more: 478 for the regular flow of income and spending, 463 for a single venture.

512 says the work should go to one who widens the sources of income (வாரி பெருக்கி) and increases the yield. 478 says that even if the channel of income is narrow (ஆகாறு அளவிட்டிதாயினும்) there is no ruin, as long as the channel of outgo is not wider (போகாறு அகலாக்கடை). 512 values enlarging income, and 478 adds that safety depends on the relation between the two channels and not on the size of the first.

479 says the life of one who lives without knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) perishes. 947 says that one who eats a great deal without regard to the measure of his digestive fire (தீயளவன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்) gets disease without measure (நோய் அளவின்றிப் படும்). Ignoring a measure brings ruin of wealth in one verse and of health in the other. 479 is printed with a corrupted character in அளவறிந்து in this edition.

218 says those who see what is due do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a time without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்). 480 says ஒப்புரவு that does not weigh the limit of one's means (உளவரை தூக்காத) quickly destroys those means.
