The Book of Virtue praises not letting scarcity stop one's helpfulness, and the Book of Wealth, speaking of a ruler's resources, makes the weighing of means a condition of it.

481 says the crow beats the owl by day (பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை), and Parimelazhagar notes that the owl is the stronger bird. 500 says a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). In both a weaker animal defeats a stronger one through a circumstance, time in 481 and ground in 500, which is how the two adjacent chapters make their cases.

482 pictures fortune (திரு) as something that leaves unless tied, and names timely action as the rope (தீராமை ஆர்க்கும் கயிறு). 617 pictures her as living in the effort of the one without sloth (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்), with her dark elder sister living in sloth. Both treat fortune as a visitor kept by conduct, and they name different conduct: timing in 482, steady effort in 617.

482 says that acting in accord with the season (பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) is the rope that keeps fortune from leaving. 1028 says those who raise their family have no season (குடிசெய்வார்க்கு இல்லை பருவம்), and that idling and thinking of one's dignity ruins it. The two conflict if பருவம் in 1028 means the right moment for action; Parimelazhagar instead takes it there as seasons of heat, rain and cold used as an excuse to put work off, which removes the conflict.

483 names two conditions that make a hard deed possible, means and time (கருவியான் காலம் அறிந்து). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள் கருவி காலம் வினை இடன்). 675 keeps 483's pair and sets it inside a fuller list.

484 says that even if one has the world in mind, it comes to hand when one considers the time and acts by the place (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும் காலம் கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்). 485 reverses the same words: those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, considering the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது ஞாலம் கருதுபவர்). 484 states the condition for acting and 485 its other side, that until the time comes the ambitious do not move.

484 says the world comes to hand if one considers the time and acts by the place (இடத்தாற் செயின்). 497, in the next chapter, uses the same phrase: one needs no support but fearlessness if one thinks everything through and acts by the place (எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்). 484 names place as a second condition beside time, and the following chapter, with 497, takes it up as its own subject.

484 says a king who considers time and place can gain even the world (ஞாலம் கருதினும் கைகூடும்). 610 says a king without sloth gains at once all the expanse crossed by the one who measured with his foot (மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான் தாஅயதெல்லாம்). Both promise the whole earth, one to timing and the other to unremitting effort, so the two chapters make the same claim for different qualities.

485 praises waiting for the right time. 671 says deliberation ends in reaching a resolve, and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (அத்துணிவு தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 671 marks the limit of 485: waiting that is fixed on the time (காலம் கருதி) is part of the plan, and holding back after the decision, for no such reason, is a fault.

485 says those who aim at the world wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது). 672 says to take one's time over what should be done slowly (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால) and not to delay what should be done without delay. Both treat waiting as a decision that fits some tasks, and 672 adds the second half that 485 leaves out.

486 says the holding back of a person of energy is like a fighting ram stepping back in order to charge (பொருதகர் தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து). 827 says not to trust humble words from an enemy, because the bending of a bow means harm (வில்வணக்கம் தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்). Both use a drawing back that comes before a blow: 486 recommends it to oneself, and 827 teaches one to see it in an opponent.

152 says always to bear with an excess done to one, and that forgetting it is better still (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று). 487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but, watching for the time, burn within (காலம் பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). Both hold back the outward response, and they differ on what happens inside: 152 wants the wrong forgotten, 487 wants the anger kept. The conflict holds if both are read as general advice; 152 belongs to the householder's virtues and Parimelazhagar takes 487 as addressed to kings facing enemies.

301 says that the one who truly guards against anger guards it where it can take effect (செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான்); where it cannot, guarding or not makes no difference. 487 has the bright hold back anger now, when showing it would not serve, and keep it inside for the right time. On the reading that 487's anger is to be released when it can succeed, it describes the restraint that 301 says does not count, and withholds the one that does.

151 says that bearing with those who scorn one, as the earth holds up those who dig into it (அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போல), is the highest thing. 488 uses a verb of carrying for the same act, bearing with those who would harm one (சுமக்க), and makes it a means: one bears them until their end comes and their head goes down. The two conflict if both are read as answers to how one should treat those who wrong one, since forbearance is the goal in 151 and a way to the enemy's fall in 488. 151 is addressed to the householder and 488 to a king, which is the other way to read them.

488 says to bear with enemies until their end comes (இறுவரை காணின்). 879 says to cut down a thorn tree while it is young, because once it has hardened it destroys the hand that cuts it (இளைதாக முள்மரம் கொல்க ... காழ்த்த இடத்து). 879 limits 488's patience: waiting serves when time works against the enemy, and not when the enemy is growing stronger.

26 says the great are those who do what is hard to do, and the small are those who cannot (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 489 uses the same phrase and adds a condition of time: hard deeds are to be done at the moment a rare opportunity arrives (செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 26 places the ability in the person; 489 says it also depends on a moment that is itself hard to come by (எய்தற்கரியது).

489 says that when what is hard to get has come, one should at that very point do what is hard to do (இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே செய்தற்கரிய செயல்). 333 says wealth has the nature of not staying, and that on getting it one should at once do what stays (அதுபெற்றால் அற்குப ஆங்கே செயல்). Both reason from something that will not last, an opportunity in 489 and wealth in 333, to acting at once, and 333 turns the king's rule of timing toward lasting good.

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து), and like its strike when the moment is right. 126 says that one who can draw in the five senses like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்) in one birth has protection for seven. Both teach restraint through an animal that draws itself in. The tortoise's withdrawal is the discipline itself, and the heron's is half of a pair that ends in a strike (குத்து).

490 holds up the heron, which stays still until the moment and then strikes, as a model for acting on enemies. 274 says that doing wrong under cover of austerity is like a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds (புதல்மறைந்து வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த்தற்று). The pattern of stillness that hides a coming strike is the same in both. It is recommended to the king waiting for his time, and it is the figure of fraud in one who wears the ascetic's appearance.

464 says those who fear disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவு இலதனைத் தொடங்கார்). 491 gives the same ban on beginning (தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும்) a concrete test: until the place has been seen (இடங்கண்ட பின் அல்லது). Read together, knowing the ground is one specific form of the clarity 464 demands before any start.

Parimelazhagar reads 491's முற்றும் இடம் as a place from which the enemy can be encircled, and tells the king neither to act nor to scorn the foe before finding one. 747 defines a fort from the other side as what cannot be taken even by encircling (முற்றியும் ... பற்றற்கு அரியது). The shared siege verb shows attacker and defender reasoning about the same ground; Manakkudavar instead reads 491 as 'the place where the task can be completed', which would loosen this link.

492 says that even for those with fighting strength (முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பினவர்க்கும்) the advantage of joining a fort (அரண்சேர்ந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) yields many gains. 741 says a fort is of value to those able to go on the offensive (ஆற்றுபவர்க்கும்) as well as to those who guard themselves in fear. Both deny that a fort is only for the weak: the chapter on place and the chapter on forts make the same point about the strong.

861 advises avoiding opposition to the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursuing enmity against the weaker. 493 says the weaker side can still become strong and win when it knows the ground and protects itself. 493 therefore sets a condition under which 861's rule about relative strength does not settle the outcome.

493 says even those without strength win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves (போற்றிச் செயின்). 878 says the enemy's pride dies when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Self-guarding plus knowledge is the common recipe; 878 generalises 493's 'place' to knowing the way of acting.

494 says those who had planned (against you) lose their plan (எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர்) when you advance knowing the place and hold close to it. 440 says the enemies' scheme becomes void (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்) when a ruler enjoys what he loves without letting the love be known. In both, the opponent's design is defeated before any fight by removing what it relied on: bad ground in one case, a known weakness in the other.

495 shows a strong animal losing outside its own element: the crocodile out of water is killed by others. 500 gives the sharper case, where a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). Together they state both halves: one's own ground makes one win, and the wrong ground lets even a much weaker creature win.

496 says chariots with strong wheels do not run on the sea and sea-going ships do not run on land (கடலோடா ... நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து); Manakkudavar takes it to mean that instruments must be made to suit the place. 675 lists means and place together (கருவி ... இடனொடு ஐந்தும்) among the five things to think through before acting. 496 shows why the two items in 675's list cannot be weighed separately: a tool is only a tool in its own medium.

497 says that one who thinks everything through and acts by the place needs no support but fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை): Parimelazhagar explains that forest or hill forts are of no use to a frightened mind. The pair shows the two sides of one claim: place is enough given courage, and place is worthless without it.

497 says no ally is needed (துணைவேண்டா) beyond fearlessness when the plan is complete and the ground right. 875 advises one who has no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்) to make one of the enemies a pleasing ally. 875 shows that the book does not treat being without allies as generally safe; 497's claim holds only under its stated condition of complete planning and the right place.

473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on out of zeal and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 498 says the large army's zeal (ஊக்கம்) is destroyed when it enters the small army's ground. In both, drive that outruns a sober measure, of one's strength in one chapter and of the ground in the other, is what gets broken.

498 says the drive of a commander with a large army is destroyed (உறுபடையான் ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்) if he enters ground suited to a small army. 744 defines a fort as having little to guard and much room, and as destroying the drive of the foe who comes against it (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்பது அரண்). The shared phrase shows that a fort is the built form of 498's principle: ground chosen so that numbers stop counting.

495 gives the image: the crocodile wins in its own deep water. 499 states the human case without an image: even people with no fortress and no great standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to engage on the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 applies the crocodile's lesson to an invader's estimate of a weak-looking people.

501 names four tests, virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life (அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம்), by which a person is examined before being trusted (தேறப்படும்). 513 names four qualities, love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire, in whoever has which trust lies (நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு). The first four are trials applied from outside (Parimelazhagar describes staged temptations); the second four are the traits such trials are meant to find.

501's fourth test is fear for one's life (உயிரச்சம்). 690 defines the envoy as one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short in securing his lord's good. The envoy chapter shows what passing that fourth test looks like in service.

502 makes birth in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து) a ground for trust alongside freedom from fault. 133 says having good conduct is itself good birth, and a lapse in conduct becomes low birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). On 133's definition, 502's first criterion cannot be checked apart from its second: family does not vouch for a person whose conduct fails.

502 places trust in one born of good family, free of faults, with a shame that recoils from blemish (குடிப்பிறந்து ... வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). 794 says the friendship of one born of good family who is ashamed of blame on himself (குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவானை) should be had even at a price. The same two criteria, birth and shame, are used to choose a king's officer and to choose a friend.

502 lists good family first and shame last among the grounds for trust. 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature (இயல்பாகச் செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு) only in those born to a good house. 951 supplies the reasoning 502 leaves unstated: family is asked for because it is taken to be where shame comes naturally.

503 says hard learning and freedom from fault still leave some ignorance when one looks closely. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own inherent understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). Both set a limit on what study can change in a person, one in the chapter on choosing officers and one in the chapter on fate.

503 observes that even in those who have learned hard things and are free of fault, it is rare on examination to find no blankness (இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு). 504 gives the rule that follows: examine the qualities and the faults and judge by what predominates (மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்). Parimelazhagar on 504 makes the bridge explicit, saying no one in the world has only qualities or only faults.

504 tells the king to examine a person's qualities and faults (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி) and take whichever predominates. 793 tells one to know a person's qualities, family, faults and kin (குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் ... இனனும்) before forming a friendship. The same inventory is used in both domains, but only 504 says how to decide when the inventory is mixed.

504 lets the predominant side decide what a person is. 965 says even those like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). 965 names a kind of fault, the degrading act, that is not outweighed by the mass of a person's merits, which limits the simple weighing of 504.

505 says a person's own deeds are the touchstone (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்) of greatness and smallness. 986 asks what the touchstone of worth is (சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின்) and answers: accepting defeat even from those not one's equal. Both use the assayer's stone for testing people; 505 names the general test, deeds, and 986 picks one particular deed as the decisive one.

506 treats having no attachment (பற்றிலர்) as a reason not to trust a person, since such a one does not fear blame. 350 tells the renouncer to hold to the one without attachment (பற்றற்றான்) in order to let attachment go. The same word is a disqualification in the chapter on choosing officers and the goal in the chapter on renunciation; the contexts differ, so this is a contrast of valuation across the books and not a contradiction.

502 puts trust in one who has a shame that recoils from blemish (நாணுடையான்). 506 warns against trusting those who are cut off (அற்றார்), because they have no attachment and are not ashamed of blame (பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி); Parimelazhagar takes அற்றார் as those without kin, Manakkudavar as those without conduct. The two verses are the positive and negative of one criterion, and 506 adds a cause: shame depends on having ties.

507 says trusting the ignorant with affection as the ground (காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்) yields every kind of folly. 515 says work is not to be assigned to someone because he is dear (சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற்றன்று), only to one who knows, endures and can do it. Both exclude affection as a ground of appointment, one at the stage of trust and the other at the stage of assigning work.

507 warns that trusting those without understanding out of fondness brings all folly on the one who trusts. 836 describes the result from the other side: when a fool who does not know how takes up a task (கையறியாப் பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்), it fails and he ends in fetters. 836 shows the outcome that 507's warning anticipates.

508 and 510 share their closing line (தீரா இடும்பை தரும்) and their first fault, trusting without examining. 510 adds a second fault of equal weight: doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Read after 508, 510 shows that the chapter's warning is not simply 'trust less': misplaced doubt is punished in the same words as misplaced trust.

508: one who trusts an outsider without examining (தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான்) gets trouble that does not end, extending to his descendants (வழிமுறை தீரா இடும்பை). 792: the friendship of one who does not inquire again and again ends in a grief that kills him (கடைமுறை தான்சாம் துயரம்). The same structure, unexamined acceptance followed by lasting harm, is stated for a king's officer and for a friend.

509 says trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்). 518 says that after examining a person's fitness for the work (வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை), make him fully entitled to it (அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்). 518 turns 509's second half into an act: the trust that follows examination is shown by handing over real authority.

509 says that once a person has been examined, what is to be trusted should be trusted. 588 says even what a spy has found and brought back should be checked through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்). For intelligence reports the book keeps verifying after the agent is chosen, which bears on 509's phrase தேறும் பொருள்: Manakkudavar reads it as the matters in which the person is reliable, not everything.

509 orders examination first and commitment after. 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, because for those who keep friendship there is no letting go once it is made (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). Friendship follows the same sequence as appointment, and 791 states the reason the order matters: the commitment is hard to reverse.

510 says doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to his work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). Both make the ruler's unfounded suspicion of a proven servant a cause of his own loss.

510 speaks to the ruler: doubt of one already trusted brings trouble that does not end. 693 speaks to the courtier: guard against grave faults, because once suspicion has arisen it is hard for anyone to clear it (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The two verses describe the same event, a ruler's suspicion, as lasting damage from each side of the relationship.

511 says the man to employ is one whose nature, having looked into good and bad (நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி), has taken to the good (நலம்புரிந்த தன்மையான்). 422 defines understanding as not letting the mind go wherever it goes but turning it from bad to good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). The test for a king's officer is the book's general definition of அறிவு applied to a person at work.

504 tells the king to examine a man's qualities and faults and judge by what predominates (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி ... மிகைநாடி). 511 uses the same verb நாடி, but now it is the candidate who examines good and bad and settles on the good. The king's weighing of the man in chapter 51 becomes, in chapter 52, a check on how the man himself weighs.

513 places trust in one who has love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire (அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை). 682 opens with the same pair, அன்பறிவு, and adds considered eloquence as the three things an envoy cannot lack. The two lists share a core of loyalty and knowledge and then differ by office: the officer handling affairs needs steadiness and no greed, the envoy needs speech.

505 makes each person's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness (தத்தம் கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்). 514 says tests of every kind before the appointment still leave many who change once in the work. Both put the decisive evidence in action, and 514 adds that the action that counts is the work itself, after trust has been given.

510 says that doubting a man one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 514 says that even when tested in every way (எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்), many people turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). Read together, 514 limits 510: testing does not settle the matter, so the ban on doubt cannot mean a ban on watching how the man changes in office.

514 observes that many who passed every test turn different through the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்). 520 tells the king to look into the one doing the work every day (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). The chapter's closing instruction answers the problem 514 raises: since office changes people, examination has to continue after appointment.

515 requires for a task one who knows and endures and can carry it through (அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு). 640 says that those without practical ability (திறப்பாடு இலாதவர்), though they plan in proper order, do things that never reach completion. 640 shows what 515's last requirement guards against: knowing is not enough without the capacity to finish.

516 asks the king to examine the doer, examine the deed, and act seeing how they fit the time (செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 675 lists five things to think through before acting: resources, means, time, the deed and the place (பொருள்கருவி காலம் வினையிடனொடு ஐந்தும்). Deed and time are in both lists; 516 adds the one item 675 lacks, the person who will do it, which is the concern of a chapter on employing people.

516: examine the doer, the deed and the fit with the time, then act (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்). 949: the trained physician acts after considering the measure of the patient, the measure of the illness and the time (உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும் ... கருதிச் செயல்). Both end in செயல் after a three-part assessment of person, matter and time, the same procedure in statecraft and in medicine.

517 says that once the king has reasoned 'this man will finish this by this means', he should leave it with him (அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்). 510 says that doubting one who has been examined and trusted brings endless trouble. Leaving the task with the man is the practical form of 510's rule: examination comes first and is then followed by a real handing over.

517 tells the king to leave the task to the chosen man (அவன்கண் விடல்). 520, in the same chapter, tells the king to look into the one doing the work daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக), because the world stays straight only if he does. The delegation in 517 is therefore not a withdrawal of attention; Parimelazhagar's note on 520 says the checking should be done privately so that the man's standing is not damaged.

519 warns the king against taking amiss the familiarity of a hard-working officer (வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மை). 700, addressed to the courtier, says that familiarity which does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதிப் பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை) brings ruin. The king must tolerate the liberty and the servant must not presume on it; each verse limits the other.

519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to the work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). 808 praises those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளாக் கெழுதகைமை). The duty not to reinterpret a close person's conduct appears in kingship and in friendship; Parimelazhagar reads 519 as the king being turned by the words of those who resent the officer, which is the situation 808 names.

520 says that if the one doing the work does not bend, the world will not bend (கோடாமை கோடாது உலகு). 546 says victory comes from the king's sceptre, provided it does not bend (கோலதூஉங் கோடாதெனின்). கோடாமை, not bending, is the mark of the just sceptre, and 520 applies the same word to the officer, on whose straightness the world's straightness is made to depend.

520: let the king look daily into the one doing his work (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்). 553: the king who does not look daily and do justice loses his land daily (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன் நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்). The same phrase of daily examination is used for officers and for justice, and both tie the state of the land to that routine.

520 requires the king to examine the worker daily. 584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்), then his kin and his enemies. 584 supplies the means by which the daily examination of 520 is carried out.

521: kin keep honouring old ties (பழைமை) even when all is lost. 806: those who keep within the bounds do not give up, even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who have stood with them from of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு). Loyalty to a long tie when fortune is gone is claimed as the mark of kin in one chapter and of true old friends in the other.

521 says that honouring the old tie even when a man's means are gone (பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமை பாராட்டுதல்) is found among kin. 1047 says that one in poverty will be looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). The conflict holds if 1047 is read as Pope reads it, of poverty in general; the verse's own qualifier அறஞ்சாரா, poverty unconnected with virtue, which Parimelazhagar and Subramuniyaswami keep, narrows it and reduces the conflict.

522 says that if a man gets kin whose love does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின்), they give many gains (ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்). 884 says that if hidden enmity of unreformed mind appears, it gives many ills that turn his circle bad (இனமாணா ஏதம் பலவும் தரும்). The two verses have the same shape with opposite content, and Parimelazhagar notes that 'whose love does not lapse' in 522 is said to exclude the inner enmity of chapter 89: kin are an asset only on that condition.

524 says the fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட ஒழுகல்). 837 says that when a fool gets great wealth, strangers eat their fill and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர்). 837 shows the failure of exactly the use 524 names: wealth that does not reach one's own people has missed its purpose.

525 names giving and pleasant speech as what surrounds a man with kin. 526 keeps giving, now great giving (பெருங்கொடை), and replaces pleasant speech with not cherishing anger (பேணான் வெகுளி), and raises the result to a following unmatched on earth. The pair is not a repetition: the second verse moves from a positive manner to the removal of what drives people away.

527 ties gain (ஆக்கம்) to those who, like the crow, call others before eating. 227 says the disease of hunger does not touch one who is habituated to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both hold that sharing food protects the sharer's own fortune, stated in the Book of Virtue as freedom from hunger and here as prosperity.

527 praises the crow for not hiding (கரவா) its food and for calling others to eat. 1035 says those who live by eating what their own hands produce do not beg and give to those who ask without hiding (கரவாது). Not concealing what one has, கரவு being the book's word for the withholder's fault in chapters 106 and 107, is the shared mark of the crow and of the farmer.

528 ends: many will live looking to that (அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்). 542 says the world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி). The phrase 'live looking to' makes the king's conduct something people depend on as they depend on rain; 528 uses it for his recognition of each person's worth.

528 says that if the king looks at people not in common but according to rank (பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்), many will live looking to that. 972 says birth is alike for all, but distinction is not alike, because of the difference in what people do (சிறப்பொவ்வா செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). 972 gives a basis for the differential regard of 528: Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை there as each person's merit, and 972 locates such difference in conduct, not birth.

529 says estranged kin return of themselves once the cause of discord is gone. 530 turns to one who left and has come back for a reason (காரணத்தின் வந்தானை) and tells the king to attend to it and accept him only after reflection (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). The pair separates two kinds of return, one that follows from the king's own correction and one prompted by the returner's interest, and prescribes welcome for the first and caution for the second.

529 says those who were one's own and left will return to kinship when the cause of the discord is absent (அமராமைக் காரணம் இன்றி வரும்). 633 lists among a minister's abilities reuniting those who have parted (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). 529 says how that reunion comes about: the ground of the estrangement has to be removed, which Parimelazhagar takes as a fault on the king's own side.

509 gives the rule: trust no one without examining, then trust (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 530 applies examination to a man who was already one's own, left, and came back for a reason: he is to be received after reflection (எண்ணிக் கொளல்). Leaving resets the earlier trust, so the test of chapter 51 has to be done again.

530 says the king should attend to the reason for which a man who left has come back, wait, and accept him after thinking it over (இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்). 830 says that when an enemy turns friend, one should be friendly in face and withhold the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). Both deal with someone who comes over after having been apart and both withhold immediate trust, but 530 ends in acceptance of the kinsman while 830 ends in letting the former enemy go.

531 states the danger: slackness from the elation of great joy is worse than excessive anger. 539 gives the practice against it: when one grows strong in one's own joy (மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து), call to mind those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக).

532 says heedlessness kills fame (பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை). 601 says the undimmed lamp called family goes out when the grime called sloth creeps over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்). In both, an inner lapse, not an outside enemy, destroys a standing built up over time.

532 uses as its comparison that constant poverty kills understanding (அறிவினை நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). 1046 describes one form of it: even when the poor speak good matter well understood, their words and meaning go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்); Parimelazhagar says nobody listens, so their learning yields nothing. Read together, the 'killing' of understanding in 532 includes its losing all effect in the world.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they possess (என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்). 534 says the heedless have no good (பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு இல்லை), which Parimelazhagar reads as: even with every kind of wealth, they get no benefit from it. The same logic of having without having is applied to lack of understanding in one verse and to lack of vigilance in the other.

534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை). 741 says a fort is of value both to those who march out and to those who, in fear, protect themselves (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள்). The conflict holds if 534's first half is taken as a plain claim about forts and the fearful; Parimelazhagar's readings ease it, since he takes 534 as fear in the mind making a fort useless and 741 as the weaker side prudently taking refuge.

750 says a fort, whatever its excellences, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). 534 says the fearful have no fort and the heedless have no good (நன்கு). Both hold that an outward advantage counts for nothing without the inner quality needed to use it, and both use the fort to say so.

429 gives the positive case: those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) meet no affliction that shakes them. 535 gives the negative: one who did not guard beforehand later grieves over his own fault (தன்பிழை பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்). Together they show foresight treated as part of understanding and its absence as heedlessness.

655 tells one not to do deeds over which one will grieve, saying 'what have I done' (எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க). 535 uses the same verb, இரங்கு, for the grief of one who failed to guard in advance. The pairing shows regret following from omission in 535 as it follows from commission in 655.

536 says nothing equals unfailing vigilance toward everyone at all times (யார்மாட்டும் என்றும்). 582 says it is the king's work to know quickly everything that happens to everyone at all times (எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்). The same universal scope appears in both, and 582 gives the general vigilance of 536 a concrete form in intelligence gathering.

611 says one must not lose heart on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்), since effort gives the greatness needed. 537 says nothing is beyond doing as 'hard' (அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை) when done with unforgetting care. Each denies that difficulty is a reason to give up, and each names its own remedy: effort in 611, sustained attention in 537.

466 says one is ruined by not doing what is fit to do (செய்தக்க செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்). 538 says what has been praised must be carefully done, and those who slight it and do not do it (செய்யாது இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு) have nothing through seven births. 538 takes the omission half of 466 and extends its cost beyond this life.

835 says a fool can make, in one birth, the mire he will sink into for seven (எழுமையும் தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு). 538 says those who neglect what is praised have no good through seven births (எழுமையும் இல்). Both attach a seven-birth consequence to conduct in this life, folly in one and neglect of duty in the other.

250 says: when you move against those weaker than you, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). 539 says: when you grow strong in your own joy, think of those ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). Both prescribe a deliberate act of recollection at the moment of feeling powerful, for the sake of compassion in 250 and of vigilance in 539.

930 asks whether a drinker, when sober and seeing another man drunk (களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்), does not reflect on the slackness of his own drinking (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). 539 tells one elated with joy to reflect (உள்ளுக) on those whom negligence ruined. Both correct an intoxicated state by looking at its effect in other people, and 930's word சோர்வு is the one 531 uses for the slackness of joy.

551 compares the oppressive king to murderers and finds him worse. 552 compares the king who demands wealth to a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over' (வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது). Together the two opening verses of the chapter set the unjust ruler beside common criminals, first the killer and then the robber.

756 names what is the king's wealth: what comes unowned, customs duty, and tribute from enemies (உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும் தன் ஒன்னார்த் தெறுபொருளும்). 552 treats a sceptre-holder's 'asking' (இரவு) of his people as highway robbery; Parimelazhagar notes that the word இரவு marks it as something other than the due tax. 756 shows the lawful sources against which 552's demand is measured.

381 lists the six things a king must have, among them people and resources (படைகுடி கூழ்...). 554 says a king who bends the sceptre and acts without reflection loses resources and people together (கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும்). The two things injustice costs him in 554 are two of the six that make a king in 381.

568 says the fortune of a king who does not think things through with his circle and then rages in anger will shrink (எண்ணாத வேந்தன் ... சிறுகும் திரு). 554 says a king who acts without reflection (சூழாது) and bends the sceptre loses wealth and people. In both, the king's loss is traced to acting without deliberation, shown in anger in 568 and in injustice in 554.

567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 555 says the tears of the afflicted are a tool that wears down wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). Both describe the effect of a king's cruelty as slow abrasion by a tool, using the same verb தேய்க்கும்.

828 says a weapon hides within an enemy's folded hands, and his shed tears are the same (படையொடுங்கும் ... அழுத கண்ணீரும் அனைத்து). 555 calls the tears shed by the afflicted the weapon that wears away wealth (அழுத கண்ணீர் ... படை). Both join the same two words, tears and weapon: in 828 the tears conceal a weapon, and in 555 the tears are the weapon.

563 says a king of cruel sceptre who goes on doing what terrifies will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 556 says kings endure through just rule (மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை) and without it their lustre does not endure. Both tie how long a king lasts to how he rules; Parimelazhagar takes what endures in 556 to be the king's fame.

In 1192 a woman says that the tender care a lover gives the one who loves him (வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி) is like the sky giving rain to those who live by it (வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் பயந்தற்று). 557 says a king's lack of அளி is to living beings what lack of rain is to the earth. The same word அளி and the same rain comparison describe dependence on a ruler in one book and on a beloved in the other.

55 says that when a wife who worships her husband says 'rain', it rains (பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை). 559 says that when a king bends justice, the sky will not rain (ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்). In both, rain responds to a person's keeping or failing the duty of their station, the wife's in the household and the king's in the realm.

239 says land that bears a body without renown declines in its blameless rich yield (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 559 says the sky holds back rain when the king bends justice, and the next verse, 560, uses the same verb for cows' yield (ஆபயன் குன்றும்). In each, nature's yield falls in response to a human moral failing, an individual's in 239 and a ruler's in 559.

19 says that if the sky does not give, giving and austerity will not remain in the wide world (தானம் தவம்இரண்டும் தங்கா). 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, cows' yield declines and the six-occupation men forget their book. In both, religious and learned life depends on a provider, the rain in 19 and the king in 560, and fails when the provider fails.

561 makes the king the one who punishes in proportion (ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து), while 579 calls it the highest quality to show kindly regard and bear with even those whose way is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும் ... பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை). The same root ஒறு sits on opposite sides. Parimelazhagar separates the cases: 561 concerns wrongs done to weaker subjects, 579 wrongs done to the ruler himself, so forbearance is limited to injuries that are the ruler's own to forgive.

562 asks for a light stroke after a stern show (மெல்ல எறிக); Manakkudavar takes this to mean the penalty should fall short of what the offence deserves. 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. The pairing marks where gentleness stops: for those 550 calls கொடியார், the book accepts the severest penalty.

562 tells those who want lasting prosperity to raise the rod sharply but strike gently (கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக). 567 names what happens when the stroke is not gentle: punishment past the bound (கையிகந்த தண்டம்), with harsh words, is a file that wears down the king's strength. 562 gives the practice and 567 the cost of abandoning it; the 'long prosperity' (நெடிதாக்கம்) of one is the 'conquering strength' (அடுமுரண்) eroded in the other.

563 says a cruel-sceptred king who keeps doing what terrifies (வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோலன்) will certainly and quickly perish (ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்). 548 says a king who is not easy of access and does not inquire and do justice will sink and perish of himself (தானே கெடும்). Neither verse needs an enemy to bring the king down: in both the misrule is itself the cause of the fall.

386 says that if a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech, his land is spoken of above others (மீக்கூறும் மன்னன் நிலம்). 564 gives the reverse case: where people say 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன்), the king quickly perishes. Both verses measure a reign by what is said about it.

564 says the king of whom the painful words 'our lord is harsh' (இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல்) are spoken will quickly perish. 555 says the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction are the weapon that wears away wealth (செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை). In both, what destroys the ruler comes from the subjects' suffering, as speech in one verse and as tears in the other.

565 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) of an inaccessible, grim-faced man is as if seen by a demon; Parimelazhagar explains that no one approaches him, so the wealth is of use neither to him nor to others. 1000 says the great wealth (பெருஞ்செல்வம்) gained by one without courtesy (பண்பிலான்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Outside the court the same judgment holds: the holder's manner ruins wealth that is sound in itself.

566 says that if the ruler is harsh of speech and 'eyeless' (கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes at once; Parimelazhagar takes கண் here to stand for கண்ணோட்டம். 577, in the next chapter, states the equation directly: those without kindly regard have no eyes (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர்). The single word in 566 is the idea the following chapter spells out.

567 calls harsh words and excessive punishment a file (அரம்) that wears down (தேய்க்கும்) the king's conquering strength. 888 says a family with enmity inside it wears away (தேயும்) like metal rubbed by a file (அரம்பொருத பொன்போல), its strength ground down. In both the file stands for slow loss of strength from within, by the king's own conduct in one and by a house's own members in the other.

306 says anger, the fire that kills what it touches, burns even the safe raft called one's people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்). 568 shows this at court: the king who neglects his circle (இனம்) and then turns his anger on them (சினத்தாற்றிச் சீறின்) loses his fortune; Parimelazhagar adds that the frightened ministers leave him. The general warning in the book of virtue becomes a specific danger for a ruler.

435 says the life of one who does not guard before a fault arrives (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்) perishes like straw before fire. 569 applies the same logic to war: the king who has not prepared his defence beforehand is overtaken when the battle arrives (செருவந்த போழ்தில்) and perishes. Both place the failure in the time before the danger, not in the moment of it.

569 says a king who has made no defence (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will be seized by fear when war comes and quickly perish. 534 says that for the fearful there is no fort (அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are no use to a frightened mind. One verse says lack of a fort produces fear, the other that fear cancels a fort, so the fort is necessary but not sufficient.

447 asks who can ruin a ruler who keeps as his own those who will rebuke him (இடிக்குந் துணையாரை யாள்வாரை). 570 shows the opposite court: the harsh sceptre gathers the unlearned around it (கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும்), because, as Parimelazhagar says, such a ruler admits only those who will go along with him. The two verses together make a ruler's choice of companions a sign of the kind of rule he runs.

557 says that a king's lack of tender care (அளியின்மை) is to those who live under him what lack of rain is to the earth. 571 states the positive side: the world exists because kindly regard exists; Parimelazhagar reads this of kings. In both verses the ruler's kindness is treated as a condition of life for the people, not as an ornament only.

571 says this world exists because the great beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy, and would otherwise sink into the earth and perish (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்). Both use the same construction, உண்டு உலகு, to say that a human quality and not power keeps the world going; 571 says it in a chapter on kings and 996 of people in general.

983 lists kindly regard (கண்ணோட்டம்) with love, shame, obligingness and truth as the five pillars that hold up worth (சால்பு). 572 gives it a wider load: the conduct of the world rests in it (கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல்). The quality that is one support of personal character in 983 is the support of social life in 572.

572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a burden to the earth (அஃதிலார் உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). 1003 says the very appearance of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown is a burden to the earth (தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை). The phrase is identical, and in both the people called a burden are those who are of no use to others.

79 asks what all the outer limbs can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (புறத்துறுப் பெல்லாம் எவன்செய்யும் ... அன்பிலவர்க்கு). 573 asks the same kind of question of the eye that lacks kindly regard. In both a visible organ is counted useless without the inner quality it should serve.

573 asks what use an eye is without kindly regard (கண்என்னாம் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), as a melody is no use that does not fit the song. 705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read another's sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). Both judge the eye by what it does for another person, kindness in one verse and understanding in the other, and not by sight.

406 says the unlearned can only be said to exist (உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர்) and are otherwise like barren saline land. 574 says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்து) and do nothing more. Both verses grant bare existence and deny any use, of unlearned persons in one case and of unkind eyes in the other.

574 says eyes without kindly regard in due measure (அளவினால் கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்) do nothing but seem to be in the face; Parimelazhagar takes அளவினால் as excluding excessive indulgence. 578 says what the measure is: kindly regard shown without ruining the task (கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்). The one word of limit in 574 becomes the whole subject of 578.

1014 asks whether shame is not an ornament (அணி) to the worthy, and whether without it their proud walk is not a disease (அஃதின்றேல் பிணி). 575 has the same shape: kindly regard is the eye's ornament (அணிகலம்), and without it (அஃதின்றேல்) the eye is a sore (புண்). In both the missing virtue does not leave the thing plain but turns it into an affliction.

393 says those who are called 'people with eyes' are the learned (கண்ணுடையர் என்பவர் கற்றோர்). 577 says those without kindly regard are eyeless and those who have eyes do not lack it (கண்ணுடையார் கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்). The same title, கண்ணுடையார், is awarded on two different tests, learning and kindly regard; the verses do not conflict, but a reader should see that the book defines 'having eyes' twice.

152 says always bear with excess against you (பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even when you are able to punish'. 579 is that case in the ruler, who has the power to punish and is asked to bear with those who harm him. 152 goes a step further than 579 by preferring forgetting the wrong to bearing it.

805 advises that when friends do something painful, one should take it as either folly or great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க). 580 describes people who drink poison they have seen poured. 805 supplies a way of construing a friend's injury that makes the conduct in 580 intelligible, though 580's own stated motive is the wish for நாகரிகம் and not a charitable reading of the giver.

520 tells the king to look daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக) into the one doing his work, since the world stays straight if he does; 582 makes constant, quick knowledge of everyone's affairs the king's own occupation (வேந்தன் தொழில்). Both treat continuous inquiry, not occasional inspection, as the core of rule; 582 widens the object from the king's officers to everyone.

582 makes it the king's work to know quickly, at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும் வல்லறிதல்), all that happens to everyone; 553 says a ruler who does not inquire daily and do justice (நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா) loses his land day by day. 553 gives the purpose and the cost: the daily knowing of 582 exists to feed daily justice, and its absence is paid for in the kingdom itself.

583 denies victory to a ruler who has things spied out but does not discern their meaning (ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா); 423 defines understanding as seeing the true substance of whatever is heard from anyone (அப்பொருள் மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது). The pairing shows the spy chapter applying the general rule about hearsay to intelligence: collecting reports is not yet knowing.

510 says that doubting a person one has examined and trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்) brings unending trouble; 584 has spies examine everyone (அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது), including the king's own officers. The conflict holds if standing surveillance of appointed officers counts as the ஐயுறவு that 510 forbids; if spying is read as routine inquiry and not suspicion of a particular person, the two can stand together.

584 defines the spy as one who examines everyone, beginning with those who do the king's work (வினைசெய்வார்); 514 observes that even people trusted after every test often turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). 514 supplies the reason for watching one's own appointed officers: the testing done before appointment does not settle how they behave afterwards.

584 puts the king's own kin (தம் சுற்றம்) among those a spy examines, alongside his enemies (வேண்டாதார்); 882 says not to fear enemies who are like a sword but to fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). The chapter on internal enmity explains why 584 does not exempt relatives from scrutiny.

585 requires of a spy an unsuspected appearance, not flinching before eyes (கண்ணஞ்சாது) and never letting anything out; 686 requires of an envoy that he not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar glosses in both verses as the angry look of the other side. The open agent and the covert one are given the same nerve; what differs is that the envoy must speak so it goes home, and the spy must give nothing away.

585 ends with the spy's ability never to let anything spill (யாண்டும் உகாஅமை); 689 wants the bearer of a king's message to be a hard man whose mouth does not let slip a damaging word (the edition prints வாய்சேரா; Parimelazhagar reads வாய் சோரா). Both make control of what leaves the mouth under pressure the test of the king's agents abroad.

276 says none are more hard-hearted than those who, unrenounced at heart, live by deceiving in the likeness of renouncers (துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வார்); 586 has the spy take the guise of renouncers (துறந்தார் படிவத்தராகி) to get into places and investigate. The conflict holds if 276 condemns the false ascetic guise as such; Parimelazhagar narrows 276 to cheating donors, and on that reading the spy's disguise in the king's service falls outside it.

695 tells those who serve a king not to listen in on or press after anything when a secret (மறை) is in progress, and to hear it only when he releases it; 587 makes the ability to hear concealed things (மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்றாகி) the definition of a spy. The pairing marks a boundary: prying into secrets is a skill the king directs at others, and a fault when his own attendants turn it on him.

587 defines the spy as able to learn what was concealed and to hold what he has learned without doubt (ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 702 ranks with a god the one who knows without doubt what is within another (ஐயப்படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானை). Both prize certain knowledge of what others hide, one gained by inquiry among informants and the other by reading a person's mind from signs.

587 requires the spy to be free of doubt about what he has learned (அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே); 588 tells the king to check even such a report (தந்த பொருளையும்) through another spy. The spy's certainty is a quality of the source and not a warrant for the king, who is to keep doubting until reports agree.

588 says that even what one spy found and brought should be confirmed through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால்); 589 adds that spies should be run so that one does not know of another, and that what three say in agreement is to be accepted (மூவர் சொற்றொக்க தேறப்படும்). 589 turns the second opinion of 588 into a procedure: sources kept independent, and a threshold of agreement.

509 says to trust no one without examining and, after examining, to trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக); 589 says to run spies unknown to one another and to accept what three say in agreement (தேறப்படும்). Both give the same two-step rule, test first and then commit, 509 for persons and 589 for reports.

440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without others knowing of his love (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' schemes come to nothing; 590 forbids showing favour to a spy where others can know of it. Both treat a ruler's visible attachments and rewards as information that others can use against him.

590 warns that a king who honours a spy so that others know of it (சிறப்பறிய) has himself let the secret out (புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை); 663 says a deed should be done so that it shows only at the end, since showing midway brings lasting trouble (இடைக்கொட்கின்). In both the actor's own conduct, not an enemy's skill, is what exposes the undertaking.

1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்); 591 asks whether those without energy really have what they have. Both separate holding goods from having them, 1005 by the test of use and 591 by the test of the holder's drive.

333 says wealth has the nature of not staying (அற்கா இயல்பிற்று) and concludes that on getting it one should at once do what stays; 592 also says goods do not stay (நில்லாது நீங்கிவிடும்) and concludes that the lasting possession is the inner drive (உள்ளம் உடைமை). Starting from the same fact, the Book of Virtue points to enduring deeds and the Book of Wealth to an inner resource that can make wealth again.

617 says the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்); 594 says prosperity finds its own way to the person of unwavering energy. Both personify fortune as choosing where it lives by the person's exertion, and neither leaves it to chance.

396 says a sand-well yields water as far as it is dug, and understanding as far as one has learned (தொட்டனைத்து... கற்றனைத்து); 595 says a water-flower's stem is as long as the water is deep, and a person's height as great as their inner drive (வெள்ளத்தனைய... உள்ளத்தனையது). Both use a water image and the same 'as much as' construction to state a strict proportion, one for learning and knowledge, the other for drive and stature.

619 says that even if a thing cannot come about because of fate (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), effort pays the wage of the body's strain; 596 says a high aim keeps its worth even when it is thrust aside, which Parimelazhagar takes as being denied by fate. Both hold that what fate withholds in outcome does not cancel the value of the striving or the aim.

774 shows a warrior who has thrown his spear at an elephant pulling out the spear lodged in his own body and laughing; 597 shows the elephant itself holding firm when struck by arrows, as the image of those who do not give way in ruin. In both, a wound taken is the occasion that shows firmness, and the Book of Wealth draws the general rule in 597 that the war chapter acts out in 774.

598 says the person without drive does not attain the pride of generosity; 614 says the beneficence of one without effort comes to nothing, like a sword in the hand of a பேடி. 614 adds what happens when such a person tries anyway: the means are present but the capacity to use them is not.

599 says an elephant, though huge and sharp-tusked, fears when a tiger attacks; 763 says a sea of roaring rats perishes when the cobra merely breathes. Both animal pairs teach that bulk or numbers do not decide a contest against an opponent with spirit, 599 of a person's drive and 763 of an army.

997 says those without human courtesy are like trees even if sharp as a file (மரம்போல்வர்); 600 says those without abundance of drive are trees, differing only in having human form (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). The tree marks the person who lacks what makes one human, but the two verses name different lacks: fellow-feeling in 997, inner drive in 600.

601 calls the family a lamp that does not dwindle (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) which dies when the grime of sloth spreads over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர). 753 calls wealth a lamp that does not fail (பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம்) which goes where its owner intends and cuts the darkness. The same 'X என்னும் ... விளக்கம்' figure is used twice in the Book of Wealth, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as a நந்தா விளக்கு; one lamp is shown dispelling darkness abroad, the other being put out from within.

602 states the negative condition for a family's standing: remove sloth. 1022 states the positive one: the family lengthens (நீளும் குடி) through long work in two things, effort and mature knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்). Read together, absence of sloth is necessary but 1022 adds knowledge beside effort.

602 tells those who want their family to be a family (குடியைக் குடியாக வேண்டுபவர்) to live treating sloth as sloth, or killing it (மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல்). 1028 says those who build the family have no season to wait for, and that if they idle and think of their dignity it is ruined (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). 1028 gives 602's rule its practical form: for the family-builder sloth shows up as waiting for the right time and standing on dignity.

605 treats sloth and its companions as something the ruin-bound choose and desire (காமக் கலன்). 371 says sloth itself arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 371 puts a cause behind what 605 describes as a preference, which matches 605's own word கெடுநீரார், people whose nature is already to perish.

605 lists delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep as the craft that those of a ruin-bound nature desire (கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்). 920 lists double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). Both verses give a short catalogue and tie it to people already marked for ruin, leaving open whether the listed things cause the ruin or are its sign.

605 makes four habits a boat (கலன்) that the ruin-bound love to board; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it as a vessel that drops its passengers mid-sea, though Parimelazhagar notes others read கலன் as an ornament. 1068 makes begging an unsafe boat (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of refusal. In both a way of living is a vessel trusted by the person in it and bound to fail him.

606: even when the holdings of those who own the earth come to them (படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும்), the slothful rarely reach an excellent fruit. 591: what makes one 'a possessor' is energy; do those without it possess even what they possess (உடையது உடையரோ)? Both deny that having things amounts to benefiting from them when the inner quality is missing. Parimelazhagar notes another reading of 606 in which the earth-owners' support, not their wealth, is what comes.

606 says the greatest possessions yield the slothful no excellent fruit (மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது). 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). The two share the 'ஆகியக் கண்ணும் / அமைந்தக் கண்ணும்' concession: resources do not work without the action of those who hold them.

607: the slothful end up hearing words of scorn (எள்ளுஞ் சொல்). 1040: seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing', the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்). Both give idleness the same penalty, being laughed at, once from people and once from the personified earth.

608: if sloth lodges in one of family standing it puts him into slavery to his enemies (அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்). 616: absence of effort puts one into want (இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). The identical closing phrase makes sloth an agent that ushers a person into a condition; the neighbouring chapters thus name two destinations, poverty and subjection, and Parimelazhagar links them in his note on 616, where want leads to destruction by enemies.

604 says that for the slothful the family dies and faults multiply (குற்றம் பெருகும்). 609 says the fault is destroyed (குற்றம் ... கெடும்) once a man changes his sloth. 609 makes 604's decline reversible; Parimelazhagar goes further and takes 609's faults to include ones that arose from other causes.

609: when a man ends the rule of sloth over him (மடியாண்மை மாற்ற), the fault that came into his குடியாண்மை is gone; Parimelazhagar splits the word into family and manhood, Manakkudavar reads it as the management of the family. 1026 says good manhood is making the management of the house one was born in one's own (நல்லாண்மை ... இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1026 supports reading the two terms of 609 together: manhood is measured in the household, and sloth is what unseats it.

610 gives the unslothful king the whole measured world. 606, in the same chapter, says that even when the wealth of earth-owners arrives the slothful get no excellent fruit from it. Together they separate two things: sloth does not only block gaining the world, it also empties the world of value when it is handed over.

611: do not flag saying 'it is hard' (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), for effort will give the greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). 26: those who do what is hard to do are great, those who cannot are small (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 26 defines greatness by hard deeds as if it were a fixed difference between people; 611 says the greatness needed is itself produced by trying.

612: guard against the work failing in the doing, because the world has left those who left the work's need undone (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு), on Parimelazhagar's reading; Manakkudavar takes the second line the other way, that the world does not leave those who finish. 670: whatever other firmness they have, the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action (வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு). Both make the world's regard answer in kind to how a person treats the task.

612 warns against abandoning a task midway (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்). 674 says the remainder of a task, like the remainder of an enmity, burns like the remainder of a fire (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). 674 supplies a reason 612 does not give: the unfinished part is not inert but goes on doing damage.

613 says the standing of a benefactor rests on labour. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their hands produce do not beg and give to those who beg without hiding anything (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்). The farming chapter shows 613's general claim in one occupation: the person who works with his hands is the one in a position to give.

614 says the generosity of a man without effort comes to nothing. 219 says that for a man of good feeling, being poor just is not being able to do the helpful things he would do (செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு). 219 shows the same blocked intention from the inside and without blame, so 614's scorn falls only on the case where the lack of means comes from not working.

615 praises the one who wants the work (வினைவிழைவான்) and not pleasure. 901 says those who desire the wife do not reach the excellent fruit, and that this is the very thing those who desire action do not want (வினைவிழையார் வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது). Both set the desire for action against a desire for enjoyment and use nearly the same word for the man of action.

615 makes the work-loving man a pillar that props his kin (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 1030 states the cost of the absence of the figure 615 praises, with the same verb ஊன்று.

616: effort makes fortune (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்) and lack of effort brings one into want. 371: unflagging effort arises from a fate of gain, and sloth from a fate of loss (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை ... போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 616 makes effort the cause of wealth; 371 makes fate the cause of effort, so on 371's account the causal chain in 616 starts one step earlier and is not in the person's hands.

616 says effort produces fortune. 594 says increase asks the way and goes to the one of unwavering drive (அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையானுழை). Both place the source of prosperity in the person's exertion, and 594 pictures it as prosperity doing the seeking. The first word of 594 is truncated in this edition (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்).

618 separates what is no disgrace (having no luck) from what is (not working). 988 says want is no disgrace to a person who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று). Both refuse to count an outward lack as shame and move the test to something in the person, effort in one and character in the other.

620 ends 'தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்', those who labour without delay, and says they see fate's back. 1024 ends with the same phrase, 'தம்குடியைத் தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்க்கு', and says that for them the outcome arrives by itself without deliberation (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). The same people are described twice, once as defeating an opposing power and once as finding the result come unsought.

621 says to laugh when trouble comes (இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக), since nothing presses it back as well. 774 shows a warrior who, having thrown his spear at an elephant, pulls out the one lodged in his own body and laughs (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்). The battlefield verse acts out the advice of 621: the laugh comes at the moment of injury, and the injury is turned to use.

Both verses turn on the same play of உள்ளம் (mind) and உள்ளுதல் (to think): in 622 a flood of suffering perishes when the wise person thinks with the mind (உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்), and in 309 all one has thought of is gained if one does not think anger in the mind (உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்). Read together they make a single act of thought decide the outcome, once by what is thought and once by what is left unthought.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that arrives to shake them; 622 says that for the person of understanding (அறிவுடையான்) even a flood of suffering already present is ended by thinking. The pair gives understanding two jobs, forestalling trouble and dissolving the trouble that came anyway, which Parimelazhagar takes in 622 to be trouble from fate.

623 says those who do not suffer at suffering (இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படாஅதவர்) make suffering itself suffer; Parimelazhagar places this in the middle of an undertaking. 261 makes bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) half of the form of தவம். The same endurance is a means to finishing work in one book and the definition of austerity in the other.

624 likens the person who pulls through every obstruction to a draught ox (மடுத்தவாயெல்லாம் பகடன்னான்) and says the trouble he meets is itself troubled. 597 says the strong do not give way where things break down (சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார்), like an elephant standing firm under arrows. Both make the same claim through a working or fighting animal; the ox adds forward motion to the elephant's holding of ground.

624 says trouble is troubled by one who hauls on like an ox through every blocked place. 620 carries the claim to its limit: those who labour on without flagging (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்) see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). What 624 says of obstacles in the road, 620 says of the power behind them.

625 says that though troubles come stacked (அடுக்கி வரினும்), those of one who is not undone (அழிவிலான்) are themselves in trouble. 989 says those called the shore of worth do not shift even if the age shifts (ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம் பெயரார்). Both define a person by not moving under pressure, one in the chapter on a king's undertakings and one in the chapter on character.

1045 states as plain fact that within the one suffering called poverty many sufferings arrive and settle (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்), and offers no remedy. 625 addresses exactly such piling up (அடுக்கி வரினும்) and says it fails against one who is not undone. Set side by side, 625's confidence is conditional on the person, while 1045 describes what the stacking is like for those in want.

629 makes freedom from pain depend on not desiring pleasure when it is present (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 4 describes the Lord as one without wanting or not-wanting (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்) and says those who reach his feet never have இடும்பை. The same link between having no pull toward or away from things and having no suffering appears as a divine attribute in Book 1 and as a human discipline here.

629 says one who does not crave pleasure in the midst of pleasure does not suffer in the midst of pain. 115 says loss and increase are both part of life and that not letting the heart bend (நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை) is the ornament of the worthy. Both ask for the same evenness across good and bad turns; 115 treats it as fairness of mind, 629 as protection against pain.

669 says to do with resolve the deed that yields joy even though pain comes thick at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும் ... இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை): pain now, joy later. 630 goes a step further and has the person take the pain itself as joy (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்). Parimelazhagar reads the pain in both as the strain of effort.

630 measures the reward by the enemy: a distinction one's foes desire or esteem (ஒன்னார் விழையும் சிறப்பு). 810 uses the same measure with the same verb: those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them (விழையார் விழையப்படுப). Each verse marks an unusual constancy, under pain or toward friends who have erred, by saying that even the hostile regard it.

641 sets the good of the tongue above every other good. 411 calls the wealth of the ear the wealth among wealths and the head of them all (செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை). The book gives the top place once to listening and once to speaking, in chapters addressed to the learner and to the minister.

The two verses end with the same formula, 'அந்நலம்/பிறநலம் யா/எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று', used in opposite directions. In 641 the goodness of the tongue (நாநலம்) is not contained in any other goodness, which Parimelazhagar takes to mean it exceeds them all; in 982 every goodness other than the goodness of character (குணநலம்) is not counted among goodnesses at all. One chapter ranks eloquence highest for a minister, the other ranks character alone for the worthy.

642 says ruin as well as gain comes from speech and asks for vigilance against slips. 128 gives the scale of the risk: if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல்), the good turns to no good (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). 128 supplies the reason why 642 treats a lapse (சோர்வு), and not only deliberate bad speech, as the danger.

Parimelazhagar reads 643 as speech that binds those who have accepted one as a friend (கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும்) and makes even those who have not want friendship. 187 gives the failure of this skill: those who do not know how to make friends with pleasing talk (நகச்சொல்லி நட்பாடல் தேற்றாதவர்) part even their own kin with divisive talk. On that reading the two verses are the positive and negative of one ability, speech as what holds or breaks alliances.

644 says to speak after knowing the திறன் of those concerned. 469 says that even in doing good there is error when it is done without knowing each person's character (அவரவர் பண்பறிந்து ஆற்றாக்கடை). Both make a good thing, a word or a deed, depend on fitting it to the particular person receiving it.

644 asks for speech fitted to its hearers and says no virtue or gain exceeds it. 696 applies this to a single hearer, the king: know his mood, consider the time, and say what is needed in a way he will want (குறிப்பறிந்து காலம் கருதி ... வேட்பச் சொலல்). The general rule for a minister's speech becomes a specific rule for speech to power.

644 says to speak knowing the திறன், which Parimelazhagar takes as the relative standing of speaker and hearers. 711 gives the method: those who know the stock of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining (அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக). Chapter 72 works out as a practice what 644 states as a principle.

645 says to speak a word only after knowing that no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 467 says to think and then commit to a task, and that saying 'we will think after committing' is a fault (எண்ணித் துணிக). Both put the testing before the irreversible step; 645 applies to an utterance the rule 467 gives for action.

646 pairs speaking well with drawing the benefit from others' words. 724 sets that pair in the assembly of the learned: make what you have learned go home to them (கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி) and take what is more from those who know more (மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்). 724 adds what 646 leaves open, that listening is how the speaker's own knowledge grows.

647 lists three things that make a person hard to beat in a contest: able to speak, free of lapses, unafraid (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்). 686 defines the envoy with nearly the same set: learned, not afraid of hostile eyes (கண் அஞ்சான்), speaking so it goes home, and knowing what fits the time. The envoy chapter puts the general portrait of 647 into the one post where it is tested before an enemy.

647 says no one can easily defeat a fearless, unfaltering speaker in a contest (இகல் வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). 872 gives the advice that follows for the other side: take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow if you must, but not of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர் பகை). Parimelazhagar takes the latter to be ministers, the people 647 describes.

648 says the world listens readily to skilled, pleasing speakers. 1046 says the words of the poor go slack even when they speak good matter that they have understood well (நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் ... சோர்வு படும்). 1046 limits 648: how the world receives speech depends on the speaker's means as well as his skill.

649 treats wanting to say many things as the sign of someone unable to say a few well. 193 says spread-out talk on useless matters (பயனில பாரித்துரைக்கும் உரை) itself announces that the speaker lacks நயன். In both, length of speech is evidence against the speaker; 193 judges his character, 649 his skill.

649 faults many words and praises a few faultless ones; the next verse faults those who cannot expound what they have learned so that others understand (உணர விரித்துரையாதார்). Manakkudavar reads the pair together: speak briefly, but also expand where it is needed. 650 keeps 649 from being taken as a rule of brevity alone.

649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words (மாசற்ற சில சொல்லல் தேற்றாதவர்) long to say many. 685 makes brevity the envoy's first mark: he speaks compactly (தொகச் சொல்லி), drops what is harsh, and speaks so as to please. 685 shows the positive skill whose absence 649 describes.

Both verses use a flower's scent (நாற்றம்) for what is inside a person. In 650 the flower is fully open and gives no scent, like the learned person who cannot convey what he knows; in 1274 the scent is held inside a closed bud, like the unspoken meaning inside the girl's budding smile. The two uses mirror each other: an open display with nothing reaching others, and a closed one whose content the lover already perceives.

651 sets வினைநலம் above துணைநலம்: support gives only ஆக்கம், good action gives all that is wanted. 455 says purity of mind and purity of action (செய்வினை தூய்மை) both come leaning on purity of company (இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்). Read together, the action that 651 ranks above one's support is itself said to depend on the people one keeps.

653 tells those who say 'ஆஅதும்' (we shall rise) to stop doing what dims their ஒளி. 962 says those who want சீர் together with பேராண்மை will not do 'சீரல்ல' even for the sake of சீர். 962 takes the harder case 653 leaves open: the dimming deed may itself be a route to fame, and it is still refused.

653 treats ஒளி as something the ambitious ('ஆஅதும் என்னுமவர்') must protect by refraining from certain deeds. 971 defines ஒளி as 'உள்ள வெறுக்கை', abundance of spirit, and இளி as saying one will live without it. Together they give ஒளி two sides: it is lost by what one does (653) and it consists in what one aspires to (971).

654 says those of unshaken sight do nothing degrading even in distress (இடுக்கண் படினும்). 174 says those of 'புன்மையில் காட்சி' who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'இலம்' (we have nothing). Both verses name a clear-sighted person (காட்சியவர்) and deny that need is an excuse; 174 applies it to coveting, 654 to action generally.

654: clear-sighted people do not do what is degrading even when trouble comes. 218: those of 'கடனறி காட்சி' do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும் ... ஒல்கார்).
