One verse says hardship does not make them do wrong, the other that it does not make them stop doing good; the two are the negative and positive halves of the same steadiness.

655 asks that one not do what will be regretted afterwards. 467 says to think and then resolve (எண்ணித் துணிக), and calls it a lapse to say 'we will think after resolving'. Both put the reflection before the act: 467 as a rule of planning, 655 as a rule about the purity of the deed.

656 forbids the blameworthy deed even when the need is a mother's hunger. 961 says to give up things that would diminish one (குன்ற வருப விடல்) even if they are indispensable (இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்). Both deny that necessity licenses a degrading act; 961 states the principle abstractly under honour, 656 gives it a concrete and painful instance.

656 uses the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள்) as the strongest pull toward wrongdoing for the sake of relief. 1047 says that one in poverty not joined with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும்). The mother marks the limit case in both: 656 holds conduct firm against her need, while 1047 says poverty without virtue loses even her regard.

657: the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) is better than wealth got by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). 408: wealth lodged with the unlearned (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு) is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமை). The same comparison of good people's poverty with bad people's wealth is made from each side, once about how wealth was got and once about who holds it.

657 ranks the utter poverty of the worthy above blame-laden wealth. 988 says poverty (இன்மை) is no disgrace (இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called சால்பு. 988 supplies the ground for 657's ranking: for the சான்றோர் poverty carries no இளிவு, whereas the wealth in 657 carries பழி.

658: forbidden deeds done without shunning them bring anguish even if they succeed (முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்). 113: give up at once gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்). Both concede success in advance and still reject the act, so the objection is not that such means fail.

658 warns that the gain of a forbidden deed turns to பீழை later. 177 says not to want gain that comes by coveting (வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம்), because at the time of enjoying it the fruit is hard to make good (விளைவயின் மாண்டற்கு அரிதாம் பயன்). Both place the harm at the stage of the result and not at the stage of getting.

658 says forbidden actions bring anguish even when they are accomplished. 931 says not to want gambling even if one wins (வென்றிடினும்), since the winnings are like the hook a fish has swallowed. The gambling verse gives an image for 658's claim: the success itself is what carries the harm.

The second half of 659 says what comes from good ways (நற்பாலவை) yields later even if it is lost (இழப்பினும் பிற்பயக்கும்). 112 says the wealth of a person of rectitude (செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கம்) does not decay and is a security for those who come after (எச்சத்திற்கு ஏமாப்பு). Both give rightly got wealth a benefit that outlasts the moment, 659 for the person later and 112 for descendants.

660: wealth made by deceit is water kept in an unfired clay vessel. 1000: great wealth obtained by one without character is good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both use a faulty கலம் for wealth that cannot be kept, but the fault differs: in 660 it is how the wealth was made, in 1000 it is the holder's character.

661: firmness in action is a person's firmness of mind (மனத்திட்பம்); everything else is something other (மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற). 34: being spotless in mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) is all of virtue; the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற). The two verses have the same shape, reducing a whole domain to a state of mind and dismissing the remainder as 'பிற', once for virtue and once for effective action.

661 locates firmness in action in the mind and sets other things aside. 600 says a person's real strength (உரம்) is abundance of spirit (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), and those without it are trees. Both place strength within the person; Parimelazhagar's note on 661 lists the outer things meant by 'மற்றைய' as the firmness of army, fort and allies.

429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming (எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்) have no affliction that comes to shake them. 662 keeps that first rule (ஊறொரால்) but adds a second for when harm arrives anyway (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 662 thus allows that foresight is not always enough; Parimelazhagar reads the second case as a task spoiled by fate.

662 gives two rules as the way of those who have studied the matter: avoid harm (ஊறொரால்) and do not give way once it has come (உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை). 442 tells a king to cherish those who remove the trouble that has come (உற்றநோய் நீக்கி) and guard beforehand against what has not (உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்). The same before-and-after pair appears as the doer's own discipline in 662 and as the quality to look for in advisers in 442.

664: saying is easy for anyone; doing as one has said (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்) is hard. 819: the bond with those whose deed is one thing and word another (வினைவேறு சொல்வேறு பட்டார்) is bitter even in a dream. 664 states the gap between word and deed as a difficulty of execution; 819 judges the same gap in a friend as a fault of character.

666: what one has thought of is obtained as thought, if one is firm. 309: all one has thought of is obtained at once (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்), if one does not think of anger in the heart. The same promise is attached to two different inner conditions, one positive (firmness) and one negative (absence of anger).

667: do not scorn anyone on seeing their form (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை), for there are people like the linchpin (அச்சாணி) of a great rolling chariot. 1032: those who plough are the ஆணி of the world's people, because they bear all who cannot plough and take up other work. Both use the pin that holds the wheel for someone small in appearance on whom everything turns; 667 leaves the person unnamed and 1032 names the farmer. Parimelazhagar supplies the smallness in 667 from the simile.

467 says to think and then resolve on a task, and that saying 'we will think after resolving' is a lapse. 668 takes up from that point: once the task has been seen without confusion (கலங்காது கண்ட), act without wavering (துளங்காது). Together they give a sequence in which doubt belongs before the decision and not after it.

668: in a task one has seen clearly and decided on (கலங்காது கண்ட வினை), act without wavering and without delay (தூக்கங் கடிந்து). 671, opening the next chapter, says deliberation ends in reaching resolve (துணிவு) and it is bad for that resolve to rest in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). The same rule closes the chapter on firmness and opens the chapter on method: once the thinking is done, delay is the fault.

669 says to carry through the worthwhile deed despite the pain it brings at first. 611 says one must not slacken on the thought that a thing is hard (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), since effort gives the greatness needed. Both refuse the difficulty of a task as a reason to hold back; 611 speaks of effort and 669 of resolve (துணிவு).

669: do with resolve the deed that yields joy (இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை), even though pain comes close at first (துன்பம் உறவரினும்). 615: one who does not want pleasure but wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினை விழைவான்) is a pillar who wipes away his kin's துன்பம். Both set இன்பம், துன்பம் and வினை against each other; 669 justifies bearing pain by the joy the deed yields, while 615 describes a doer who is not after pleasure at all and whose work removes others' pain.

670: whatever other firmness they have attained (எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும்), the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action. 750: whatever excellences it has (எனைமாட்சித்து ஆகியக் கண்ணும்), a fort is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண்). The two chapter-closing verses are built alike and make the same point, that other strengths count for nothing without the capacity to act, once of a minister and once of a fort's defenders.

490 says to be like the heron in the season for folding up (கூம்பும் பருவத்து) and like its strike when the moment is right (சீர்த்த இடத்து). 672 gives the same double instruction without the image: take time over what is to be done slowly, and do not delay what must not be delayed. Both hold that waiting and speed are each correct in their place.

671 calls it a fault when a resolved deed lingers in delay (தாழ்ச்சியுள் தங்குதல் தீது). 672 immediately limits this: there are deeds to be done slowly, and over those one should take time (தூங்குக தூங்கிச் செயற்பால); only the deed that must be done without delay must not be slept on. Delay is therefore wrong by the nature of the task, not in itself.

485 says those who have the world in mind wait, unshaken, with their mind on the time (காலம் கருதி இருப்பர்). Manakkudavar reads the second half of 673 in that sense: when the deed is not possible, keep it in mind and act on seeing the place where it becomes possible. Parimelazhagar reads 673 differently, as open force where one is stronger and one of the other three expedients where one is not, so the link holds on Manakkudavar's reading.

462 says nothing is hard to attain for those who act after examining a matter with chosen company (தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு) and thinking it over themselves. 677 narrows whose counsel counts for a particular task: the one who knows that deed from inside (அவ்வினை உள்ளறிவான்), whom Parimelazhagar takes to be someone who has done it before. General consultation in 462 becomes, in 677, learning the mind of the person with experience of the task.

678 says to get one deed done by means of another, as one binds an elephant with a rutting elephant (யானையால் யானையாத் தற்று). Manakkudavar takes this as setting an enemy's own enemy against him. On that reading 875 is the case worked out: one who is alone with two enemies should take one of them as an ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க அவற்றின் ஒன்று). Parimelazhagar reads 678 more generally, as making a task in hand the means to another like it.

875 says that one without allies and facing two enemies should take one of them as a pleasing ally. 679 says that winning over ஒட்டார் is more urgent than favours to friends; Manakkudavar takes ஒட்டார் as one's enemies, Parimelazhagar as those not allied with one's enemy. On either reading both verses treat alliance as something to be made out of the hostile or uncommitted when one is pressed.

488 says to bear with enemies on meeting them (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க), for when their end comes their head will go down; Parimelazhagar glosses சுமக்க as bowing. 680 has the small bow to the great to obtain terms. 488 adds what 680 does not say: that such bowing can be a way of waiting for the stronger side's fall.

861 says to avoid standing against the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). 680 describes what that means for a weak party: those of small domain, fearing the trembling of their own side (உள்நடுங்கல் அஞ்சி), bow to the greater and accept terms if they can get them (குறைபெறின் கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). 861 gives the rule and 680 the settlement that follows from it.

967, on honour, says it is better to be called ruined as one stands than to live by going behind those who are hostile to one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்று வாழ்தலின்). 680 says the small will bow to the great and take what terms they can. The conflict depends on reading 967's ஒட்டார் as covering a stronger enemy; Parimelazhagar limits it to following scorners for a living, but he also remarks on 680 that bowing is not the wish of those with honour, which is why the verse says 'they will accept' as a report of worldly practice.

502 places trust in one born in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து), free of faults and with a shame that recoils from blemish. 681 makes birth in a fit family (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) one of the envoy's three marks. Family is used in both as evidence about a person before he is given a charge, for trust in general in 502 and for the embassy in 681.

681 asks of the envoy 'qualities that kings desire' (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை) without saying what they are. Manakkudavar glosses the phrase as not desiring what the king desires, which is the content of 692 (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை), and Parimelazhagar says this quality is obtained from the following chapter on conduct around kings. 692 therefore supplies, on the commentators' reading, what 681 leaves unstated.

The first line of 681 and of 992 is the same: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். 992 says these two are what is called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); 681 lists them and adds a third, the qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), as the nature of one who carries a message. The envoy's qualification is thus the book's general definition of courtesy with a courtly requirement added.

722 says those who can make what they have learned go home before the learned are called learned among the learned (கற்றாருள் கற்றார்). 683 uses the same construction for the envoy: he must be strong in the treatises among those who know treatises (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன்). Both measure learning by standing among the learned, not against the unlearned.

684 counts presence (உரு) among the three things an envoy needs. 407 says the fine looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-made clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). 407 supplies the limit on 684's உரு: appearance counts only in the union (செறிவு) with understanding and learning that 684 itself demands.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have keen intelligence together with the treatises (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு). 684 requires of the envoy understanding and well-examined learning (அறிவு ... ஆராய்ந்த கல்வி) held together. Parimelazhagar glosses the first term in each verse as natural intelligence and the second as acquired learning, so both verses ask for the two in combination, for the minister and for the envoy.

696 tells one who serves a king to say what is needed and not disliked, in a way that is wanted (வெறுப்பில வேண்டுப வேட்பச் சொலல்). 685 has the envoy remove what offends and speak so as to please (தூவாத நீக்கி நகச்சொல்லி) while securing good for his own side. The same manner of speech is prescribed toward one's own king in 696 and toward a foreign king in 685; in both the pleasing manner serves what has to be said.

724 says to make what one has learned go home before the learned (கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லி). 686 uses the same two terms for the envoy: having learned (கற்று), he speaks so that it goes home (செலச்சொல்லி). In both, learning is complete only when it can be delivered to a demanding audience, the assembly in 724 and a hostile court in 686.

675 says to act after thinking through resources, means, time, deed and place (காலம் ... இடனொடு ... எண்ணிச் செயல்). 687 uses the same terms for speech: consider the time, know the place, think it through and then speak (காலங் கருதி இடனறிந்து எண்ணி உரைப்பான்). The envoy's speech is planned by the same checklist the book gives for any deed.

696 tells the courtier to read the king's mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) before speaking. 687 has the best envoy know what is due, consider the time (காலங் கருதி) and know the place before he speaks. The phrase காலங் கருதி is common to both, so the discipline for speaking to one's own king is the same as for speaking to another's.

712 says those who know how words work should discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), understand well and then speak; Parimelazhagar takes இடை as the receptive moment of the assembly. 687 asks the envoy to consider the time, which Parimelazhagar likewise glosses as the listener's receptive state (செவ்வி). Both make the listener's readiness a condition of speaking.

298 says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth (அகந்தூய்மை வாய்மையால் காணப்படும்). 688 names தூய்மை first among the envoy's marks and then requires வாய்மை along with all three. 298 gives the reason the two words belong together: truthfulness is how inner purity shows.

383 names three things that never leave a ruler: promptness, learning and resolve (தூங்காமை கல்வி துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றும்). 688 has the same frame for the envoy who repeats the king's message: purity, support and resolve, these three (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை இம்மூன்றின்). துணிவுடைமை is the term common to king and envoy; the other two differ with the office.

501 says a man is to be trusted after being tested by virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life. 688 lists the faithful envoy's marks as purity, support, resolve and truthfulness (தூய்மை துணைமை துணிவுடைமை ... வாய்மை). Parimelazhagar explains தூய்மை as being clean in respect of wealth and pleasure and துணிவு as not holding back for fear of harm, which makes 688's qualities the passes of 501's tests.

139 says that for people of good conduct it is not possible to speak evil with the mouth even by a slip (வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்). 689 asks the same of the envoy in his own field: a firmness whose mouth does not let slip a word that brings blemish (வடுமாற்றம் வாய்சோரா). What Book 1 treats as a result of character, 689 makes a condition for carrying the king's word. (This edition prints வாய்சேரா; the commentaries read வாய்சோரா.)

642 says to guard against a lapse in speech (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு) because both gain and ruin come from it. 689 is that rule at the point where the stakes are the king's: the envoy must not let a word that discredits slip from his mouth (வாய்சோரா); Parimelazhagar adds that the slip in question would come from fear for himself. The verb சோர் is shared, and 689 names the hardness (வன்கண்) that prevents the lapse 642 warns of.

638 says that even if the king destroys good counsel and knows nothing himself, the one at his side owes it to him to say what is good for him (உறுதி ... கூறல் கடன்). 690 says the envoy secures the lord's good (உறுதி) even at the cost of his own life. Both use உறுதி for the king's real interest and hold the servant to it under threat, from his own king in 638 and from a foreign one in 690.

723 says those who will die among enemies are easy to find and those who do not fear in an assembly are rare (பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர் அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 690 asks the envoy to face death (இறுதி) while speaking in a hostile court. 723 separates the two kinds of courage and rates the second as rarer; the envoy of 690 needs both together, which indicates how much the verse asks.

778 says warriors who do not fear for their life when battle comes (உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா மறவர்) do not lose their distinction even if their lord is angry. 690 says the envoy is one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short and secures what is good for his lord (இறைவற்கு உறுதி). The envoy's office is given the soldier's standard, with both verses naming the lord (இறைவன்) as the one served.

691 compares the king to a fire one warms at from a measured distance. 896 says one burned by fire may still survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம் உய்யார் பெரியார்ப் பிழைத்தொழுகுவார்). Read together, the fire in 691 understates the danger: 896 ranks the offended great above fire, though Parimelazhagar takes its பெரியார் as those great in austerity, not kings.

691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings (இகல்வேந்தர்) to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor closing in (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). In 1104 a lover asks where she got a fire that burns when he withdraws and is cool when he comes near (நீங்கின் தெறூஉம் குறுகுங்கால் தண்ணென்னும் தீ). The king's fire burns at close range and the lover's reverses that rule, so the court calls for a kept middle distance and the love speech for none.

692 says that not desiring what kings desire (மன்னர் விழைப விழையாமை) brings lasting prosperity through those same kings; Parimelazhagar takes விழைப as the enjoyments, adornment and precedence proper to a king. 179 says Fortune herself comes to the wise who, knowing virtue, do not covet (அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும் ... திரு). Both make not-wanting the route by which wealth arrives, once as court prudence and once as virtue.

693 says those who would guard themselves should guard against the gravest things (போற்றின் அரியவை போற்றல்), which Parimelazhagar reads as faults a king cannot forgive. 891 says not slighting the power of those able to act is the chief of all the guarding done by those who guard themselves (போற்றுவார் போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை). Both use போற்றல் for self-protection and locate its first object in one's dealings with the powerful.

694 says that in the presence of the great one should suppress whispering and shared smiles (செவிச்சொல்லும் சேர்ந்த நகையும் அவித்தொழுகல்). 715 calls the restraint of not speaking first among elders (முதுவருள் முந்து கிளவாச் செறிவு) the best of good things. Court and assembly get the same rule of holding speech back before superiors; 694 extends it to private asides and laughter, which Parimelazhagar says the king would take as aimed at himself.

695 treats the king's secret (மறை) as something to be heard only when he lets it go. 1076 says the base are like a beaten drum because they carry to others the secrets they have heard (தாம் கேட்ட மறை பிறர்க்கு உய்த்துரைக்கலான்). The two give the two ends of handling a secret: restraint in acquiring it in 695, and the failure to hold it in 1076.

696 opens with குறிப்பறிந்து, knowing the king's mood, as the first condition of speaking to him. 701 praises the one who looks and knows what is meant without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்) as an ornament to the earth. The skill 696 names in passing is taken up as the subject of the next chapter, beginning with 701.

697 says to speak what is wanted and never to say what has no use, even if asked (வினையில எஞ்ஞான்றும் கேட்பினும் சொல்லாவிடல்). 200 gives the general rule: say words that have use, do not say words that have none (சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்). The court verse applies the household rule and tightens it, since here even the king's own request does not license useless talk.

698 forbids belittling a king on the grounds of youth or kinship (இளையர் இனமுறையர் என்றிகழார்). 667 says one must not scorn by outward form, since the great rolling chariot depends on its linchpin (உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்). Both reject judging a person by a surface measure, whether age, family relation or size, and point instead to the function he carries.

700 says the familiarity (கெழுதகைமை) that does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதி) brings ruin. 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு). The liberty that defines friendship between equals is thus withdrawn where the other party is a king, as Parimelazhagar reads 700.

700 says intimacy that does what is improper brings ruin (பண்பல்ல செய்யும் கெழுதகைமை கேடு தரும்). 805 says that when friends do something hurtful one should understand it as folly or as great intimacy (பேதைமை ஒன்றோ பெருங்கிழமை என்றுணர்க நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்). The conflict holds on Manakkudavar's gloss of 700, which speaks of the nature of friendship in general; on Parimelazhagar's, 700 concerns a king and the two verses address different relationships.

701 praises the one who knows what is meant by looking, without its being said (கூறாமை நோக்கிக் குறிப்பறிவான்). 1100, in the love chapter that has the same title குறிப்பறிதல், says that when eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use (வாய்ச்சொற்கள் என்ன பயனும் இல). Reading without speech is a minister's rare skill in 701 and the ordinary condition of two lovers in 1100.

703 urges the king to pay any price for those who read signs. 445 says that since counsellors serve as the ruler's eyes (சூழ்வார் கண்ணாக ஒழுகலான்), he must choose them with care. 445 gives the reason behind 703: the king sees through his advisers, so an adviser who can read what is unsaid is worth what Parimelazhagar lists as wealth, land, elephants and horses.

703 says to give whatever it takes from one's resources and secure those who read a sign by a sign (யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 794 says the friendship of one of good family who is ashamed of blame should be had even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு). The shared formula marks the two kinds of person the book thinks worth paying for, the perceptive adviser and the friend with a sense of shame.

704 stops at saying that those who cannot grasp the unspoken are 'different' (வேறு) from those who can. 410 says others stand to those who have studied the shining books as beasts stand to people (விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர்). Parimelazhagar glosses the வேறு of 704 with this very comparison, the idea being that they are animals, so 410 states outright what 704 leaves implied.

704 says those who grasp what is meant without being told and the rest are alike in limbs (உறுப்போ ரனையரால்) and yet different. 993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால்), and true likeness is likeness of character. Both deny that the shared body makes people alike, with perception the dividing line in 704 and பண்பு in 993.

704 says readers of the unspoken and others share the same limbs but are different (வேறு). 1071 says the base look just like people (மக்களே போல்வர் கயவர்), a resemblance the speaker has seen nowhere else. The same figure of outward human likeness hiding an inner difference serves a point about intelligence in 704 and about moral baseness in 1071.

705 says eyes that cannot read another's meaning are of no use. 393 says only the learned have eyes, and the unlearned have two sores in the face (முகத்திரண்டு புண்ணுடையர் கல்லாதவர்). In both the physical eye is treated as worthless without a trained capacity behind it, learning in one and the reading of signs in the other.

705 asks what use eyes are among the limbs if they cannot read a sign by a sign (என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்). 574 asks what eyes without measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face (உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் ... கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்). Each denies the eye its name unless it does more than see, perceiving another's mind in 705 and looking kindly in 574.

706 says the face shows what fills the heart, as crystal shows what is beside it. 959 says the sprout shows what lay in the ground, and the spoken word shows the lineage of the one born in it (நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும்). Both rest on காட்டும்: something visible discloses a hidden source, mood in the face and family in speech.

707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 830 advises that when an enemy turns friend one should befriend with the face and let go in the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்). If the face always runs ahead of the mind, as 707 says, the control 830 recommends should not be possible; the two agree only if 707 describes the unguarded face.

707 says the face is ahead of the person in showing pleasure or anger (தான் முந்துறும்). In 1277 a woman says her bangles knew before she did that her lover had left (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). Both give the body a knowledge that arrives before the mind's own, a general observation in 707 and a lover's remark on her thinning arms in 1277.

708 says that if one has people who look within and understand what has happened, it is enough to stand looking them in the face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). 1100 says that once eyes agree with eyes, spoken words are of no use. Both make speech unnecessary between the right pair; Parimelazhagar adds for 708 that going on to speak would lessen both parties, a concern for dignity the love verse does not have.

710 says the measuring rod (அளக்குங்கோல்) of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye. 796 says ruin has one benefit: it is a rod that measures one's people to full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). The book uses the measuring rod twice for gauging other people, the eye taking a present reading of a mind in 710 and adversity testing loyalty over time in 796.

Both verses end with the identical line சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மையவர். 711 commands such people to know the assembly before speaking; 721 says that, having known the kinds (வகையறிந்து), they do not let their speech slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). The repeated line makes 721 the outcome of 711's instruction: knowing the assembly is what removes the fear that causes slips.

712 asks the speaker in an assembly to discern the opening (இடைதெரிந்து), which Parimelazhagar glosses as the hearers' readiness to listen. 696 asks the same of one speaking to a king: know his mood and consider the time (குறிப்பறிந்து காலங் கருதி) and say it so that it is wanted. The timing rule is the same before an assembly and before a single ruler.

713 says those who take up speaking without knowing the assembly (அவையறியார்) do not know the kinds of speech and have no ability at all. 401 says holding forth in an assembly (கோட்டி கொளல்) without full learning is like playing dice with no marked board. Each names a different missing precondition for speaking in an assembly, knowledge of the hearers in 713 and knowledge of the books in 401, and each treats the speech that results as empty.

714 tells the speaker to change with the audience, bright before the bright and blank before the blank. 425 says understanding is what does not open and close (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது அறிவு). If 425's second half is read generally, as steadiness of bearing, the two disagree about whether the wise adapt their display; on Parimelazhagar's reading, where 425 is about constancy in friendship with the world, the conflict disappears.

714 uses a colour pair for intelligence: be bright (ஒள்ளியர்) before the bright, and take the colour of white plaster (வான்சுதை வண்ணம்) before the blank (வெளியார்). 844 uses the same pair: whiteness (வெண்மை) is the conceit that says 'we have brightness' (ஒண்மை உடையம் யாம்). Read together, the learned person of 714 puts on whiteness knowingly before those who, by 844, are white because they think themselves bright.

715 praises the restraint (செறிவு) of not speaking first among elders. 419 says a mouth that bows (வணங்கிய வாய்) is hard to have for those without fine listening. Both treat modest speech as a mark of what a person has learned, and 419 supplies the source 715 leaves unstated: the habit of listening.

642 gives the general rule: since gain and ruin come from speech, guard against a lapse in it (சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு). 716 applies it to one setting, a slip before the widely learned, and measures the damage by comparing it to falling from the path (ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந்தற்று), which Parimelazhagar reads as a renouncer's lapse from the good path.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those who have taken in wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path. 957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high, like the spot on the moon (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). In both, the weight of a fault depends on where it is seen, the standing of the witnesses in 716 and of the person in 957, and not only on its size.

717 says the learning of those who have studied and understood shines among those able to examine words without fault (சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து). 404 says the wise do not accept an unlearned person's brightness (ஒட்பம்), however good it is. The same expert hearers decide both cases: before them real learning becomes visible and untaught cleverness is not accepted.

719 and 728 share the phrase நல்லவையுள் நன்கு செலச் சொல்லு-. 728 says those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are of no use though they have learned much; 719 tells those who can do so not to speak in a mean assembly even by forgetting (பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க). Together they set the limits: silence in a good assembly is a failure, and silence in a mean one is required.

719 forbids speaking good things in a mean assembly. 849 gives a reason in another chapter: one who shows something to a person who does not see becomes himself unseeing (காணாதான் காட்டுவான் தான்காணான்), while that person goes on seeing as he saw. Parimelazhagar makes the same point on 719, that both assemblies would then look down on the speaker.

720 says holding forth before those not of one's kind is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). 1000 says great wealth in the hands of one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). Both describe a fine liquid ruined by where it lands, and so place the loss in the receiver and not in the thing given.

721 says those who know the body of words and the kinds of assembly do not let their speech slip before the capable (வாய்சோரார்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not slipping out of fear. 647 lists the same qualities, able to speak, without slips, without fear (சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான்), and says such a person is hard for anyone to defeat. 647 states the payoff of the fearlessness that 721 describes.

716 says a slip (இழுக்கு) before those of wide learning is like falling from the path. 721 answers from the next chapter: those who know words and know the assembly do not slip before the capable (வல்லவை வாய்சோரார்). One verse gives the cost of the slip and the other says what prevents it.

722 says those who make what they have learned go home before the learned (கற்ற செலச் சொல்லுவார்) are called learned among the learned. 424 defines understanding with the same verb: saying things so that they go in easily (எண்பொருளவாகச் செலச்சொல்லி) and seeing the subtle meaning in what others say. Both measure learning or understanding by whether it reaches the hearer, not by what the speaker holds.

722 gives the title 'learned among the learned' to those who can convey their learning to the learned. 650 gives the reverse case: those who cannot unfold what they have learned so that others understand (கற்றது உணர விரித்துரையாதார்) are like flowers that bloom in clusters without scent. Together they treat communication as part of learning itself.

723 calls those who die amid enemies எளியர், easy to find. 762 says the hardness that does not fear wounds when the king falters is rare except in an old army (தொல்படைக்கல்லால் அரிது). If 723's first half is read as saying battle courage is common, the two disagree about how rare it is; if 762 is limited to courage in defeat and with reduced numbers, they do not.

723 says those who will die amid enemies are easy to find, and those who do not fear within an assembly are hard to find (அவையகத்து அஞ்சாதவர்). 872 says one may take on the enmity of those who plough with the bow but not of those who plough with the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). Both rank the word above the weapon, 723 by how rare the courage is and 872 by how dangerous the opponent is.

724 joins two acts: convey your learning (செலச்சொல்லி) and take in what those more learned have. 424 joins the same two as its definition of understanding: say things so that they go in (செலச்சொல்லி) and see the subtle meaning in what others say (பிறர்வாய் நுண்பொருள் காண்பது). What 424 calls understanding, 724 presents as what a fearless speaker gains from an assembly.

Both verses open with the command to learn. 391 says learn without flaw and then stand in keeping with it (கற்க கசடற ... நிற்க அதற்குத் தக); 725 says learn with measure so as to give a fearless reply (மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு). 391 gives learning its end in conduct, and 725 gives it a second end in public speech.

725 says to learn by the proper path and with measure (ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க) in order to reply in the assembly without fear; Parimelazhagar takes அளவு as the science of logic. 645 says to speak a word only after knowing no other word can defeat it (வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து). 725 names the training that makes 645's test possible.

726 asks what a sword is to those who are not hard-eyed, and what books are to those who fear a subtle assembly (நுண்ணவை அஞ்சுபவர்க்கு). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை), which Parimelazhagar explains as a fortress being of no use to them. In each, fear cancels an instrument that is sound in itself: sword, books, fort.

726 says books are nothing to one who fears a subtle assembly. 647 says the one who can speak, does not slip and does not fear (அஞ்சான்) is hard for anyone to defeat, and Parimelazhagar takes that fearlessness as fearlessness of the assembly. 647 states positively the condition whose absence 726 says makes learning useless.

728 and 140 have the same form: 'though they have learned much'. In 140, those who have not learned to live in accord with the world are without understanding though they have learned much (பலகற்றும்). In 728, those who cannot speak well in a good assembly are without use though they have learned many things (பல்லவை கற்றும்). Each names a practical ability without which the amount learned does not count.

395 calls the unlearned the lowest (கடையரே கல்லாதவர்). 729 uses the same word to put someone beneath them: those who have studied and understood and still fear an assembly of the good are lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை). 729 thus limits 395's ranking, since learning that is not voiced does not lift a person above the bottom rank and, as Parimelazhagar explains, leaves them with only the labour of having studied.

730 counts those who cannot voice their learning as equal to those who are not, though they exist. 214 says one who knows what is fitting truly lives and anyone else is placed among the dead (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both apply the figure of a living person counted as dead or absent to someone who gives nothing to others, wealth in 214 and learning in 730; Parimelazhagar reads 730's இல்லார் as the dead.

731 sets unfailing yield and worthy people (தக்கார்) side by side as marks of a land. 239 says land that bears a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) declines in its blameless rich produce (வண்பயன் குன்றும்). 239 makes a causal claim where 731 only lists: the land's yield depends on the quality of the people it carries.

731 makes unfailing yield (தள்ளா விளையுள்) one of three things that must come together (சேர்வது) for a land. 545 says rain and yield (பெயலும் விளையுளும்) gather (தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as it should be wielded. Read together, the yield that defines a land in 731 is traced in 545 to just rule.

Parimelazhagar takes விளையுள் in 731 to stand for the cultivators, since the verse lists it beside two kinds of people (தக்கார், செல்வர்). 1032 calls those who plough the linchpin (ஆணி) of the world because they carry all who go off to other work. 1032 gives the reason the cultivators come first in 731's list.

732 says a land yields greatly because ruin is rare there (அருங்கேட்டால் ஆற்ற விளைவது). 15 says rain is what ruins (கெடுப்பதூஉம்) and also what raises up the ruined. Parimelazhagar's list of the கேடு meant in 732 begins with too much rain and no rain, so 15 names the chief source of the ruin that 732 wants to be rare.

732 asks that ruin be rare (அருங்கேடு) so that the land yields abundantly. 736 goes a step further: the foremost land does not know ruin, and its richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 732 states the ordinary standard and 736 the highest one.

733 defines a land as one that bears burdens arriving all at once and still agrees to give the king his whole due (இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது). 552 says that asking (இரவு) by one who stands with the sceptre is like a man standing with a spear saying 'hand it over'. The land's willingness to pay in 733 is not a licence for the king to demand: Manakkudavar reads 733's burdens as levies beyond the fixed due, which is the situation 552 condemns.

In 733 the land bears the load that comes upon it (பொறை ... தாங்கி). In 990 the great earth will not bear its load (தாங்காது ... பொறை) if the worthy decline in worth. The same words describe a land's capacity to carry weight, and 990 makes that capacity depend on the character of its best people.

734 lists what must not reach a land from outside or by nature: hunger, disease and the enemy who destroys (செறுபகை). 735 lists what must not exist inside it: many factions (பல்குழு), the inner enemy that lays waste (உட்பகை) and murderous bands that harass the king. The two verses divide the threats into external and internal.

735 says a land has no murderous bands that harass the king (வேந்தலைக்கும் கொல்குறும்பு). 550 says a king's punishing the cruel with death (கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல்) is like weeding the young crop. 550 gives the ruler's means of producing the condition 735 describes; Parimelazhagar on 735 likewise says these three are to be removed by the king and the inhabitants.

735 requires a land to be without the inner enemy that lays waste (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை). 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவு), holds ruin within it (உள்ளதாங் கேடு). 889 explains why 735 demands its complete absence and not just its reduction.

736 calls foremost the land whose richness does not shrink even where ruin has come (கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா). 955 says an old family does not part from its character even when what it has to give has fallen away (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் ... பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று). Both use the same 'even when' construction to test excellence by what remains after loss, one for a land and one for a family.

737 names a strong fort (வல்லரண்) among the limbs (உறுப்பு) of a land, with its waters and hill. 381 names the fort (அரண்) and the people or land (குடி) as two of the six things a king must have, which Parimelazhagar calls his six limbs (அங்கம்). 737 nests one of the king's limbs inside another, which fits the order of the chapters: land, then fort.

738 lists five ornaments (அணி) of a land: freedom from disease (பிணியின்மை), wealth, yield, happiness and protection (ஏமம்). 734 defines a land by three absences: severe hunger, unceasing disease (ஓவாப் பிணி) and destructive enemies. The two lists match as positive and negative: yield answers hunger, பிணியின்மை answers disease, and ஏமம் answers the enemy, while 738 adds wealth and happiness.

739 says lands are those whose riches come without being sought (நாடா வளத்தன). 594 says prosperity itself asks the way and goes (ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும்) to the person of unwavering drive. Both picture wealth arriving unsought, but 594 makes it the result of the person's energy, where 739 makes it a property of the land.

739 praises land whose riches need no seeking. 1040 says the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்) at those who say 'we have nothing' and sit idle (அசைஇ இருப்பாரை). 1040 limits 739: the land has riches to give, but not to those who do nothing.

740 says a land's excellences bring no benefit (பயமின்று) without accord between it and its king. 558 says that under the sceptre of a king who does not do justice, having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). 558 shows one way the wealth praised in this chapter turns useless or worse under the wrong ruler.

740 says that a land with every excellence is of no use without accord with its king. 770 says that though an army has plenty of steadfast men (நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும்), there is no army where there are no leaders (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). In both, a body that is complete in its own parts is counted as nothing without its head.

741 says a fort matters to those who fear attack and look to their own safety. 569 says a king who has not made his defences (சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்) will, when war comes, be struck with fear and quickly perish (வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்). 569 states the cost of ignoring 741: without a fort prepared beforehand, fear has nowhere to turn.

742 says a fort has clear water (மணிநீர்), open ground, a hill (மலை) and a forest of fine shade. 737 lists as limbs of a land the two waters (இருபுனல்), a well-placed hill (வாய்ந்த மலை), the water that comes from it, and a strong fort. The same features of the terrain, water and hill, are counted first as a land's resources and then as a fort's defences, and 737 already names the fort as part of the land.

743 defines the fort as a wall complete in four measures: height, breadth, strength and difficulty of approach (உயர்வு அகலம் திண்மை அருமை). 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin and an inner fort that enemies cannot destroy (செறுவார்க்கும் உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்). 421 moves the fort inside the person: the quality 743 seeks in masonry, that it cannot be broken into, 421 claims for understanding.

745 says a fort is hard to take, holds stored food (கொண்ட கூழ்த்து) and is easy for those inside to hold their position in (அகத்தார் நிலைக்கு எளிது). 499 says that even people with no good defences or standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to take on in the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 shows that the insiders' advantage of position, which 745 asks the fort to give, already belongs to home ground without walls.

746 wants in a fort good men who help at the place where it would otherwise fall; Parimelazhagar glosses இடத்து as the point of destruction by those outside. 762 says the hardness that does not fear a wound when things give way and the force is reduced (உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண்) is rare except in an ancient army. Both measure fighting men by what they do at the moment of collapse, in the fort and in the field.

746 says a fort has every needed thing and good men who help at the critical place (இடத்துதவும் நல்லாள்). 1030 says a family with no good man to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. The same word நல்லாள் names the person on whom a fort and a family each depend at the moment of danger; goods alone hold up neither.

747 says a fort is hard to seize by encircling, by assault without encircling, or by subversion (அறைப்படுத்தும்), which Parimelazhagar explains as undermining those inside through people they trust. 764 defines an army as one that does not break and cannot be subverted (அறைபோகாதாகி). The same word அறை marks treachery from within as a danger that fort and army must both be proof against, beside open force.

748 says a fort is where those who hold it keep their hold (பற்றாற்றி) and defeat even those strong enough to besiege them; Parimelazhagar notes that the smaller force does not just endure but wins. 493 says even those without strength become strong and win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves. 748 is 493's rule about place applied to the fort.

749 says a fort has its distinction from what is done in action (வினைமுகத்து வீறெய்தி) so that enemies fall at the front of battle. 750 says that whatever excellence a fort has, it is nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). 750 turns 749's praise into a condition; Parimelazhagar says the two verses together show that a fort cannot do without its defenders.

749 places a fort's distinction in the actions by which enemies are brought down as soon as battle is joined (முனைமுகத்து); Parimelazhagar explains these as recognising the attack begun and choosing the acts that defeat it. 767 says an army is one that knows the way to bear the battle coming at it (தலைவந்த போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து) and advances. Both ask for trained response to the enemy's opening move, from the walls and in the field.

750 says a fort's excellences do not exist for those who lack excellence in action. 727 says the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is like a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி amid enemies (பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). In both a good instrument, a fort or learning, is worth nothing in the hands of someone who cannot act when the test comes.

751 treats wealth's power to give standing to persons of no account as its distinction. 241 notes the same fact, that material wealth is found even among the base (பொருட்செல்வம் பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள), and uses it to rank wealth below grace, the 'wealth among wealths'. What 751 counts in wealth's favour, 241 counts against it.

752 reports that all scorn the poor and all honour the rich. 988 says lack is no disgrace to one who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 752 describes how the world behaves; 988 denies that the scorn is deserved where character is present, which Parimelazhagar's gloss on 752 (scorned 'even if they have every good') makes pointed.

752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1046 gives a particular case: even when the poor understand a good matter well and say it, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The general contempt of 752 is shown reaching what a poor person says.

752's 'everyone' (எல்லாரும்) scorns the have-nots. 1047 carries that to the limit case: one in poverty not joined to virtue is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல). The pairing shows how far 'everyone' reaches, with 1047 adding the condition அறஞ்சாரா.

753 says wealth cuts away darkness (இருளறுக்கும்), which Parimelazhagar takes to be enmity. 759 says no steel is sharper than wealth for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). Both use the verb அறு for what wealth does, once as a lamp and once as a blade; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 753 they make the same claim.

754 says wealth that came by knowing the right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 39 says only what comes through virtue is pleasure (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்). 754 fits wealth into 39's rule: wealth produces real pleasure only when it was itself acquired without wrong.

754 limits its promise to wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 659 says what was taken making others weep leaves with weeping, while what came by good ways pays later even if lost (பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பாலவை). Both make the manner of acquisition decide what wealth yields.

755 says a gain of wealth that does not come with grace and love should be let go, not embraced (புல்லார் புரள விடல்). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day even if it brings only good (அன்றே யொழிய விடல்). Both end on the same command, விடல், for gain acquired the wrong way, one naming love and grace as the test and the other fairness.

755 tells one to refuse wealth that comes without grace and love. 1009 says what becomes of such wealth: bright wealth amassed by setting love aside and not looking to virtue (அன்பொரீஇ ... அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய) is taken by others. 1009 supplies a consequence for the wealth 755 rejects.

757 says the child grace, born of love, is reared by the nurse called wealth (பொருளென்னும் செல்வச் செவிலி). 247 sets the two side by side: that world is not for those without grace, as this world is not for those without wealth. Both pair அருள் with பொருள்; 247 keeps them parallel, while 757 makes grace depend on wealth to grow.

757 says grace is raised by wealth. 755, in the same chapter, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாரா) is to be let go. The dependence runs both ways: grace needs wealth, but only wealth that itself came with grace and love.

758 says doing a task with something in one's own hand (தன்கைத்தொன்று உண்டாக) is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, which Parimelazhagar explains as acting without fear or strain. 449 says those without capital have no profit (முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை). Both make resources in hand the precondition of an undertaking; 758 adds the safety they give.

758 praises acting with wealth in hand (கைத்து உண்டாக). 593 says those who hold steady energy as what is in their hand (ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார்) do not grieve that they have lost their gains. The same word கைத்து is used for money in 758 and for drive in 593, which treats energy as the holding that matters when the money is gone.

759 says wealth is sharper than any steel against foes. 546 says it is not the spear that gives victory but the king's sceptre, if it does not bend (வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது). In both the literal weapon is set below something else, wealth in one and just rule in the other.

759 says to make wealth, since no steel is sharper for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). 878 says the pride found in enemies dies (மாயும் பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு) when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Both aim at the enemy's செருக்கு; Parimelazhagar glosses 878's தற்செய்து as enlarging oneself, and 759 names wealth as the means.

759 calls wealth the sharpest steel (எஃகு) against enemies' pride. 985 says bowing is the weapon (படை) by which the worthy turn their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Each names a non-military thing as the real weapon against foes: resources for the ruler, humility for the person of character.

760 makes wealth the route to the other two aims, virtue and pleasure. 31 makes virtue the source of distinction and wealth (சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்). Each verse, speaking from within its own book, puts its own aim first as the one from which the others follow.

760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in full, the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easy to have together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 754 says the wealth that yields virtue and pleasure is wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 754 supplies the condition; Parimelazhagar reads it into 760's ஒண்பொருள் as wealth that comes by the right way.

760 says abundant wealth makes virtue and pleasure easy to get. 1002 calls it a delusion to hoard without giving on the thought that everything comes from wealth (பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும் மருள்), and says it leads to a low birth. 760's claim holds for wealth that is made and used; held back by a miser, the same belief is called delusion.

761 says a conquering army, complete in its parts and unafraid of wounds, is the chief of all a king's wealth (வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 381 lists the six things a king must have and puts the army first (படைகுடி கூழ் ...). The placing in 381's list and the ranking in 761 agree.

761 counts the army as a form of the king's wealth (வெறுக்கை). 759 counts wealth as a weapon, the sharpest steel against foes (எஃகு). The two neighbouring chapters describe each thing in terms of the other: wealth is a weapon and the army is wealth.

762 says steadfastness in defeat is rare except in an old army (தொல்படை). 764 defines an army by courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்), along with not collapsing and not being turned by subversion. 764 makes a requirement of what 762 observes, and both use வன்கண் for the quality.

762 says the hardness that does not fear harm in a time of decline (தொலைவிடத்து) is found only in an old army (தொல்படை). 806 says those who keep to the bounds do not give up, even in decline (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who stood by them of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார்). Both use the same two words to tie loyalty in bad times to length of standing, in an army and in friendship.

762 says only a long-established army stays firm when it is reduced and the king is faltering. 955 says an old family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its nature even when its means of giving have shrunk. In both, age of standing is what keeps character intact under loss.

763 says a crowd of weak enemies is nothing to one strong fighter. 873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்). 763 holds only where the one is a cobra and the many are rats; 873 is the warning for a lone person who assumes that.

764 says an army has courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்). 766 lists the four things that protect an army: valour, honour, walking the excellent path of those before (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு) and தேற்றம். 766 spells out the inherited quality of 764 as following the path of earlier warriors, which is how Parimelazhagar reads வழிச்செலவு.

768 says an army gains stature through its array (படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்) even if it lacks striking power and endurance; Parimelazhagar takes படைத்தகை as splendour of appearance. 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with people who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). They conflict if 768's பாடு is read as real military worth; if it means only repute, 768 is a concession and 750 still stands.

769 names a resentment that will not leave (செல்லாத் துனி) among the things an army must be free of to win; Parimelazhagar says it arises from degrading treatment. 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 567 gives a cause on the king's side for the condition 769 warns of.

769 says an army wins if it is free of dwindling, of resentment that does not leave, and of poverty (வறுமை). 759 says to make wealth because it is the sharpest weapon against foes. Parimelazhagar links them from both sides: under 769 he says desertion and want arise when the king does not pay, and under 759 that making wealth brings a large army.

770 says an army does not exist without leaders. 1030 says a family with no good person to prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. Both make a group's survival depend on a capable person at its head, in the army and in the household.

771 dismisses the enemy by pointing to the many (பலர்) who faced his lord and became stones. 763 asks what it matters if a host of rats roars like the sea, since they perish when the cobra merely breathes (நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்). Both say numbers on the other side count for nothing against one real fighter; Parimelazhagar reads 763 as the hero not fearing a crowd of non-heroes.

771 has a warrior warn enemies not to stand before his lord (என்ஐமுன் நில்லன்மின்), since many who did now stand as memorial stones (கல்நின்றவர்). 894 states the rule behind the warning: for the unable to do harm to the able is like beckoning Death with the hand (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்று). The battlefield taunt and the political maxim give the same counsel, one from the strong side and one addressed to the weak.

771 is a warrior's boast about a might that turns opponents into memorial stones. In 1088 a lover says his பீடு, which even enemies who had not met him feared in battle (ஞாட்பினுள் நண்ணாரும் உட்கும்), has broken before her bright forehead. The Book of Love borrows the same figure of the warrior whose name alone frightens foes, here as a speaker's way of measuring her effect on him.

772 prefers the failed throw at an elephant to the successful shot at a hare, and Manakkudavar takes it with 771 as saying the warrior should send the weak away and fight those who can oppose him. 861 advises the reverse: avoid meeting the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and keep up enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). The conflict holds if 772 is read as a rule for choosing opponents and 861 as Parimelazhagar reads it; it is the warrior's pride against the king's policy. Kalaignar's gloss of 861 turns it into fighting the strong, which would remove the conflict.

773 makes help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; Parimelazhagar illustrates it with the king of Ayodhya telling his disarmed enemy to go and come back tomorrow. 987 asks what use worth (சால்பு) is if one does not do what is sweet even to those who did one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே). The ideal of the worthy person in the chapter on சால்பு appears here as the height of a soldier's manhood.

775 asks whether it is not a rout (ஒட்டு in this edition, which Parimelazhagar glosses as turning the back) for the fierce if the eye glaring at the enemy closes in a blink when a spear is thrown. 686 requires the envoy to be one who does not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the hostile king's angry stare; 585 says the same of the spy. Holding one's gaze under threat is a test in the court as on the field.

775 treats a single blink (இமைப்பின்) before a flung spear as equal to flight. In 1129 the woman says she will not blink because her lover, who lives in her eyes, would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). Both make the refusal to blink a measure of devotion, to valour in one and, in the speaker's conceit, to the beloved in the other.

777 says that for those who want fame that circles the earth and do not want life (வேண்டா உயிரார்), tying on the war-anklet is an adornment. 235 says a ruin that is growth and a death that is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains by the body of fame outliving the body of flesh. 235 gives the reasoning for the warrior's choice in 777.

777 describes warriors who prefer fame (இசை) to life. 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both rank a value above staying alive; in one it is public renown won in battle, in the other an inner restraint.

779 asks who could fault for failure (பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற்பவர்) those who die so as not to break what they vowed (இழைத்தது இகவாமை); Parimelazhagar explains that dying before the vow is accomplished still counts as keeping it. 772 says the spear that missed (பிழைத்த வேல்) the elephant is better to hold than the arrow that hit a hare. Both verses turn on பிழை, a miss, and deny that it is a disgrace when the attempt was great.

781 praises friendship as the best protection. 815 says the poor friendship of small people, which gives no safety even after it is made (செய்து ஏமம் சாரா), is better not had than had. The protection claimed in 781 belongs only to friendship with the right people; made with the wrong ones it guards nothing.

782 contrasts friendships that grow and friendships that wane according to the kind of person. 811 says that with people without character, however ardent they look, it is better for the friendship to shrink than to grow (பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது). The waning that 782 observes in bad friendships is in 811 what one should want for them.

783 says that with people of character (பண்புடையாளர்) the bond grows sweeter with practice. 811 says that with those who lack character (பண்பிலார்), friendship is better shrinking than growing, even if they seem to drink one up with affection. The reward of long practice in 783 depends on பண்பு; without it, more closeness is worse.

784 gives rebuke as friendship's purpose. 795 turns it into a test for choosing friends: examine and take the friendship of those able to speak so that one weeps, to rebuke (இடித்து) and to teach what is proper. What 784 says a friend is for, 795 tells the reader to look for beforehand.

Manakkudavar reads 785 as saying many days of acquaintance are not needed to judge a friendship, because for those of the same understanding (உணர்ச்சி) one meeting gives the claim. 792 says the friendship of one who does not examine again and again (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான்) ends in grief that kills him. On Manakkudavar's reading the two differ on whether friendship can safely be formed quickly; on Parimelazhagar's, 785 only says that feeling, more than contact, is what makes the bond, and there is no conflict.

786 says friendship in which only the face smiles is not friendship (முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று), and that friendship in which the heart within smiles is. 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா). The face and heart contrast that defines true friendship in 786 becomes in 824 the mark of a false friend to be feared.

787 ends with the friend who suffers along in ruin (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பது). 799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when remembered at the hour of death. 799 shows the cost of the failure of the third duty that 787 lists.

In 788 the hand goes at once to the slipping garment (உடுக்கை). In 1023, for one who says he will raise his family, தெய்வம் tucks up its garment (மடிதற்று) and goes ahead of him. Both use a gesture with one's clothing for help that comes unasked and promptly, from a friend in one and from the divine in the other.

789 defines the height of friendship as a firm state of propping the other up (ஊன்றும் நிலை). 449 says those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு) have no standing (நிலை), as those without capital have no profit. 789 describes the supporter and 449 the one who needs supporting, in the chapter on a king's reliance on the great.

789 places friendship's throne in supporting the friend without wavering wherever it is possible (ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை). 818 says to let slip without a word the friendship of those who make difficult a task they could do (ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்றுபவர்). The same word for what lies within one's power sets the standard in 789 and identifies the friend who fails it in 818.

790 says friendship looks shabby (புல்லென்னும்) even when friends dress it up in words (புனையினும்) such as 'they are this to us and we are that to them'. 978 says greatness always bows while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In both, the verbal ornament is the sign of the lesser thing: real friendship, like real greatness, does not advertise itself.

791: inquire first, since after befriending there is no leaving (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 467: think and then resolve on a task, and to say 'we will think after resolving' (துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம்) is a lapse. The same order of thought before an irreversible step is applied to friendship and to action.

791 grounds the need for inquiry on the claim that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 800 tells one to leave the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார், even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக), and Parimelazhagar takes this as the remedy for a friendship taken up unknowingly. If வீடில்லை is read as a flat 'there is no release', the two conflict; if it describes only what a true friend will not do, 800 is the exception the chapter allows.

793 includes a person's இனன், his circle, among the things to learn before befriending him (Parimelazhagar takes it as kin). 453 says that the word 'he is such a one' comes from a person's company (இனத்தானாம் இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்). 453 gives the reason the circle belongs on 793's list: it is where a person's character is read from.

794 picks out as a friend the well-born person who is ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவான்). 951 says that integrity and shame together are found by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை ... செப்பமும் நாணும்). 951 gives the book's reason for 794 pairing birth with shame as the test.

795 says to choose as friends those who can rebuke (இடித்து) and bring one to tears over a wrong. 448 says a king without those who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத) perishes even with no one to ruin him. The rebuker counts as a safeguard both for the private person choosing friends and for the king choosing his support.

797 counts leaving the friendship of fools as gain (ஊதியம்). 450 says that letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Whether breaking a tie is profit or harm depends on who is at the other end of it.

797 says leaving a fool's friendship is gain. 816 says that being a stranger to the wise (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை) is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு); Pope and Subramuniyaswami render ஏதின்மை as enmity. Both verses put a fool's friendship below having no tie at all.

797 calls it gain to give up and leave the friendship of fools (பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). 839 uses the same phrase, பேதையார் கேண்மை, and says it is very sweet because there is no pain in parting from it. Read together, 839 is the ironic version of 797: the one good thing about such a friendship is the leaving of it.

798 says not to take the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்). 106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு துறவற்க). The two prohibitions, கொள்ளற்க and துறவற்க, are complementary: how a friend behaves in trouble decides both whom not to take and whom not to drop.

798 begins: do not think of what makes the spirit shrink (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ). 596 gives the positive form: in all one thinks, think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்). Both treat the direction of one's thoughts as something to be chosen for the sake of the spirit; 798 then sets fair-weather friends beside the shrinking thoughts as things to refuse.

798 uses ஆற்றறுப்பார் for friends who fail one in distress. 814 uses the same expression of the untrained horse that fails its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா) and says solitude is better than such people as one's own. 814 supplies the picture for 798's word: support that holds until the moment it is needed.

799 says the thought of false friends burns the heart (உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). 293 says that after a lie one's own heart burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). In 293 the heart burns for one's own fault, in 799 for another's desertion, so the same inner fire is given two different causes.

799 ends உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்: even to think of the deserter's friendship burns the heart. 1207 ends with the same words in the mouth of the parted woman, for whom even remembering her lover burns. The phrase is used once for betrayal and once for separation in love; in both the pain comes from memory of a bond, not from a present injury.

794 says the friendship of the well-born man who fears blame is worth getting even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 800 says the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார் is worth leaving even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). The chapter uses the figure of payment in both directions, for acquiring a good friend and for getting free of a bad one.

800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at a cost. 818 says how to leave one kind of bad friend, those who make hard work of what they could do: without speaking of it, let the friendship slip (சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்). 818 adds a manner of leaving to 800's instruction to leave.

802 calls it the duty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கடன்) to take a friend's liberties well. 981 says that for those who take on worthiness knowing what is due, all good things are கடன். 802 is one instance of 981's general statement, with the same word கடன்.

803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as though one had done it oneself (செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை). 790 says friendship looks shabby even when friends describe each other as 'they are this to us, we are that to them'. Both deny a separation of 'mine' and 'theirs' between friends: 790 in how they speak of each other, 803 in whose act an act is counted to be.

804 says that when friends act without asking, out of intimacy (கெழுதகையாற் கேளாது), it is welcomed. 788 compares friendship to the hand of a man whose garment slips, removing the distress there and then (ஆங்கே). The hand in 788 does not ask leave before acting; 804 states the same thing from the receiving side, that such unasked action is to be wanted and not resented.

805 says a hurtful act by a friend is to be understood as folly or as great intimacy (பெருங்கிழமை). 109 says that even an injury like killing is cancelled when one thinks of a single good the person did. Both teach a way of reading an injury so that the bond survives it; 109 does it by remembering a past benefit, 805 by a charitable account of the cause.

187 says that those who cannot make friends by pleasant speech will divide even their own people by divisive talk (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 808 describes the friend on whom that does not work, who does not listen to reports of a friend's lapse. 187 gives the talebearer's side and 808 the hearer's refusal.

808 speaks of those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளா); Parimelazhagar takes this as not accepting it even when others report it. 510 says that doubting one who has been trusted after examination (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. Both rule out reopening a settled trust, in friendship and in a king's appointments. The second half of 808 is read in opposite ways by Parimelazhagar (the day of the lapse is a day well spent) and Kalaignar (the days are wasted), so the link rests only on the first half.

791 says that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (வீடில்லை). 809 says the world wants (விழையும் உலகு) those who do not leave (விடாஅர்) the friendship of friends of unbroken long standing. What 791 gives as a reason for caution before befriending, 809 presents as what earns a person general regard.

In 1266 the waiting wife says that when her husband returns she will drink him in (பருகுவன்) so that her pain ends. 811 uses the same verb for friends who look as though they would drink one up (பருகுவார் போலினும்), which Parimelazhagar glosses as from excess of love. The pair shows 'drinking' as the book's figure for consuming affection, sincere in the wife's mouth and only an appearance in the bad friend.

812 treats the friendship of those who leave when the gain ends (அறின் ஒரூஉம்) as a matter of indifference, gained or lost. 799 says that the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when recalled at the hour of death (உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). Read together, losing such a friend is no loss, yet having trusted one is not painless.

Both verses name the ஒப்பிலார். 812 says it makes no difference whether their friendship is had or lost; 800 goes further and says to leave it even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). Parimelazhagar explains the word differently in each place: here as those who fit with no one because they look only to their own gain, there as those who do not accord with the world.

839 says, with irony, that the friendship of fools is very sweet because parting from them brings no pain (பிரிவின்கண் பீழை தருவதொன்றில்). 812 asks what it matters whether one gains or loses (பெறினும் இழப்பினும் என்) the friendship of those who befriend when there is profit and leave when there is none. Both measure a worthless friendship by the same test: its loss costs nothing.

813 sets friends who weigh what will come to them (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) beside 'those who take what they get' (பெறுவது கொள்வார்), whom Parimelazhagar identifies as courtesans, and thieves. 912 describes those women directly: they weigh the profit and then speak of character (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The later chapter spells out the comparison 813 makes in a phrase, with the same verb தூக்கு for the calculating look.

788 defines friendship by the moment of need: like the hand of a man whose garment slips, it removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது). 814 pictures the reverse, a horse that gives way in the battle itself (அமரகத்து). Both locate the test of a friend at the instant of crisis, one by the hand that acts unasked and one by the mount that fails.

106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு). 815 says the friendship of the small, which gives no safety (ஏமம்), is better not obtained at all. The same measure, support in trouble, decides in one verse which friends must be kept and in the other which should never be acquired.

799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin burns the heart even to think of at the time of death (அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும்). 819 says the bond with those whose words and deeds differ is painful even in a dream (கனவினும் இன்னாது). Each verse extends the harm of a false friend beyond ordinary waking life, to the deathbed in one and to sleep in the other.

188 asks what people whose habit is to broadcast even the faults of those close to them (துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும்) would do to strangers. 820 warns against the bond with those who are friendly in private and blame one in public. Both take the public exposure of an intimate as the mark of a person no one should be near.

487 says the bright do not flare up outwardly at once but watch for the time and burn within (காலம்பார்த்து உள்வேர்ப்பர்). 821 warns that those who keep close without inner consent will strike when they see the right place. The patience the book recommends to a ruler in 487 is the same conduct it tells him to expect from a false friend in 821.

883 says to fear the enemy within, because at the moment of weakness (உலைவிடத்து) it cuts like the tool that cuts the potter's clay (மட்பகை). 821 says the friendship of those who join without inner accord (நேரா நிரந்தவர்) is an anvil (பட்டடை) for striking once they find the right opening (சீரிடம் காணின்). Both verses use a craftsman's tool for the hidden enemy and both place the blow at the moment that suits him.

882 says not to fear enemies who are like swords but to fear the bond with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 822 says the friendship of those who seem one's own and are not (இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார்) will turn. Both identify the enemy in the guise of kin as the dangerous one; 882 gives the instruction and 822 the reason, that such a bond does not stay what it looks like.

920 lists two-minded women (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்) with liquor and dice as the company of those fortune has left. 822 compares false friendship to women's minds that become other (வேறுபடும்). The divided or shifting female mind serves in both as the book's figure for a tie that cannot be relied on, and 920 suggests which women the figure has in view.

822 uses women's minds as its example of something that changes (மகளிர் மனம்போல வேறுபடும்); Parimelazhagar takes this of women in general and supports it with a line from the Valaiyapathi. 974 takes single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) as its model of the constancy that greatness needs. On Parimelazhagar's general reading of 822 the two figures conflict; if 822's மகளிர் is limited to the courtesans of chapter 92, they do not.

509 says to trust no one without examining them and, having examined, to trust what is to be trusted (தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது). 825 says that those who are not at one with you in mind are not to be judged trustworthy by their words in any matter (சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று). 825 adds to the rule of examination a statement of what cannot count as evidence.

890 says that life with those who are not in accord (உடம்பாடு இலாதவர்) is like living with a snake in a hut. 825 says those whose minds are not settled with yours (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are not to be trusted on their words. Both make inner agreement, not outward closeness or speech, the thing that decides whether a person near you is safe.

709 says the eye itself tells of enmity and friendship (பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும்) to those who know how to read it. 826 says an enemy's words are soon recognised even when they sound like a friend's.
