Both hold that hostility shows through the surface; 709 makes this depend on a skilled reader, a condition 826 leaves unstated.

826 says the words of the unreconciled are quickly seen through although they say good things as friends do. 828, in the same chapter, says a weapon can lie hidden in hands joined in worship (தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்) and in an enemy's tears. 828 limits the confidence of 826: the speech may give itself away, but gestures of submission and grief can still conceal the intent.

488 advises that on meeting an enemy one should bear him, which Parimelazhagar glosses as bowing, until his end is in sight (செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை). 827 says not to accept an enemy's bowing speech (சொல்வணக்கம்), because the bending of a bow signals harm. The humility 488 teaches as a tactic is the humility 827 teaches one to distrust in the other side.

985 says that bowing (பணிதல்) is the strength of those who accomplish and the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). 827 says that an enemy's verbal bowing should not be accepted, since it points to harm as a bent bow does. Bowing is a means of working on an adversary in both; 985 praises it in the worthy, and 827 says that from an enemy it must not be taken as goodwill.

488 says to bear an enemy when you meet him until his final limit comes, and then his head goes down. 829 says to keep the false friend pleased and hold him in the appearance of friendship while it dies inwardly. Both advise outward accommodation of an enemy who cannot yet be opposed openly, in the chapter on timing and in the chapter on false friendship.

824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face while bitter within. 829 says that those who make much of you outwardly and despise you (மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளுவார்) should be made to smile and be embraced within the friendship so that it dies (நகச்செய்து நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லல்). The response 829 prescribes has the same form as the conduct 824 warns against; Parimelazhagar notes that it is allowed as royal policy although such doubleness is otherwise unfitting.

488 advises bearing with enemies when one meets them until their end is in view. 830 advises a friendly face toward enemies at a time when, as Parimelazhagar explains, they cannot be openly put aside. Both treat outward civility toward an enemy as a matter of timing and not of feeling.

831 defines folly as taking up what harms and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 422 defines understanding as the reverse movement: turning away from evil and steering toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). Read together, the two definitions are mirror images, so folly in 831 is not a lack of information but the wrong choice between two things in view.

831 says folly is to let gain go (ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 797 uses the same two words to say what gain is: giving up and leaving the friendship of fools (ஊதியம் என்பது ... பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). The fool lets gain go, and for everyone else letting the fool go is the gain.

831 says folly is accepting harm and letting gain go. 925 gives a concrete case in drinking: handing over wealth to receive ignorance of one's own body (பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல்), which it traces to கையறியாமை, not knowing what to do. The drinker's purchase is 831's exchange carried out literally.

832 names as the worst folly a liking (காதன்மை) for what is not fit for one. 439 gives the matching instruction: do not set your desire on a deed that yields no good (நயவற்க நன்றி பயவா வினை). Both locate the error in the wanting, before any deed is done.

833 lists four absences as the fool's work: no shame, no inquiry, no tenderness, no care for anything (நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும் பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்). 428 defines folly as not fearing what should be feared and calls fearing it the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில்). Both define folly as a missing response where one is due, and both set it out as a characteristic தொழில்.

833 describes the fool by four negations. 865 describes the ideal enemy to have by a similar string: he does not look to the way, does not do what is fitting, does not look to blame, has no character (வழிநோக்கான் ... பழிநோக்கான் பண்பிலன்), and so is sweet to his foes. The same profile that 833 treats as a moral portrait is, in the chapter on enmity, a strategic weakness.

833 puts shamelessness (நாணாமை) first among the fool's traits. 1018 says what that trait costs: if one is not ashamed of what makes others ashamed, the fault is one that virtue itself would be ashamed of (அறம் நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads it as virtue leaving him. 1018 supplies the consequence that 833 leaves unstated.

130 praises the one who guards against anger and, having learned, is restrained (கற்றடங்கல் ஆற்றுவான்): virtue itself seeks him out. 834 names the one who has read, understood and taught but is not restrained (ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் ... தானடங்கா) the greatest of fools. Both treat learning and அடங்கல் as a pair in which the learning is judged by the restraint.

834 presents a puzzle: a person who has studied, understood and taught, and still does not restrain himself. 373 offers the chapter on fate's account of such a person: however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்), which Parimelazhagar takes as the folly given by fate. 373 explains how the fool of 834 is possible.

835 calls the fool's destination an அளறு, a mire or hell, into which he enters and sinks (புக்கழுந்தும்). 919 calls the shoulders of women who draw no line the அளறு in which base men sink (பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு). 919 uses for one present indulgence the image that 835 uses for the result of a whole life of folly.

836 says that when a fool who does not know the way of doing (கையறியாப் பேதை) takes up a task, the task fails (பொய்படும்) and he himself ends in fetters. 468 says effort not made by the right means will collapse (பொத்துப் படும்) even with many standing by to protect it. Parimelazhagar glosses both verbs as புரைபடும்; 468 states the rule about method and 836 adds the cost to the doer.

836 describes the fool as கையறியா, not knowing how to act. 925 uses the same compound, கையறியாமை, as the cause of paying money to lose awareness of oneself in drink. In both verses the word names a practical ignorance that ends in the person binding or losing himself.

837 speaks of great wealth that has come to a fool (பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக்கடை) and benefits the wrong people. 1000 says great wealth obtained by one without character (பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம்) is like good milk spoiled by its vessel. Parimelazhagar notes on both verses that the verb marks wealth received and not made; both hold that the holder's defect ruins what the wealth could do.

837 says a fool's great wealth feeds strangers (ஏதிலார்) while his own go hungry. 1009 says wealth amassed by giving up love, denying oneself and ignoring virtue will be taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The miser and the fool arrive at the same result by opposite routes, one by holding wealth back and one by letting it go to the wrong people.

838 likens a fool's possession to drunkenness added to derangement. 408 says fortune lodged with the unlearned is more painful than poverty lodged with the good (கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு). Both deny that wealth is a good independent of its holder; 838 gives the image and 408 the comparative judgment.

840 treats the fool's mere entry (புகல்) into the company of the worthy as a defilement; Parimelazhagar adds that the assembly itself is lowered by it. 403 allows that even the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned (கற்றார்முன் சொல்லாதிருக்கப் பெறின்). 403 leaves a condition under which presence is acceptable, though its subject is the unlearned and 840's is the fool.

840 likens a fool entering an assembly of the worthy to setting an unwashed foot on a bed (கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்று). 720 likens speaking before those not of one's own kind to nectar spilled in an unclean yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்து). The two are mirror images of the same mismatch: the unclean thing brought into the clean place, and the precious thing let fall in the unclean place.

842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing but the receiver's தவம். 70 says a son's service to his father is to make people ask what the father did as penance (என்நோற்றான் கொல்) to have him. Both use the same figure, explaining a good by the stored merit of the one who benefits; 70 uses it as praise of the son and 842 to deny the giver any credit.

92 treats giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்) as a real good, surpassed only by a glad face and sweet speech. 842 takes the same act, giving with a glad heart (நெஞ்சுவந்து ஈதல்), and says that in a person without understanding it reflects only the receiver's merit. 842 limits 92's valuation: the glad gift counts for the giver only when understanding is behind it, which is how Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it.

843 says the suffering those without understanding inflict on themselves is hard even for their enemies to inflict (செறுவார்க்கும் செய்தல் அரிது). 165 says that for the envious, envy is enough: it brings ruin even when enemies fail to (ஒன்னார் வழுக்கியும் கேடீன்பது). Both measure an inner defect against an outside enemy and find the defect the more effective.

843 says the fool harms himself beyond what an enemy could. 434 says one's own fault is the enemy that brings ruin (குற்றமே அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை) and is therefore the thing to guard against. 434 gives the general principle of which 843 is the case of the person who cannot do the guarding.

843 states generally that those without understanding torment themselves (தாந்தம்மைப் பீழிக்கும் பீழை). 847, in the same chapter, names one way it happens: the person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip and so does great harm to himself by himself (பெருமிறை தானே தனக்கு). 847 is a specific instance of 843's claim, with the same stress on தானே.

844 says the claim to ஒண்மை is itself what வெண்மை is. 404 says that however good an unlearned person's ஒட்பம் may be, those with understanding do not accept it (கொள்ளார் அறிவுடையார்). 404 shows the other side of 844's self-assessment: the brightness one credits to oneself is not credited by those able to judge.

844 locates want of understanding in the pride (செருக்கு) of saying 'we are bright'. 978 says smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து) while greatness bows. Both make self-admiration the identifying mark of the deficient state, one for understanding and one for stature.

845 says one false claim to learning casts doubt on what one has mastered without flaw. 128 says that if even one bad word has its effect, the good comes to nothing (நன்றாகாதாகி விடும்). Both describe a single lapse spreading backward over what was sound, in knowledge and in speech.

391 tells one to learn what is to be learned without flaw (கற்க கசடற) and then stand by it. 845 uses the same phrase for what a person has truly mastered (கசடற வல்லதூஉம்) and says that carrying on as if one knew what one has not learned (கல்லாத மேற்கொண்டொழுகல்) brings doubt even on that. Pretence undoes the standing of the very learning 391 asks for.

405 says an unlearned person's standing gives way once he meets others and speaks (சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்). 845 describes a further loss for one who has some real learning: by taking on what he has not learned, he puts even his genuine mastery in doubt (ஐயம் தரும்). 405 is the exposure of a claim; 845 is the damage the exposure does to what was true.

846 asks whether covering one's nakedness is not itself small-minded when one's faults are left uncovered (தம்வயின் குற்றம் மறையா வழி); Parimelazhagar takes covering faults to mean removing them. 278 speaks of many who, with stain in the mind, bathe and go about concealed (மனத்தது மாசாக ... நீராடி மறைந்தொழுகு). Both set a bodily propriety, clothing or bathing, against an inner fault it does nothing about.

846 treats clothing the body as trivial beside dealing with one's faults. 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for any living being, and the distinction of humans is having shame (ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). 1012 gives the reason behind 846: dress is common to all, and what marks a person is shame at fault.

Parimelazhagar reads 847 as a person who receives rare instruction and lets it run out without taking it in, harming himself. 418 says ears not pierced by listening are deaf even though they hear (கேட்பினுங் கேளாத் தகையவே). On that reading both describe teaching that reaches a person and does not enter; 847 adds that the loss is self-inflicted.

847 says a person without understanding lets the precious மறை slip (அருமறை சோரும்) and so harms himself. Manakkudavar takes மறை as a secret let out to others, a reading Parimelazhagar reports and rejects. On that reading the verse meets 1076, where the base are like a beaten drum because they carry every மறை they hear to others; 1076 notes the harm to others, 847 the harm to the leaker.

448 says a king without people who rebuke him will perish even with no one to ruin him (கெடுப்பாரிலானுங் கெடும்). 848 takes the case one step further: a person who has people to direct him and still does not act on it, and cannot work it out alone. 448 makes having correctors the safeguard; 848 shows the safeguard is useless to one who will not be corrected.

848 calls the life of one who neither heeds nor understands a disease until it leaves (போஒம் அளவுமோர் நோய்); Parimelazhagar takes this as a burden hard for the earth to bear, while Kalaignar takes the disease as the person's own. 572 says the existence of those without kindly regard is a weight on the earth (உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை). On Parimelazhagar's reading the two share the figure of a person whose mere being alive is an affliction to the world.

848 describes one who does not act when told and does not see for himself (ஏவவும் செய்கலான் தான் தேறான்), and calls that life a disease until it departs. 638 describes a king in the same two terms, one who destroys what the knowing say and does not know himself (அறிகொன்று அறியான்), and says the minister must still tell him what is sound. The same double failing appears in both; 848 gives the verdict on the person and 638 the duty of those beside him.

849 ends with the unseeing person continuing to see as he saw (தான்கண்டவாறு). 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own underlying understanding prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). Both hold that what is brought from outside, a teacher in 849 and books in 373, does not displace the understanding a person already has.

849 says one who tries to show something to a person who does not see ends up the unseeing one, while that person goes on having seen it his own way (கண்டானாம் தான்கண்டவாறு). 929 says giving reasons to a drunk man is like searching with a flame for someone sunk under water (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று). Both describe instruction that cannot reach its target, and in both the effort reflects on the one making it.

850 condemns the one who denies what the world affirms. 140 says those who have not learned to conduct themselves in accord with the world (உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல்) lack understanding however much they have studied. Parimelazhagar takes 'the world' in both as the high-minded many, so both make their consensus a test that private cleverness does not override.

851 names the fault as பகல், splitting apart, and its chapter closes (860) by setting நகல் against இகல். 187 uses the same pair of roots: those who do not know how to make friends by நகச்சொல்லி will பகச்சொல்லி and separate even their kin. The chapter on backbiting already holds the contrast between dividing and laughing together that the chapter on hostility is built on.

851 defines இகல் as the disease (நோய்) that spreads பகல், the ill nature of division, among all living beings. 886 takes the same division to its end inside one's own circle: if ஒன்றாமை arises among ஒன்றியார், escaping death (பொன்றாமை) is hard at any time. The general diagnosis of 851 becomes a specific warning about a ruler's own people; Parimelazhagar reads 886 of a king.

852 ranks not harming a provoker as தலை, the best course. 203 uses the same ranking word: the head of all understanding (அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை) is not to do evil even to those who hate you (செறுவார்க்கும்). Together they show the text treating non-retaliation as a matter of good sense as well as of virtue; Parimelazhagar on 852 explains that retaliating feeds the enmity while refraining lets it die out.

853 says that removing the painful disease of hostility gives a brightness that neither fails nor is flawed (தவலில்லாத் தாவில் விளக்கம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as lasting fame. 156 says those who punish have one day's pleasure while those who forbear have praise until the end (பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்). Both make enduring renown the result of declining the quarrel, one in the householder's ethics and one in public life.

854 offers இன்பத்துள் இன்பம், the joy of joys, as what follows when hostility goes. 629 uses the same two phrases differently: one who does not crave pleasure within pleasure (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்) does not feel pain within pain (துன்பத்துள் துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்). Read together, the joy 854 promises is a result of removing a cause of suffering, and 629 warns against making such joy an object of desire.

855 says no one sets out to defeat a person who can lean away from hostility. 874 goes a step further: the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்). 855 describes safety gained by not answering hostility; 874 describes actively turning the enemy into a friend and gives it a public value.

855 asks who would be inclined to overcome those able to lean away when hostility confronts them (இகலெதிர் சாய்ந்தொழுக வல்லாரை). 985 says the strength of the capable is to bow (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Both treat yielding as what disarms an opponent; 985 states it as a trait of the சான்றோர், 855 as a skill (வல்லார்), which Parimelazhagar says is hard for kings.

855 holds that the one who gives way before hostility cannot be beaten. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' sulk the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. The speaker in 1327 is a lover talking about play-quarrels, so this is the same pattern of winning by yielding in a different setting, not a doctrine shared with 855.

856 says the life of one who declares it sweet to excel in hostility (இகலின் மிகல் இனிது என்பவன்) is close to failure and ruin. 307 says the ruin of one who takes anger to be a thing of worth (சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன்) is as sure as the hand of one who strikes the ground. In both the fault is the valuing of the passion, and both attach certain or imminent ruin to it.

423 defines understanding as seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு) in whatever one hears from anyone. 857 says those of harmful understanding who are attached to hostility (இகல்மேவல் இன்னா அறிவினவர்) do not see the மெய்ப்பொருள் that carries victory. So 857 names hostility as one thing that turns அறிவு against its defining task; Parimelazhagar narrows மெய்ப்பொருள் here to the content of the treatises on statecraft and says hostility clouds the understanding.

860 says all ills come from hostility, and from friendly gladness (நகல்) comes 'the pride called good conduct' (நன்னயம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 180 has the same shape and the same closing phrase: coveting without thought yields destruction, and 'the pride called not-wanting' (வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு) yields victory. In both the verse sets a ruinous impulse against its absence and calls that absence a செருக்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses in both places as wealth.

860 says இகலான் ஆம் இன்னாத எல்லாம்: every painful thing arises from hostility. 303 says to forget anger toward anyone, because the birth of evils comes from it (தீய பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்). The Book of Virtue makes anger the source of evils and the Book of Wealth makes hostility the source, with nearly the same construction.

860 credits நகல், glad friendliness, with producing good conduct and its dignity. 999 describes those without the capacity: for people not able to laugh with others (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the wide world lies in darkness even by day. 860 gives what நகல் yields and 999 what its absence costs; Parimelazhagar reads நகல் in both as rejoicing in company with others.

862 asks how a man with no love, no worthy allies (ஆன்ற துணையிலன்) and no strength of his own can wear down an enemy's might. 449 states the principle: those without capital have no profit, and those without the prop of supporters (மதலையாஞ் சார்பிலார்) have no standing. 862 applies to a contest with an enemy what 449 says of a ruler's position in general.

862 describes the man without love, allies or strength as unable to resist an enemy. 873 judges the man in that position who nevertheless provokes: one who, alone (தமியனாய்), takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad. 862 gives the weak position seen by an attacker; 873 gives the advice that follows for the one who is in it.

863 puts fear first among the traits that make a man easy for his enemy. 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை); Parimelazhagar explains that defences are of no use to one with fear in his mind. Both say that fear cancels whatever other protection a person has.

863 lists fear and ignorance among the weaknesses that make a man easy prey (அஞ்சும் அறியான்). 869 keeps just those two and states them from the other side: joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are without understanding and afraid (அறிவிலா அஞ்சும் பகைவர்ப் பெறின்). The chapter moves from describing the weak enemy to stating what the attacker gains from him.

864 says one who does not leave off anger (நீங்கான் வெகுளி) and has no நிறை is easy for anyone, at any time, anywhere. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger, because unguarded anger kills oneself (தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்). 305 states the self-destruction as an ethical fact; 864 shows how it works in a contest, by making the angry man open to any opponent.

864 says the man who cannot leave anger is easy for anyone to overcome. 526 gives the opposite case: no one on earth has more people at his side than one who gives greatly and does not cherish anger (பேணான் வெகுளி). Put together, anger decides whether a man stands with many around him or exposed to all.

866 says the enmity of a man of blind anger and excessive lust (காணாச் சினத்தான் கழிபெருங் காமத்தான்) is to be welcomed. 360 names the same two, with delusion, as what must perish for suffering to perish (காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம்). What the chapter on true knowledge treats as obstacles to release, the chapter on enemies treats as what makes an opponent beatable; Parimelazhagar says such men destroy themselves.

867 advises paying to have a certain man as an enemy rather than keep him near. 800 advises paying to be rid of a certain friend: give something (ஒன்று ஈத்தும்) and leave the friendship of those who are not a match. Both accept a cost to end a harmful closeness; the commentators differ on who the man in 867 is, Parimelazhagar taking him as one who begins a task and acts unsuitably, Kalaignar as one who stays beside you.

504 tells the ruler to examine a man's qualities, then his faults, and judge by what predominates (மிகை நாடி மிக்க கொளல்). 868 describes the result when the tally is all on one side: with no qualities and many faults (குணனிலனாய்க் குற்றம் பலவாயின்) he is left without companions, and that is a support to his opponents. The test used for choosing servants in 504 is applied by 868 to the ruler himself, with his enemies as the ones who benefit.

868 says a man without qualities and with many faults comes to have no one with him (இனனிலனாம்). 525 gives the positive case: one who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in rows (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). Both make a person's following a product of his character; 868 adds the military consequence of losing it.

869 says joy does not go far from those who fight if they get enemies who are ignorant and afraid. 772 says holding the spear that missed an elephant is sweeter (இனிது) than holding the arrow that hit a forest hare. One locates the pleasure of fighting in the easy opponent and the other in the hard one; the conflict holds if both are read as claims about what a fighter should want, and eases if 869 is a king's reckoning of advantage and 772 an individual warrior's sense of honour.

871 says enmity, a thing without good in it (பண்பிலதனை), is not to be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும் வேண்டற்பாற்று அன்று). 867 says the enmity of one who stays close and does unfitting things must certainly be got, even by paying for it (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற). The conflict holds if 871 is read as a rule about all enmity; Parimelazhagar narrows it to enmity that brings no benefit, which would leave room for 867.

872 says that even if you take on the enmity of those whose plough is the bow (வில்லேர் உழவர்), you should not take on that of those whose plough is the word (சொல்லேர் உழவர்). 129 says a wound burned by fire heals within, but the scar burned by the tongue (நாவினாற் சுட்ட வடு) does not. Both rank harm done by words above harm done by a physical instrument, one in statecraft and one in personal conduct.

873 states the folly of standing alone (தமியனாய்) against many enemies. 875 gives the working rule for the smallest such case: with no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்), make one of them a pleasing ally (இன்துணையாக் கொள்க). 875 turns 873's condemnation into a remedy.

874 praises the one who takes enmity as friendship (பகைநட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும்) without saying how it is done. 985 names a means: bowing (பணிதல்) is the weapon by which the worthy change their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Parimelazhagar glosses this as ending the opponents' enmity, so 985 reads as the method behind 874.

874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of character who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship (பண்புடையாளன் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு). 996 says the world exists by resting on those of character (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம்), and would otherwise sink into the earth. Both make பண்பு the thing the world stands on; 874, in the chapter on enmity, specifies it as the capacity to turn enemies into friends.

875 advises a ruler caught alone between two enemies to make one of them an ally. 633 lists among a minister's abilities dividing (பிரித்தல்), which Parimelazhagar explains as separating the enemy's supporters from him, and rejoining those who broke away (பிரிந்தார்ப் பொருத்தல்). The advice to the king in 875 is the skill required of the minister in 633.

876 says that whether or not one has trusted the enemy before, in a time of ruin (அழிவின்கண்) one should neither join him nor break from him (தேறான் பகாஅன் விடல்); Parimelazhagar explains that joining lets him destroy from inside and breaking makes him add to the ruin. 691 tells those who serve quarrelsome kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither moving off nor coming close (அகலாது அணுகாது). Both prescribe a deliberate middle distance from a dangerous party, once toward an enemy and once toward one's own king.

877 says not to let softness show before enemies (மேவற்க மென்மை பகைவர் அகத்து); Parimelazhagar takes மென்மை as lack of strength, which enemies watch for. 440 says that if a ruler can enjoy what he loves without that love being known (காதல் அறியாமை), his enemies' designs come to nothing (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்). In both, what an enemy can use is what he is allowed to learn about one's inner state, weakness in one verse and desire in the other.

879 speaks of those who remove the thorn tree with the word களையுநர், weeders. 550 compares a king's putting the cruel to death to weeding the green crop (பைங்கூழ் களைகட்டதனொடு நேர்). Both picture the removal of dangerous people as a cultivator's weeding; 879 adds that timing matters, since the weed grown hard injures the weeder's hand.

880 states the cost of not breaking the pride of one's enemies (செயிர்ப்பவர் செம்மல் சிதைக்கலாதார்): one cannot be counted as living. 759 names the instrument for that task: wealth, the sharpest steel for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும் எஃகு). One verse gives the necessity and the other the means.

881 says the nature of one's own people is bad if it does harm (தமர்நீரும் இன்னாவாம் இன்னா செயின்). 522 says kin whose affection does not lapse (விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம்) yield many gains that keep branching; Parimelazhagar notes that this wording is chosen to exclude inner enmity. The condition written into 522 is the case 881 describes, so each verse marks the limit of the other.

881 says even shade and water are bad when they do harm (நிழல்நீரும் இன்னாத இன்னா), and so is the nature of one's own people when it does harm. In 1309 the man says water is sweet in the shade (நீரும் நிழலது இனிதே), and sulking is sweet only with those who love. Both take shade and water as the standard of what is pleasant and then make the pleasantness depend on a condition, which in both cases is the real disposition of those closest to one.

882 uses the verb of fear for kin-like enemies (அஞ்சுக கேள்போல் பகைவர் தொடர்பு). 824 uses it for deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப்படும்). The chapter on false friendship and the chapter on inner enmity reach the same instruction: what is to be feared is hostility presented as closeness.

882 contrasts the enemy who is like a drawn sword (வாள்போல் பகைவர்) with the one who looks like kin, and fears the second. 828 says a weapon hides even within an enemy's hands folded in worship (தொழுதகையுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும்), and his tears are the same. In 882 the visible sword is the safer one; 828 shows where the other sword is kept.

883 says to fear the enemy within and guard oneself (உட்பகை அஞ்சித் தற்காக்க), or it will destroy one. 305 says that if you would guard yourself, guard against anger (தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க); unguarded, anger kills oneself. The same formula of self-guarding against something lodged inside is applied in one verse to people within the household or court and in the other to a passion within the mind.

885 says an inner enmity that comes in the form of kinship (உறல்முறையான் உட்பகை) brings many ills of a deadly kind (இறல்முறையான் ஏதம்) to the ruler. 735 defines a land as one without many factions, without ruinous inner enmity (பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகை) and without murderous marauders who harass the king. The danger 885 describes for the king's person and household is, in 735, something whose absence is part of what makes a country a country.

886 says that if disunity arises among those who are one with a ruler (ஒன்றாமை ஒன்றியார் கட்படின்), it is always hard for him to escape perishing. 764 defines an army as one that is not destroyed, cannot be undermined from within (அறைபோகாதாகி) and has inherited hardness. Both treat the loyalty of one's own side as a condition of survival, stated once as a warning and once as a requirement.

887 uses the casket and its lid for a family that fits together outwardly while divided within. 277 uses the kunri seed for false ascetics, red on the outside (புறங்குன்றி கண்டனையர்) and black within like its tip. Each verse chooses an everyday object to show an outside that does not match the inside, one for kin and one for renouncers.

887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined, though it joins like a casket and its lid (செப்பின் புணர்ச்சிபோல் கூடினும் கூடாதே). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship is what makes the heart within smile (நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). Both deny the name of union to a joining that is only on the surface, in the family and in friendship.

889 holds that inner enmity is ruinous even at the size of a split sesame seed. 433 says those who are ashamed of blame take a fault the size of a millet seed (தினைத்துணை) to be as large as a palmyra. 433 describes the attitude that 889 calls for: treating the small thing at its eventual size.

889 says inner enmity carries ruin even when it is as small as a split sesame seed. 879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young (இளைதாக), since grown hard it destroys the cutter's hand. The two neighbouring chapters, on open and on inner enmity, make the same point that hostility should be judged by what it will grow into; only 879 goes on to say what to do about it.

889 says that inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed (எட்பகவன்ன சிறுமைத்தே ஆயினும்), has ruin in it. 965 says even those like a hill will be lowered if they do a lowering thing the size of a kunri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). Both use a tiny seed as the measure of something that brings down what is large, a family or kingdom in 889 and a person's standing in 965.

891 makes not slighting the able the chief safeguard; 861 tells the ruler to avoid standing against the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). The chapter on enmity gives as a tactical rule what 891 gives as a rule of self-protection.

892 says disregard of the great brings unending trouble (பேரா இடும்பை); 450 says letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Both chapters on the great rank a bad relation to them above ordinary dangers, 450 by a number and 892 by permanence.

892 warns that going on without cherishing the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகின்) brings, through them, ills that do not leave. 976 says the intent to cherish and win the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு) is simply absent from the minds of the small. The shared verb பேணு ties them: 976 names who it is that fails to cherish, 892 what the failure costs.

893 states as irony what 861 states as a plain command: offending those with the power to destroy (அடல்வேண்டின் ஆற்றுபவர்) is a way to seek one's own ruin, and 861 says to avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக).

893 says: if you want ruin (கெடல்வேண்டின்), go ahead without listening and wrong those able to destroy. 922 says: do not drink, but if anyone will, let it be those who do not want the regard of the worthy (எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). Both forbid by an ironic permission addressed to whoever wants the bad result, once about offending the powerful and once about liquor.

894 says the unable doing harm to the able (ஆற்றுவார்க்கு ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்) is like beckoning Death with the hand. 250 asks one about to go against someone weaker (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து) to think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன்). Both reason from the weak facing the strong: 894 uses it as prudence in the Book of Wealth, 250 turns the same experience into a ground for compassion in the Book of Virtue.

895 says those who draw the anger of a king of fierce might (வெந்துப்பின் வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) cannot go on existing anywhere they go. 691 gives the working rule for those who serve such kings: like people warming at a fire, neither move off nor come close (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). 895 states the danger, and 691 the conduct that lives beside it.

895 makes the king's anger inescapable for those under him; 899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), the king himself (வேந்தனும்) breaks midway and loses his kingship. Within the chapter the pair sets up an order of power: the king who destroys others can himself be destroyed by the anger of the great. Parimelazhagar takes வேந்தன் in 899 as Indra.

207 says those who incur any enmity whatever survive it (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும் உய்வர்), and only the enmity of one's own evil deeds follows and kills. 896 says those who keep offending the great do not survive (உய்யார்). If எனைப்பகை is taken literally as every human enmity, the two conflict; the conflict eases if 207's phrase is read as a rhetorical foil for the enmity of deeds, or if the harm in 896 is understood as itself the fruit of a wrong deed.

444 says living so that those greater than oneself become one's own is the head of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 897 gives the other side: a fully appointed life and great wealth count for nothing (என்னாம்) once the worthy great are angered. Together they make one's standing with the great, and not one's possessions, the deciding strength.

897 asks what a life excellent in every part and lofty wealth (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும்) come to if the worthy of great stature are angered (தக்கார் செறின்). 900 says even those with support beyond measure (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு) do not survive if those of the highest distinction are angered (சீரார் செறின்). The two close on the same word செறின் and between them cancel a person's own assets and then his outside supports.

898 plays on குன்று (hill) and குன்ற (to diminish): if the hill-like intend diminishment, the seemingly permanent vanish. 965 uses the same play: even the hill-like (குன்றின் அனையாரும்) will diminish (குன்றுவர்) if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri seed. In 898 the hill-like bring others low; in 965 they themselves can be brought low by their own act, so height gives power over others but no protection from one's own lapse.

900 says that even those with support beyond measure will not survive (உய்யார்) if those of the highest distinction are angered (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்). 29 says the anger (வெகுளி) of those standing on the hill of good qualities is hard to ward off (காத்தல் அரிது) even for a moment. The Book of Wealth applies to kings and their resources what the opening chapters said in praise of renouncers.

303 says to forget anger toward anyone at all (யார்மாட்டும்), because every evil is born from it. 900 treats the anger of the most distinguished (சீரார் செறின்) as a force no support can save one from, and Parimelazhagar and Pope take these as people of great austerity. If they are ascetics, the chapter on not being angry would have them without anger; the conflict depends on that identification and on reading 900 as accepting such anger, where it may only be warning the offender of what follows.

45 says that when household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), these are its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்); Parimelazhagar takes the love as that owed to one's wife. 901 says those who fix their desire on the wife (மனைவிழைவார்) miss the excellent fruit (மாண்பயன்). The pair marks a line between love within the household, which is its fruit, and விழைவு that lets the wife rule the man, which loses it; Parimelazhagar reads 901 as men who follow the wife's lead for pleasure's sake.

903 calls a man's stooping before his wife (இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த) இயல்பின்மை, something against the natural order, which shames him among the good. 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband (கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள்). The two show that the book fixes the direction of deference in marriage: it is a merit in the wife and a disgrace in the husband.

978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை), and elsewhere the book calls bowing good for everyone. 903 names one bowing that brings shame: lowering oneself before one's wife (தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை), which Parimelazhagar explains as arising from fear. The pair separates humility that comes from the absence of pride from submission that comes from fear.

904 denies வீறு (distinction) to the action of the wife-fearing man: வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று. 665 says the firmness in action (வினைத்திட்பம்) of those who have attained distinction (வீறெய்தி மாண்டார்) reaches the king and is held in regard. The same phrase வீறு எய்து names what capable action normally earns and what, in 904, fear of the wife withholds.

904 says the man who fears his wife gets no distinction from his command of action (வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று). 1026 defines good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) as making the mastery of one's house one's own (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as leading one's family. Both build on ஆண்மை as mastery: the man of 904 has given up mastery at home, and his mastery of work earns no honour.

905 says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; 908 says those who act as she wishes (பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) neither meet their friends' needs nor do good (நன்றாற்றார்). Both state the cost to others: the wife-ruled man fails the good in 905 and his friends in 908.

906 says that even if they live like the gods (இமையாரின் வாழினும்), men who fear their wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no dignity (பாடிலர்). In 1088 a lover exclaims that his might (பீடு), feared by enemies in battle, has broken before her bright forehead alone. Both show male standing giving way before a woman's bodily feature; the Book of Wealth counts it a disgrace, while in the Book of Love it is a lover's speech in the moment and carries no judgment.

1011 ranks shame at one's deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்) as true shame and sets aside the shame of fair-browed women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாண்) as another kind. 907 says a woman who has shame (நாணுடைப் பெண்) has more greatness than the manhood of one who lives doing a woman's bidding. So the woman's modesty that 1011 treats as the lesser kind still outranks, in 907, manhood that has given up command.

907 pairs நாண் and ஆண்மை: manhood that obeys a woman is worth less than womanhood with shame. In 1134 a lover says the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft made of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). Both treat shame and manliness as the two things a man loses together under a woman's hold; 907 states it as a judgment, 1134 as a lover's own complaint.

907 gives greatness to the woman with shame over the submissive man's manhood (பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து). 1137, a speech in the Book of Love, says nothing has more worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்). In both, a woman's restraint is measured against a man's lack of it and ranked higher.

908 describes men who live as the woman wishes, பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்; 141 speaks of the folly of living in desire for another man's woman, பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை. The same pairing of பெட்டு (desire, wish) with ஒழுகு (to conduct oneself) describes a life steered by desire in both, in 141 the man's own desire for a forbidden woman and in 908 the wishes of his own wife.

788 defines friendship as removing a friend's distress on the spot (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand of a man whose garment slips. 908 says those who live as the woman of the fine brow wishes (நன்னுதலாள் பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) do not see their friends' needs through (நட்டார் குறைமுடியார்). 908 names a condition under which the duty of 788 goes unmet: the man's actions are no longer his own to direct.

754 says wealth that comes by right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன் ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 909 lists the same three goods as missing in men who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்). Where 754 treats the three as flowing from one sound source, 909 treats them as shut off by one fault.

760 says that for those who have made abundant wealth the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easily had together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 909 says that deeds of virtue, ample wealth and the other pursuits (அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்) are all absent in those who do a woman's bidding; Parimelazhagar and Pope take பிறவினை as pleasure. Both use the three aims as the measure of a life: 760 shows how they are gained together, 909 a way they are lost together.

910 says those with deliberation and firmness of heart never fall into the folly of attachment to a woman. 917, in the next chapter, says it is those without a firm heart (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace with their minds on other things. Both locate the safeguard in the man's own நெஞ்சம், stated positively in 910 for the wife-ruled man and negatively in 917 for the client of courtesans.

911 warns that the இன்சொல் of women who want a man's wealth brings him harm. In 1258 a woman calls the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her lover, a 'thief of many deceptions' (பன்மாயக் கள்வன்), the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Both treat gentle words as an instrument that undoes the hearer, though 1258 is a lover's complaint in the Book of Love, not a warning the book gives in its own voice.

103 says help given by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்) proves, when its worth is weighed (நயன்தூக்கின்), greater than the sea. 912 uses the same pair of words in the same order: the women weigh the gain (பயன்தூக்கி), and the man is to weigh their conduct (நயன்தூக்கி) and not join them. Weighing the return is what spoils a relationship in both verses, and weighing worth is the observer's proper response.

80 says the seat of life follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). 913 likens the false embrace (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) of women who want wealth to embracing an unknown corpse in a dark room (ஏதில் பிணம்). 913 applies 80's premise to a particular case: a body offered without love is, for the one who holds it, a dead one.

285 says that a loving nature with grace in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's unguarded moment. 914 opposes those who examine அருட்பொருள் to women for whom பொருள் is the only thing of value. In the chapter on theft and in this one, the same pair, aiming at grace or aiming at goods, sorts people into two kinds that do not mix.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have native acuteness together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 915 says those whose knowledge is made excellent by goodness of intellect (மதிநலத்தின் மாண்ட அறிவினவர்) do not touch the favours of women common to all; Parimelazhagar reads this too as natural intellect perfecting acquired knowledge. The pairing shows the same compound of mind being credited in statecraft with seeing through stratagems and here with keeping a man from a private vice.

915 calls the women பொதுநலத்தார், those whose favours are common to all, and says the wise will not touch them. In 1311 a wife tells her husband that all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), calls him பரத்த, and refuses his chest. The reproach of being 'common' is turned on the man there, and it is a sulking wife's charge in the Book of Love, not a judgement the book makes itself.

57 says confinement does little to guard women, and that the guard kept by their own நிறை, firmness, is the chief one. 917 says it is men without a heart of நிறை (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace while their hearts tend other things. The same inner firmness that 57 names as a wife's real protection is here named as what a man lacks when he goes to such women.

864 says the man who does not let go of anger and has no நிறை (நிறையிலன்) is easy prey for anyone, at any time and place. 917 says those without நிறைநெஞ்சம் are the ones who go to women whose hearts are set on something else. In both the lack of self-command is what exposes a man, to enemies in 864 and to women who want what he has in 917.

910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman never exists in those whose hearts hold deliberation (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து இடனுடையார்). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an affliction to those who lack examining understanding (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு). The neighbouring chapters, on subservience to a wife and on courtesans, give the same safeguard: a mind that thinks the matter through.

918 says that for those without discerning understanding the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses as the touch of a spirit-woman who takes life through desire. In 1082 a lover says that her returning his look is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) arriving with an army. The same figure of the woman as an afflicting spirit is a lover's praise in the Book of Love and a warning in 918.

920 says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the companions of those whom Fortune has removed from herself (திருநீக்கப்பட்டார்). 936 says those covered by the goddess of misfortune named gambling (சூதென்னும் முகடி) do not eat their fill and suffer. Both verses describe a vice through the two sister goddesses: in 920 the vices attend the man Tiru has already left, in 936 one of them is Mugadi herself.

920 names women of two minds (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்), which Parimelazhagar explains as a mind that joins and does not join a man at once. 974 says greatness, like women of one mind (ஒருமை மகளிர்), exists only by guarding oneself. The two phrases are opposites, and where single-mindedness is 974's model for keeping greatness, doubleness in 920 goes with dice and drink as the company of the unfortunate.

653 tells those who mean to rise to leave off any deed that dims their lustre (ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை). 921 says those who live in love of liquor (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்) are never held in awe and lose their lustre (ஒளியிழப்பர்). 921 gives a named instance of the kind of act 653 warns against in general.

939 says that clothing, wealth, food, lustre (ஒளி) and learning do not come near a man who takes to gaming. 921 says those devoted to liquor lose their ஒளி and are not feared. The adjoining chapters on drink and dice both count the loss of ஒளி, the standing that makes a man regarded, among the costs.

922 forbids drinking and adds that if anyone drinks, it should be those who do not want to be counted by the worthy (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). 656 forbids any act the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை), even to relieve one's own mother's hunger. In both the judgement of the சான்றோர் is the measure of conduct; 922 states it as the price a drinker must be willing to pay.

924 says shame turns away from the drinker. In 1288 the speaker tells her lover that his chest is to her as liquor is to those who have enjoyed it, wanted even though it does harm that brings disgrace (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The simile in the Book of Love takes for granted what 924 teaches, that drink disgraces, and uses it to describe a desire that persists in spite of shame.

838 says a fool getting something into his hand is like a deranged man getting drunk (மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று). 925 says paying out wealth to buy oblivion shows ignorance. 838 uses drunkenness as the image for what a fool does with property, and 925 describes drunkenness itself as a fool's use of property.

271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the hidden conduct of a man with a deceitful mind. 927 says those who drink and droop are seen through and always laughed at by their own town (உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர்); Parimelazhagar takes கள்ளொற்றி as drinking in concealment. In both, concealed conduct has a witness that laughs, the elements within the body in 271 and the neighbours who infer what is going on in 927.

293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn the liar afterwards. 928 concerns one such lie, 'I have never been drunk' (களித்தறியேன்), about something the speaker's heart knows, and says that drink brings the hidden thing out. 293 gives the inner penalty for this kind of lie and 928 adds an outward one, exposure.

928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk, because what he hid in his heart shows all the more at that moment (ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்). In 1161 a woman says she would hide her pain, but like spring water for those who draw it, it increases (ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). Both end on மிகும்: the attempt to conceal an inner state is answered by its overflowing, in drink and in love.

113 says to let go, that very day, of gain that comes from leaving fairness even if it yields only good (நன்றே தரினும்). 931 uses the same concession, 'even if you win' (வென்றிடினும்), and still refuses the gain, calling it a swallowed hook. In both the apparent success of a wrong source is conceded and set aside.

385 defines a king as one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும்). 933, which Parimelazhagar reads of a king, says both the gathered wealth and its sources (பொருள் ஆயம்) leave him if he keeps at the dice. One habit undoes the gathering and the guarding that 385 makes the mark of rule.

933 says that if one keeps calling the rolling dice-throw (உருளாயம்), wealth and its income (பொருளாயம்) go and fall outside (புறமே படும்); Parimelazhagar takes 'outside' as into enemies' hands. 1009 says the wealth a miser gathered without love, self-regard or virtue is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்). The gambler and the hoarder, by opposite habits, both end with their wealth in strangers' hands.

934 says nothing gives poverty like gambling, which does many small harms and ruins standing (சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும்). 1045 says that within the one affliction called poverty many sufferings arrive (பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்). Read together they form a chain: gambling brings harms on the way to poverty, and poverty then brings its own.

935 says those who clung (இவறியார்) in pride to dice, gaming hall and skilled hand became people with nothing (இல்லாகியார்). 437 uses the same word of the miser: the wealth of one who clings (இவறியான்) without doing what should be done perishes. இவறுதல், holding on and not letting go, ends in loss in both verses, whether the thing held is money or the game.

539 advises thinking, when swollen with one's own joy, of those who were ruined by negligence (இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக). 935 supplies such a memory: those who took pride (தருக்கி) in the dice and came to nothing; Parimelazhagar reads them as kings of former times and names the Pandavas. 935 does for gambling what 539 asks a ruler to do in general.

167 says the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). 936 names that sister, முகடி, as gambling itself, covering those who play. Envy hands a person over to misfortune; gambling, in 936, is misfortune under another name.

937 says time spent in the gaming hall ruins long-held wealth and character (பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்). 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's தோல் (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்), which Pope takes as dignity of speech. The two sentences have the same shape: an inherited standing and a personal quality lost at one stroke, with gambling as a cause and poverty as a cause.

938 lists what gambling does: it destroys wealth (பொருள் கெடுத்து), makes one take up lying, destroys compassion (அருள் கெடுத்து) and drives one through misery. 248 ranks two of these losses: those without wealth may flower again one day (பூப்பர் ஒருகால்), but those without அருள் are finished. By 248's measure the third item in 938's list is graver than the first.

757 calls அருள் a child born of love that is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called பொருள். 938 has gambling destroy both பொருள் and அருள். Parimelazhagar assigns the losses in 938 to separate causes (losing, winning, resentment), but 757 suggests a link between them: with the nurse gone, the child is harder to raise.

166 says the kin of one who envies a gift perish without anything to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றி). 939 begins its list of what gaming keeps away with the same pair, clothing and food (உடை ... ஊண்). Envy and gambling are both measured by the loss of the plainest necessities.

939 names five things, among them learning (கல்வி), that 'அடையா' the one who takes to gaming. Parimelazhagar glosses this as 'do not come to him', but Pope's verse rendering and Kalaignar take the five as departing from him. On that second reading 939 conflicts with 400, which calls learning the wealth that cannot perish (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்); on Parimelazhagar's reading there is no conflict, since the gambler never acquires it.

In 1145 a lover says love grows sweeter each time it is exposed, as drinking is wanted more each time one is drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்). 940 has the same 'each time ... the more' construction with another vice, the dice, as the comparison (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்). The lover uses the figure to praise his state, while 940 uses it to describe an attachment fed by its own losses.

941 says the three humours counted by the learned, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they exceed or fall short (மிகினும் குறையினும்); Parimelazhagar refers the excess and shortfall to food and activity. 466 says one is ruined by doing what is unfit and also by not doing what is fit (செயக் கெடும் ... செய்யாமையானும் கெடும்). Both verses locate harm on two sides of a right amount, in the body and in action.

943 says to eat knowing the measure once digestion is complete, as the way one who has a body can carry it long (நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு). 479 says the life of one who does not live knowing the measure (அளவறிந்து வாழாதான்) seems to exist and then perishes; Parimelazhagar refers that measure to one's wealth. The same phrase governs both the stomach and the purse. (This edition prints 'அறவறிந்து' in 943; Parimelazhagar's gloss reads அளவு அறிந்து.)

946 says disease stays with the one of very great feed (கழிபேர் இரையான்), as pleasure stays with the one who eats knowing to stop short (இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்). 420 asks what it matters whether those live or die who know taste only by the mouth and not by the ear, and calls them மாக்கள். Both verses use a word with an animal sense for the person ruled by the mouth: இரை, feed, and மாக்கள்.

289 says those who know nothing but stealth do what is beyond measure and perish right there (அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர்). 947 says the one who eats beyond the measure of his fire gets disease beyond measure. Chapter 29 uses அளவு as a moral measure and chapter 95 as a bodily one, and in each case overstepping it brings its own penalty.

947 says that if one eats greatly without discerning the measure of the fire within (தீயளவு), disease arises without measure (நோயளவின்றிப் படும்). 475 says even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if they are piled too high (சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்). In both a fixed capacity, the digestive fire or the axle, is what excess breaks, whatever the quality of the load.

948 tells the healer to look for the root of the disease (நோய்முதல்) before the remedy. 360 does this for suffering in general: when desire, anger and confusion perish even in name, the நோய் perishes. The chapter on true perception treats pain as chapter 95 treats illness, by naming causes and removing them.

948 sets out an order of enquiry: look into the disease, then its root, then the means that subdue it, and act so that it works (நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி ... வாய்நாடி). 504 has the same threefold நாடி for judging a person: examine the qualities, examine the faults, examine which predominates, and take that. Diagnosis of a patient and assessment of a candidate are given the same grammar of step-by-step examination before a decision.

637 says that even when one knows the method of doing a thing, one should act knowing how the world goes (செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்); Parimelazhagar glosses the method as what the treatises teach. 949 addresses the one who has learned (கற்றான்) and still requires him to consider this patient, this illness and this moment. Both hold that book learning has to be fitted to the particular case.

952 says the well-born do not slip (இழுக்கார்) in conduct, truthfulness and shame. 133 says having conduct is itself குடிமை and that a lapse (இழுக்கம்) turns into low birth (இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). Read together, 952's claim is close to a definition: whoever slips has by 133 already left the class of the well-born, a point Parimelazhagar makes on 133 while keeping it within varna.

952 lists three things the well-born keep: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை, நாண். 983 lists five pillars that hold up சால்பு: love, shame (நாண்), obligingness, kindly regard and truthfulness (வாய்மை). Two of the three marks of lineage reappear as supports of personal worth, so the same core is described once as inherited and once as a structure a person stands on.

953 names a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the share of a true lineage. 92 takes three of these and ranks them: being sweet-spoken with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The list in 953 is flat; 92 shows the book elsewhere weighing its items against one another.

953 puts giving and not scorning (ஈகை ... இகழாமை) side by side among the marks of a good family; Parimelazhagar takes all four as the way one meets the poor who come. 1057 gives the receiver's side: on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்), the asker's heart rejoices within. The pairing shows why 'not scorning' sits next to 'giving' in the list.

954 says the well-born will not do diminishing things (குன்றுவ) even if they get crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும்). 311 says the stainless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction (சிறப்பீனும் செல்வம் பெறினும்). Both use the same 'even if they gained' (பெறினும்) form to set a fixed refusal against a large reward, once for family standing and once for non-harm.

954 says no amount of wealth makes the well-born do what lowers them. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above gain reached by taking on blame (பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கம்). Both rank standing above wealth; 657 states the comparison outright, in the context of a minister's clean action.

954 says the well-born do not do things that diminish (குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்), whatever the gain. 965 uses the same word to say what follows if they do: even those like a hill sink (குன்றுவர்) if they do a diminishing thing (குன்றுவ) the size of a kundri seed. 954 gives the rule and 965 the cost of breaking it, at a scale far below crores.

955 says an ancient family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its character when its means shrink. 1043 says poverty destroys together one's ancient descent and one's speech (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). They conflict if 1043 is read as plain poverty undoing lineage; the conflict eases on Parimelazhagar's reading, which stresses that 1043 calls poverty a craving (நசை), so it is the wanting, not the lack, that ruins.

956 says those who mean to keep to a spotless line do not do what lacks worth (சால்பில செய்யார்); Parimelazhagar adds 'even in poverty'. 656 says one should not do what the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை) even if one must see one's mother hungry. Both set a standard of worthy conduct above need, 656 naming the hardest case.

956 says those resolved to live by their spotless lineage will not do unworthy things by taking to deceit (சலம் பற்றி). 660 uses the same word for wealth-making: securing wealth made by deceit (சலத்தால் பொருள் செய்து) is like keeping water in an unfired clay pot. 956 rules deceit out on grounds of family honour; 660 adds that its gains do not hold anyway.

958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a man, people will doubt his lineage (குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப்படும்). 992 names having love and being born in a seasoned family (அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல்) as the two things that make up courtesy. 992 pairs love and birth as partners; 958 shows that when the first is missing the second is no longer believed.

960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward everyone (யார்க்கும் பணிவு). 125 says bowing is good for all (எல்லார்க்கும் நன்றாம் பணிதல்) and is a further wealth for the rich. Both make humility general, and each singles out the highly placed, by family or by wealth, as those it most becomes.

960 asks for humility toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு) from anyone who wants to keep a lineage. 963, in the next chapter, limits when bowing is called for: in abundance one must bow (பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல்), but in reduced circumstances one must stand high (சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). The humility of 960 is thus not meant to cover bending under want.

960 pairs நலம் with shame and குலம் with humility: want நலம், then want நாணுடைமை; want குலம், then want பணிவு toward all. 1019 uses the same pair in negative form: a lapse in principle burns one's குலம், and settled shamelessness burns one's நலம் (நலஞ்சுடும் நாணின்மை). The two verses share the குலம்/நலம் pairing and agree that நலம் depends on shame.

Parimelazhagar reads 961's இன்றி அமையா as things without which one would not survive, so the verse puts standing above life. 131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence. The same ranking, a value kept ahead of survival, is made for honour in one chapter and for conduct in the other.

962 refuses unworthy acts even when they would bring renown (சீரினும்). 113 says to let go at once of gain that departs from fairness even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கம்). Both have the form 'even if it yields the thing you want, not by this means', applied to fame in one and to profit in the other.

652 says to avoid any action that yields neither renown nor good (புகழொடு நன்றி பயவா வினை), which makes renown one of the tests of an act. 962 says those who want renown together with great manliness will not do unworthy things even for renown (சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யார்). 962 therefore narrows 652's test: bringing fame does not by itself make an act fit to do.

963 says that in small and shrunken circumstances one must hold oneself high (சிறிய சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு). 680 says those whose domain is small (உறைசிறியார்), fearing their own people's trembling, will bow to the greater and accept terms (கொள்வர் பெரியார்ப் பணிந்து). They conflict if 963's 'reduced state' includes weakness of position before a stronger party; if 963 is only about poverty and personal bearing, 680 is separate advice on statecraft.

963 asks for an upright bearing (உயர்வு) when one's means have shrunk. 988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று) for one who has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 988 supplies the ground for 963's demand: want does not itself lower a person, so there is no reason to stoop in it.

124 says the stature of one who is restrained without shifting from his position (நிலையின் திரியாது அடங்கியான்) is far greater than a mountain. 964 uses the same word for the opposite case: those who descend from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்த) are like hair off the head. Together they give the two ends of one scale, both measured by whether a person keeps to their நிலை.

964 says people who have come down from their position (நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை) are like hair fallen from the head. 973 says those who are not low are not low even when placed low (கீழிருந்தும் கீழல்லார் கீழல்லவர்). They conflict if 964's நிலை means outward rank or station; on Parimelazhagar's reading it means the high standard the well-born hold themselves to, so the fall is their own doing and the verses agree.

966 asks what is gained by going and standing behind those who scorn you (இகழ்வார் பின் சென்று நிலை). 1033 says only those who eat by their own ploughing truly live, and all others bow to eat and go behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). Both use 'going behind' another as the picture of a dependent life, and 1033 names the livelihood that avoids it.

966 says standing in the train of those who scorn you brings neither renown nor the gods' land. 1053 says that even asking has a certain beauty (ஏஎர் உடைத்து) when one stands before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று). What 966 rejects is therefore not dependence as such but dependence on people who despise the one who comes to them.

967 prefers being called ruined to a life got by following those who reject you. 230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even that is sweet when giving is out of reach (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). In both, a life that cannot be lived on one's own terms, without honour or without the power to give, is ranked below death.

968 asks whether a life that tends the flesh is a medicine (மருந்தோ) once greatness has lost its dignity; Parimelazhagar takes this as a medicine against dying. 82 says that eating while the guest waits outside is not to be wanted even if the food were the medicine of deathlessness (சாவா மருந்தெனினும்). Both raise the idea of an immortality-medicine only to rank it below a duty, honour in one and hospitality in the other.

968 questions the worth of a life that merely feeds the body (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) when dignity is gone. 1017 says those governed by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் ... நாண் துறவார்). The chapters on honour and on shame reach the same ordering of life and self-respect.

969 says those like the கவரிமா give up life when their honour is at stake (உயிர் நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 779 asks who could reproach as failures those who die so that what they vowed is not broken (இழைத்தது இகவாமைச் சாவார்). Dying to avoid going back on what one stands for appears as a matter of civil honour in 969 and as a soldier's vow in 779.

970 says the world worships and praises the radiance of the honourable who do not live on in disgrace. 235 says that a ruin which is growth and a death which is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are hard to reach except for the skilled. 235 gives the general idea that 970 applies: a death can leave a person present in fame.

970 sets disgrace against radiance: the world worships the ஒளி of those who will not live when இளி comes. 971 defines the same two words: one's ஒளி is abundance of aspiration, and one's இளி is saying 'we will live without it' (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்). In both, disgrace is a way of going on living, and radiance belongs to those who refuse it.

981 says that for those who know what is due (கடன் அறிந்து) and take on worth, every good thing is கடன்; Parimelazhagar glosses this as the good qualities being natural to them. 218 uses the same phrase, கடனறி காட்சியவர், for people who do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 218 shows one concrete case of 981's general claim: a duty that is felt as one's own does not wait on circumstances.

982 says the worthy have only the goodness of character (குணநலம்), and that other goodness is not counted among goodnesses; Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் to be the goodness of the bodily limbs. 79 asks what all the outer limbs (புறத்துறுப்பு) can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (அகத்துறுப்பு). Both verses rank an inner quality over the body's outward parts, one for worth and one for love.

982 denies that any goodness other than character counts for the worthy. 407 says the handsome looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both dismiss outward நலம் that has nothing inside it, though 407 measures by understanding and 982 by character.

983 calls its five qualities the pillar planted to bear worth (சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண்). 615 calls the man who wants the work and not pleasure a pillar that wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்து ஊன்றும் தூண்). The same figure, with the same verb ஊன்று, is used once for qualities holding up a character and once for a person holding up a family.

983 lists five pillars that bear worth: அன்பு, நாண், ஒப்புரவு, கண்ணோட்டம், வாய்மை. 1013 singles out one of them: as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த), சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame (நாண் என்னும் நன்மை குறித்தது). Read together, shame is one support among five in 983 and the seat of worth itself in 1013.

985 says the strength of those who accomplish is bowing (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes. 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both attach bowing to the strong and not the weak; 985 adds that it has an effect on opponents.

986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat (தோல்வி கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equal. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. Both treat yielding as the better outcome; 1327 is a lover's remark about a sulk, while 986 states a test of character.

987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm. 998, in the next chapter, says failing in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்) is lowness (கடை). Both verses use the particle 'even to' (-க்கும்) to extend the virtue to hostile people, one for சால்பு and one for பண்பு.

988 calls சால்பு a firmness (திண்மை) that keeps poverty from being a disgrace. 1064 describes that firmness at work: the worth that will not consent to begging even when no means remain (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு) is too large for all space to hold. 1064 shows what the poor but worthy person of 988 does and does not do.

990 says the earth cannot carry its burden (பொறை) once the worthy lose their worth. 572 says those without kindly regard are, by merely existing, a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The same figure is used from two sides: the worthy are what lets the earth carry its load, and people without கண்ணோட்டம் are dead weight on it.

991 and 548 share the word எண்பதம், easy access. In 548 a king who is not accessible (எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா) and does not examine and do justice falls and perishes by himself; in 991 being accessible to all makes courtesy easy to attain. The quality whose absence ruins a ruler is the one whose presence makes a person courteous.

994 says the world honours the character (பண்பு) of those whose usefulness (பயன்) comes from doing good with fairness (நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த). 97 uses the same four words of speech: words that yield benefit (பயன்) and do not part from பண்பு produce நயன் and bring forth நன்றி. Parimelazhagar glosses நயன் as justice in both, so the cluster describes good speech in 97 and a good life in 994.

994 praises people of நயன் whose doing good makes them useful (பயனுடையார்). 216 says wealth falling to one who has நயன் (நயனுடையான்) is like a fruit-bearing tree (பயன்மரம்) ripening in the middle of the town. 216 supplies the picture for 994: the person of நயன் is of பயன் to everyone within reach.

995 says courtesy is present even in enmity (பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள) in those who understand others. 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of courtesy who treats enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடையாளன்). 874 takes the step beyond 995, from staying courteous toward an enemy to turning him into a friend; Parimelazhagar reads 874 as a matter of policy.

995 warns that இகழ்ச்சி, scorn, wounds even as a joke. 953 lists not scorning (இகழாமை) with a smile, giving and sweet words as the four marks of a true family. 953 names the trait as a mark of good birth, and 995 gives the reason for it.

998 calls it lowness (கடை) to fail in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness. 579 calls it the highest thing (தலை) to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose nature is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்). The verses mark the two ends of the same scale: good conduct toward the hostile is தலை, and its failure is கடை.

998 requires courtesy even toward those who do unfriendly, unkind things. 852 says that even if someone does what one cannot bear, intending division (பகல் கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), it is best not to do harm in return out of hostility. 852 gives the minimum, no retaliation, and 998 asks for more, that courtesy itself not lapse.

999 says that for those not able to laugh (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the great world lies in darkness even by day; Parimelazhagar takes நகல் as mixing with others and being glad at heart. 523 says the life of one who does not mingle freely (அளவளாவு இல்லாதான்) is like a tank filling without a bank. On Parimelazhagar's reading both describe the cost of not mixing with people, as lost wealth in 523 and a darkened world in 999.

1000 says great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). 1008 says the wealth of a man nobody seeks out is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village (நச்சு மரம் பழுத்தற்று). Both say a good thing is made useless or harmful by the character of its holder; Parimelazhagar reads 1000 as wealth that benefits no one.

229 says eating alone in order to fill up one's store (நிரப்பிய தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging; 1001 takes the case one step further, the man who does not even eat it (அஃதுண்ணான்), and calls him dead. Read together they grade the misuse of wealth: unshared use is wretched, no use at all is not living.

751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). 1002 names nearly the same thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as what the miser thinks, and says that when it leads to not giving (ஈயாது இவறும்) it is delusion. The chapter on making wealth is thus limited here: the claim holds only for wealth that is given and used.

114 says whether people were worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம்; 1004 asks what எச்சம் the unwanted man imagines for himself. Parimelazhagar takes the word as offspring in 114 and as what remains after death, i.e. renown, in 1004, so the pairing shows the same test of a life by what it leaves, applied with two senses of the word.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்); 1005 says the same of those who neither give nor enjoy, even with crores. The same form of argument, that owning is not having unless some further quality is present, is used for understanding in one place and for use and giving in the other.

1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று); 1006 says the man who neither uses nor gives is ஏதம் to பெருஞ்செல்வம். In both the wealth is good in itself and the holder is what spoils it, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 1006 (others take the wealth to be a misery to him).

226 says ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has got wealth stores it. 1007 says the wealth of one who does nothing for the destitute (அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான்) is like a very beautiful woman growing old alone. 226 says where wealth is kept safe; 1007 shows what happens to wealth kept anywhere else: it passes its time unused.

1039 says land whose owner stays away sulks like a wife (இல்லாளின் ஊடிவிடும்); 1007 likens ungiven wealth to a beautiful woman who ages alone (தமியள் மூத்தற்று). Both picture a good left unattended as a woman without her partner, for farmland in one verse and for money in the other; Parimelazhagar notes for 1007 that the wealth itself loses its fruit.
